title: Representing Numbers Using Continued Fractions and the TRIP Framework
text: My undergraduate thesis was about a family of generalized continued-fraction algorithms called TRIP maps. I think they’re neat algorithms, and they’re beautiful, so I wanted to make some visualizations to help others apprecaite and understand them. Expand the tabs below to see what I mean!

title: Representing Numbers Using Continued Fractions and the TRIP Framework
text:
Representing fractions with vectors
A two-dimensional vector can represent a single fraction, or equivalently a point on the one-dimensional unit interval,
\[
\begin{pmatrix}p\\q\end{pmatrix}
\longleftrightarrow
x=\frac pq\in[0,1].
\]
Similarly, a three-dimensional vector can represent an ordered pair of fractions, or equivalently a point in the two-dimensional triangle
\[
\begin{pmatrix}q\\p\\r\end{pmatrix}
\longleftrightarrow
(x,y)=\left(\frac pq,\frac rq\right)\in\Delta,
\qquad
\Delta=\{(x,y):0\le y\le x\le1\}.
\]
For example, \((10,8,3)^\top\) represents the point \((4/5,3/10)\) in the triangle. These are called homogeneous coordinates, multiplying every entry by the same positive constant leaves the represented point unchanged.






Remark: Higher Dimensions





The intuition extends naturally: one number lives on an interval and uses \(2\times2\) matrices; two numbers live in a triangle and use \(3\times3\) matrices; three numbers live in a tetrahedron and use \(4\times4\) matrices. More generally, an \(n\)-dimensional vector represents \(n-1\) numbers, corresponding to a point in an \((n-1)\)-dimensional simplex.

title: Representing Numbers Using Continued Fractions and the TRIP Framework
text:
The Farey maps
We can generate ordinary continued-fraction expansions by iterating the Farey map, defined on the unit interval \([0,1]\). Although the input is a single number \(x\), each branch can be represented by a \(2\times2\) matrix acting on \((x,1)\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
F_1(x)
&=\frac{x}{1-x},
&
\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\-1&1\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}x\\1\end{pmatrix}
&=\begin{pmatrix}x\\1-x\end{pmatrix},
&&0<x\le\frac12,\\[10pt]
F_0(x)
&=\frac{1-x}{x},
&
\begin{pmatrix}-1&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}x\\1\end{pmatrix}
&=\begin{pmatrix}1-x\\x\end{pmatrix},
&&\frac12<x\le1.
\end{aligned}
\]
Taking the ratio of the two entries in each resulting vector recovers the corresponding map. Applying \(F_1\) exactly \(k\) times and then \(F_0\) gives an accelerated (Gauss-type) step, \(G_k=F_0\circ F_1^k\).
For our original fraction,
\[
\frac{2}{17}\xrightarrow{G_7}\frac12
\xrightarrow{G_1}0.
\]
The successive indices \(k=7,1\) correspond to the ordinary continued-fraction digits \(8,2\).
We can extend the same idea to the triangle \(\Delta\). Now the input is an ordered pair \((x,y)\), and the corresponding Farey map has two branches represented by \(3\times3\) matrices acting on \((1,x,y)\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
F_1(x,y)
&=\left(\frac{x}{1-y},\frac{y}{1-y}\right),
&
\begin{pmatrix}
1&0&-1\\
0&1&0\\
0&0&1
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}1\\x\\y\end{pmatrix}
&=
\begin{pmatrix}1-y\\x\\y\end{pmatrix},
&&x+y\le1,\\[12pt]
F_0(x,y)
&=\left(\frac{y}{x},\frac{1-x}{x}\right),
&
\begin{pmatrix}
0&1&0\\
0&0&1\\
1&-1&0
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}1\\x\\y\end{pmatrix}
&=
\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\\1-x\end{pmatrix},
&&x+y>1.
\end{aligned}
\]
This time, dividing the second and third entries by the first recovers the transformed pair. Just as the interval is partitioned into branches that generate continued-fraction digits, the triangle is partitioned into regions that generate a sequence describing two numbers together.

title: Representing Numbers Using Continued Fractions and the TRIP Framework
section: From Farey branches to Gauss regions
text:
From Farey branches to Gauss regions
Each Farey step subdivides the interval or triangle into two regions, labeled \(0\) and \(1\). Repeating this process gives a binary sequence recording which branch contains a point at each step.
The accelerated Gauss map groups consecutive applications of branch \(1\), followed by branch \(0\), into a single step. This produces regions labeled by nonnegative integers,



Gauss region
Farey branches
Meaning




\(\Delta_0\)
\(0\)
No \(1\) steps before \(0\)


\(\Delta_1\)
\(10\)
One \(1\) step before \(0\)


\(\Delta_2\)
\(110\)
Two \(1\) steps before \(0\)


\(\Delta_3\)
\(1110\)
Three \(1\) steps before \(0\)


\(\vdots\)
\(\vdots\)
\(\vdots\)



More precisely, let \(V\) contain the vertices of our original interval or triangle in homogeneous coordinates. The region \(\Delta_k\) is constructed from
\[
VF_1^kF_0,
\qquad k=0,1,2,\ldots,
\]
by projecting its columns back into the interval or triangle. Thus, the region number \(k\) counts how many times branch \(1\) occurs before branch \(0\), rather than describing the region’s geometric position.
A Farey itinerary such as
\[
110\,10\,1110\,0\cdots
\]
therefore becomes the accelerated sequence
\[
(2,1,3,0,\ldots).
\]
This is the connection to ordinary continued fractions, instead of tracking every binary subdivision individually, we record how many consecutive steps occur before switching branches. The same idea works on triangles, even though their geometry is considerably more complicated.
The interactive tools in the dropdown menus above let you explore the expansion formulas (or explosion formulas, as I like to call them, given their tendency to explode across the page), partitions, and orbits of these algorithms.

title: Representing Numbers Using Continued Fractions and the TRIP Framework
text:
Families
For 3d we have 216 permutation settings falling into 15 families of subdivision patterns and

Same family: their partition lines match at every depth, either directly or after rearranging the triangle’s three outer vertices.
Different families: no rearrangement of the outer vertices makes their partition lines match.

There are 6 ways to arrange three vertices, but multiple permutation settings can produce the same partition even without rearranging them. Consequently, families contain more than six settings: 12 families contain 12 settings each, and 3 contain 24 each, accounting for all 216.
Each family therefore has one representative picture. Its members share that geometry, but may label the pieces differently and move points differently.

title: Probability Theory, Statistical Models, and Setting Up Inference
text:
Probability theory provides the mathematical foundation for statistical modeling. It defines random variables, probability distributions, conditional distributions, expectations, and dependence, allowing uncertainty to be represented mathematically. It also describes how random data behave under repeated sampling through results such as the law of large numbers and central limit theorem.
A useful distinction is that probability and statistics operate in opposite directions. Probability is the forward problem: given a probability distribution or data-generating mechanism, say \(P_0=P_{\theta_0}\), determine the behavior of observable random variables and statistics generated under \(P_0\). Statistics is the inverse problem: given observed data generated from some unknown \(P_0\), use the statistical model \(\mathcal P\) and the data to learn about \(P_0\) or particular features of \(P_0\).
Schematically,
\[
\text{Probability: }
P_0
\longrightarrow
\text{distribution of observable data},
\]
whereas
\[
\text{Statistics: }
\text{observed data}
\longrightarrow
\text{inference about }P_0
\text{ or a functional of }P_0.
\]
The role of the statistical model \(\mathcal P\) is therefore to specify the collection of probability distributions regarded as plausible data-generating mechanisms, while \(P_0\in\mathcal P\) denotes the true, generally unknown, data-generating distribution.
We focus below on the probability and measure-theoretic foundations needed for parametric statistical modeling. The forward-versus-inverse distinction will become increasingly concrete as we develop random variables, distributions, likelihoods, and statistical inference.

title: Probability Theory, Statistical Models, and Setting Up Inference
section: Conditioning, Densities, and Changes of Measure
text:
Conditioning, Densities, and Changes of Measure
Conditional probability can also be understood as a change of probability measure. Rather than assigning probabilities over the entire sample space \(\Omega\), conditioning on an event \(B\) restricts our attention to \(B\) and renormalizes the probabilities so that \(B\) has probability one.
Formally, given a probability space \((\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\) and an event \(B\) with \(P(B)>0\), define the conditional probability measure
\[
P_B(A)\coloneqq P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}.
\]
This new measure satisfies \(P_B(B)=1\) and \(P_B(B^c)=0\). Moreover, \(P_B\) is absolutely continuous with respect to \(P\), and its Radon–Nikodym derivative is
\[
\boxed{
\frac{dP_B}{dP}(\omega)
=\frac{\mathbf 1_B(\omega)}{P(B)}.
}
\]
Consequently, conditional probability can be expressed as an integral under the original measure:
\[
\begin{aligned}
P(A\mid B)
&=\int_A\frac{dP_B}{dP}\,dP\\
&=\frac{1}{P(B)}\int_A\mathbf 1_B\,dP\\
&=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The same principle appears when working with conditional densities. If \((X,Y)\) has joint density \(f_{X,Y}\) and marginal density \(f_Y\), then, for \(f_Y(y)>0\),
\[
\boxed{
f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)
=\frac{f_{X,Y}(x,y)}{f_Y(y)}.
}
\]
Intuitively, we restrict the joint distribution to a particular value of \(Y\) and normalize by its marginal density. Unlike conditioning on an event with positive probability, however, conditioning on \(Y=y\) for a continuous random variable requires a conditional distribution, since \(P(Y=y)=0\).
More generally, conditioning on a \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F\) is formalized through the Radon–Nikodym theorem. For an event \(A\), define \(\nu_A(G)=P(A\cap G)\) for \(G\in\mathcal G\). Then
\[
P(A\mid\mathcal G)
=\frac{d\nu_A}{d(P|_{\mathcal G})}
=E[\mathbf 1_A\mid\mathcal G].
\]
Thus, conditional probability, conditional densities, and conditional expectation are closely connected through restricting, normalizing, and disintegrating probability measures.

Definition: Mean/Expectation



The mean or expectation of a random variable \(X\) is its probability-weighted average. The same quantity can be expressed in several useful ways: by averaging values, averaging quantiles, accumulating tail probabilities, or first conditioning on another variable.
Assume \(\mathbb{E}[|X|]<\infty\), and let \(F_X\) denote the CDF of \(X\).








Representation
Expression
Conditions or interpretation




Probability space
\(\mathbb{E}[X]=\int_\Omega X(\omega)\,dP(\omega)\)
The underlying measure-theoretic definition


Distribution
\(\mathbb{E}[X]=\int_{\mathbb{R}}x\,dF_X(x)\)
Average values according to the distribution of \(X\)


Discrete
\(\mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_{x\in\mathcal{S}}x\,p_X(x)\)
\(p_X(x)=P(X=x)\) is the probability mass function


Density
\(\mathbb{E}[X]=\int_{\mathbb{R}}x f_X(x)\,dx\)
Applies when \(X\) has a density \(f_X\)


Quantiles
\(\mathbb{E}[X]=\int_0^1F_X^{-1}(u)\,du\)
Uniformly average all quantile levels


General tails
\(\mathbb{E}[X]=\int_0^\infty P(X>t)\,dt-\int_0^\infty P(X<-t)\,dt\)
Expected positive part minus expected negative part

\(\mathbb{E}[X]=\int_0^\infty[1-F_X(t)]\,dt-\int_{-\infty}^0F_X(t)\,dt\)
Express the tail integrals using the CDF


Iterated expectation
\(\mathbb{E}[X]=\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y]]\)
Average conditional means over the distribution of \(Y\)


Change of measure
\(\mathbb{E}_P[X]=\mathbb{E}_Q[X\,dP/dQ]\)
Requires \(P\ll Q\); reweight an expectation under another probability measure


Characteristic function
\(\mathbb{E}[X]=\varphi_X'(0)/i\), where \(\varphi_X(t)=\mathbb{E}[e^{itX}]\)
Recover the mean from the derivative at zero



Here \(F_X^{-1}(u)=\inf\{x:F_X(x)\ge u\}\) is the generalized quantile function, so the quantile representation also applies to discrete and mixed distributions. For nonnegative \(X\), the nonnegative integral and sum representations remain valid when \(\mathbb{E}[X]=\infty\).
A related optimization characterization, assuming \(\mathbb{E}[X^2]<\infty\), is \[
\boxed{\mathbb{E}[X]=\underset{a\in\mathbb{R}}{\arg\min}\;\mathbb{E}[(X-a)^2].}
\] Thus, the mean is the constant that minimizes expected squared prediction error.

title: Probability Theory, Statistical Models, and Setting Up Inference
section: What are Empirical Processes?: A Functional Perspective
text:
What are Empirical Processes?: A Functional Perspective






Example: ECDF as a Random Empirical Function



Thinking more generally, the ECDF \(F_n\) can be viewed as a random function obtained by empirically averaging functions from the deterministic indicator class
\[
\mathcal F_{\mathrm{CDF}}
=
\left\{
f_t:f_t(x)=\mathbf 1\{x\leq t\},\ t\in\mathbb R
\right\}.
\]
The empirical measure \(P_n\) acts as the empirical-average operator \(f\mapsto P_n f\). Therefore, for each \(f_t\in\mathcal F_{\mathrm{CDF}}\), we can write
\[
F_n(t)
=
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n f_t(X_i)
=
P_n f_t
\]
The functions \(f_t\) themselves are not random. The ECDF is random because the empirical-average operator \(P_n\) depends on the random observations \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\). Equivalently, for each \(i\), the mapping \(f_t:t\mapsto\mathbf 1\{X_i\leq t\}\) is a random step function, and \(F_n\) is the average of these random functions.


The empirical distribution is an equally weighted sum (mixture) of Dirac probability measures, each concentrated at one observed data point.
For observations \(X_1,,X_n\),
\[ \]
Each \(_{X_i}\) assigns probability \(1\) to \(X_i\), and multiplying by \(1/n\) assigns each observation probability mass \(1/n\).
For any measurable set \(A\),
\[ P_n(A)=1n_{i=1}^n(X_iA). \]
Thus, \(P_n(A)\) is simply the proportion of observations belonging to \(A\).
The particularly useful consequence is
\[ \]
This is why empirical process theory expresses sample averages as integrals with respect to the empirical distribution.
Strictly speaking, these are Dirac measures, rather than ordinary probability density functions.
As with the ECDF, the empirical-average operator can be used to define many common statistics, and empirical-process theory studies the asymptotic behavior of these empirical averages directly. Writing \(P=P_X\) for the true distribution of \(X\), the empirical measure is
\[
P_n=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{X_i}
\]
For a measurable and \(P\)-integrable function \(f\), the empirical and population averages are
\[
P_n f
=
\int f\,dP_n
=
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n f(X_i),
\qquad
Pf
=
E_P[f(X)]
\]
A statistical procedure typically determines a particular class of functions \(\mathcal F\) that is evaluated using the empirical measure






Example: Common Statistical Procedures Through Empirical Processes



Even without using likelihoods, different statistical procedures use different indexing classes \(\mathcal F\).

The empirical distribution function corresponds to the class \[
\mathcal F_{\mathrm{CDF}}
=
\{f_t:f_t(x)=\mathbf 1\{x\leq t\},\ t\in\mathbb R\},
\]since\[
P_n f_t
=
P_n\mathbf 1\{x\leq t\}
=
F_n(t).
\]
An \(M\)-estimator may instead involve a loss-function class \[
\mathcal F_M
=
\{\ell_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\},
\] where the empirical criterion is maximizing \(P_n\ell_\theta\) over \(\Theta\)
A moment- or Z estimator/estimating-equation-based procedure may involve a class of score or moment functions \[
\mathcal F_Z
=
\{\psi_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\},
\] where the empirical estimating equation is typically \(P_n\psi_\theta=0\)



Given a function class \(\mathcal F\) the corresponding empirical process, indexed naturally by \(f \in \mathcal F\), is
\[
\mathbb G_n(f)
=
\sqrt n(P_n-P)f,
\qquad
f\in\mathcal F
\] Empirical-process theory studies the stochastic behavior of \(P_n\), through the scaled empirical process \(\mathbb G_n\), uniformly over function classes \(\mathcal F\). Thus, the statistical procedure determines the relevant function class, while the complexity and structure of that class determine which empirical-process tools are needed to establish consistency, convergence rates, and asymptotic distributions. This perspective places the asymptotic behavior of many seemingly different statistical procedures and functionals of interest within a single unifying framework.

A Note on Indexing
An empirical process is fundamentally indexed by functions \(f\in\mathcal F\):
\[
\mathbb G_n(f),
\qquad
f\in\mathcal F
\]
When the function class has a natural parameterization \(\mathcal F=\{f_t:t\in T\}\), where \(T\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), we can equivalently index the empirical process by \(t\) and write
\[
\mathbb G_n(t)
:=
\mathbb G_n(f_t)
\]
This is only a change in notation: the parameter \(t\) labels the function \(f_t\) on which the empirical process acts.






Example: Indexing Function Classes Differently




For the CDF indicator class,\[
f_t(x)=\mathbf 1\{x\leq t\},
\qquad
t\in\mathbb R,
\]so we can index the empirical process by \(t\) and write \[
\mathbb G_n(t)
=
\mathbb G_n(f_t)
=
\sqrt n\{F_n(t)-F(t)\}
\]
For the class of interval indicators, define \[
f_{a,b}(x)
=
\mathbf 1\{a<x\leq b\},
\qquad
(a,b)\in
\left\{
(a,b)\in\mathbb R^2:a<b
\right\}
\]The empirical process can then be indexed by the vector \((a,b)\),$$\begin{aligned} G_n(a,b) &= G_n(f_{a,b})\ &= n [ {F_n(b)-F_n(a)}
{F(b)-F(a)} ]. \end{aligned}$$
For a multivariate random variable \(X\in\mathbb R^d\), the multivariate CDF indicator class is \[
f_t(x)
=
\mathbf 1\{x_1\leq t_1,\ldots,x_d\leq t_d\},
\qquad
t=(t_1,\ldots,t_d)\in\mathbb R^d
\] Here the empirical process is naturally indexed by \(t\in\mathbb R^d\),\[
\mathbb G_n(t)
=
\sqrt n\{F_n(t)-F(t)\}
\]
An \(M\)-estimation problem provides a different type of indexing. For a loss-function class \[
\mathcal G_M
=
\{\ell_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\},
\qquad
\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p,
\] we can index the empirical process by the parameter \(\theta\), \[
\mathbb G_n(\theta)
:=
\mathbb G_n(\ell_\theta)
=
\sqrt n(P_n-P)\ell_\theta
\]

Thus, depending on the structure of the function class, an empirical process may be indexed by a scalar threshold, a vector of thresholds, or a model parameter.


Not every function class has a useful finite-dimensional parameterization. Classes of nuisance functions or other infinite-dimensional objects may still need to be indexed directly by the functions \(f\in\mathcal F\).

title: Probability Theory, Statistical Models, and Setting Up Inference
section: Asymptotics and “Well-Behaved” Classes of Functions for EP
text:
Asymptotics and “Well-Behaved” Classes of Functions for EP
The ordinary law of large numbers gives pointwise convergence: for each fixed \(P\)-integrable function \(f\in L_1(P)\),
\[
P_n f\overset{P}{\longrightarrow}Pf
\]
We can prove this using Chebyshev’s inequality under the stronger condition \(f\in L_2(P)\), but the ordinary i.i.d. law of large numbers itself requires only the moment condition \(E_P|f(X)|<\infty\).
The classical Glivenko–Cantelli theorem strengthens this pointwise convergence for the CDF indicator class to uniform convergence over all thresholds \(t\in\mathbb R\). Inspired by this result, we call a function class \(\mathcal F\) a \(P\)-Glivenko–Cantelli class if
\[
\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}
\left|
P_n f-Pf
\right|
\overset{P}{\longrightarrow}0
\]
Glivenko–Cantelli classes, however, are not enough for every asymptotic question. This property establishes the uniform consistency of the empirical averages \(P_n f\), but it does not describe their scaled stochastic fluctuations or provide their asymptotic distributions.
If \(\mathcal F={f_1}\) contains a single square-integrable function \(f_1\in L_2(P)\), then its variance exists and the ordinary central limit theorem gives
\[
\mathbb G_n(f_1)
=
\sqrt n(P_n-P)f_1
\rightsquigarrow
N(0,\sigma_{f_1}^2),
\]
where
\[
\sigma_{f_1}^2
=
\operatorname{Var}_P\{f_1(X)\}
=
P(f_1-Pf_1)^2
\]
More generally, if \(\mathcal F={f_1,\ldots,f_K}\) is a finite class of square-integrable functions, then the multivariate central limit theorem gives
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
\mathbb G_n(f_1)\\
\vdots\\
\mathbb G_n(f_K)
\end{pmatrix}
\rightsquigarrow
N_K(0,\Sigma),
\]
where
\[
\Sigma_{jk}
=
P(f_jf_k)-Pf_j\,Pf_k
\]
For an infinite class \(\mathcal F\), the same argument gives finite-dimensional convergence: for every fixed finite collection \(f_1,\ldots,f_K\in\mathcal F\), the corresponding vector of empirical-process evaluations converges to a multivariate normal distribution. Finite-dimensional convergence alone, however, does not control the behavior of \(\mathbb G_n(f)\) simultaneously over all \(f\in\mathcal F\).
The space
\[
\ell^\infty(\mathcal F)
=
\left\{
z:\mathcal F\to\mathbb R:
\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}|z(f)|<\infty
\right\}
\]
is equipped with the supremum norm
\[
\|z\|_{\mathcal F}
=
\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}|z(f)|
\]
Thus, \(\mathbb G_n\) is viewed as the random function
\[
f\mapsto\mathbb G_n(f)
\]
on \(\mathcal F\). To establish weak convergence of \(\mathbb G_n\) in \(\ell^\infty(\mathcal F)\), we generally need two ingredients:

finite-dimensional convergence; and
asymptotic tightness of the entire process.

Tightness is commonly established using the \(L_2(P)\) semimetric
\[
\rho_P(f,g)
=
\left\{
P(f-g)^2
\right\}^{1/2}
\]
and by showing that the empirical process is asymptotically equicontinuous:
\[
\lim_{\delta\downarrow0}
\limsup_{n\to\infty}
P^*
\left(
\sup_{\rho_P(f,g)<\delta}
\left|
\mathbb G_n(f)-\mathbb G_n(g)
\right|
>
\varepsilon
\right)
=
0
\]
for every \(\varepsilon>0\), together with suitable total boundedness of \(\mathcal F\) under \(\rho_P\). In practice, entropy bounds, bracketing numbers, and VC-class results provide sufficient conditions for this tightness.
A function class \(\mathcal F\) is called \(P\)-Donsker if
\[
\mathbb G_n
\rightsquigarrow
\mathbb G_P
\qquad
\text{in }\ell^\infty(\mathcal F),
\]
where \(\mathbb G_P\) is a tight mean-zero Gaussian process. Its covariance function is
\[
\operatorname{Cov}\{\mathbb G_P(f),\mathbb G_P(g)\}
=
P(fg)-Pf\,Pg
\]
Therefore, square integrability of each \(f\in\mathcal F\) gives the required pointwise and finite-dimensional central limit theorems, but it does not by itself imply that \(\mathcal F\) is \(P\)-Donsker. The Donsker property additionally requires enough control over the size and complexity of the entire function class to obtain asymptotic tightness.

Gaussian Processes

title: Probability Theory, Statistical Models, and Setting Up Inference
text:
EP for Functionals
Donsker convergence describes the joint asymptotic behavior of the centered and scaled empirical averages over \(\mathcal F\). However, it does not automatically give the asymptotic distribution of every nonlinear functional of the empirical measure. If a statistic can be written as \(T(P_n)\), we still need sufficient regularity of the map \(T\), such as Hadamard differentiability, to transfer the empirical-process convergence through \(T\). The functional delta method then gives
\[
\sqrt n\{T(P_n)-T(P)\}
\rightsquigarrow
T'_P(\mathbb G_P).
\]
Thus, Glivenko–Cantelli classes provide uniform laws of large numbers, Donsker classes provide uniform central limit theorems, and the functional delta method transfers these process-level results to sufficiently regular functionals of interest.

title: Probability Theory, Statistical Models, and Setting Up Inference
text:
EP Decomposition for Asymptotics
A useful way to organize an asymptotic analysis is to start from the empirical score at the truth and apply the empirical-process decomposition for an estimated score: \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb P_n\psi(W;\tau_0,\hat\eta)-\underbrace{P\psi(W;\tau_0,\eta_0)}_{=0}
&=
\mathbb P_n\psi(W;\tau_0,\hat\eta)-\textcolor{blue}{\mathbb P_n\psi(W;\tau_0,\eta_0)}
+\textcolor{blue}{\mathbb P_n\psi(W;\tau_0,\eta_0)}\\
&-\textcolor{red}{P\psi(W;\tau_0,\hat\eta)}
+\textcolor{red}{P\psi(W;\tau_0,\hat\eta)}
-P\psi(W;\tau_0,\eta_0)
\\[0.5em]
&=
\underbrace{(\mathbb P_n-P)\psi(W;\tau_0,\eta_0)}_{\text{first-order empirical fluctuation / influence}}+
\underbrace{(\mathbb P_n-P)\big[\psi(W;\tau_0,\hat\eta)-\psi(W;\tau_0,\eta_0)\big]}_{\text{empirical-process remainder}}\\&+
\underbrace{P\big[\psi(W;\tau_0,\hat\eta)-\psi(W;\tau_0,\eta_0)\big]}_{\text{plug-in bias}}.
\end{aligned}
\] 
This decomposition separates the score into three parts:

The first term, \[
(\mathbb P_n-P)\psi(W;\tau_0,\eta_0),
\] is the leading first-order empirical fluctuation term. Since the estimating equation is centered at the truth, \[
P\psi(W;\tau_0,\eta_0)=0,
\] this term is a mean-zero empirical average: \[
(\mathbb P_n-P)\psi(W;\tau_0,\eta_0)
=
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \psi(W_i;\tau_0,\eta_0).
\] It therefore lives on the natural \(n^{-1/2}\) scale and is the term that drives the asymptotic distribution. This is why it is closely related to the influence function: it is the raw first-order empirical process term built from the true score.
To see how the influence function arises, let \[
\Psi(\tau,\eta):=P\psi(W;\tau,\eta).
\] Since \(\hat\tau\) approximately solves the estimating equation, \[
\mathbb P_n\psi(W;\hat\tau,\hat\eta)\approx 0,
\] and since the nuisance remainder terms are shown to be negligible, the leading behavior comes from replacing the empirical score near \(\hat\tau\) by its idealized first-order form. A first-order Taylor expansion of the population moment map in \(\tau\) around \(\tau_0\) gives \[
\Psi(\hat\tau,\eta_0)
=
\Psi(\tau_0,\eta_0)
+
\dot\Psi_\tau(\tau_0,\eta_0)(\hat\tau-\tau_0)
+
o(|\hat\tau-\tau_0|),
\] where \[
\dot\Psi_\tau(\tau_0,\eta_0)
=
\frac{\partial}{\partial\tau}P\psi(W;\tau,\eta_0)\bigg|_{\tau=\tau_0}.
\] Because \(\Psi(\tau_0,\eta_0)=P\psi(W;\tau_0,\eta_0)=0\), this becomes \[
\Psi(\hat\tau,\eta_0)
\approx
\dot\Psi_\tau(\tau_0,\eta_0)(\hat\tau-\tau_0).
\] Combining this linearization with the empirical fluctuation term yields \[
0
\approx
(\mathbb P_n-P)\psi(W;\tau_0,\eta_0)
+
\dot\Psi_\tau(\tau_0,\eta_0)(\hat\tau-\tau_0),
\] so \[
\hat\tau-\tau_0
\approx
-\dot\Psi_\tau(\tau_0,\eta_0)^{-1}
(\mathbb P_n-P)\psi(W;\tau_0,\eta_0).
\]
This is exactly where the influence function comes from in the earlier definitions. In the RAL viewpoint, the influence function is the function \(\varphi\) in an expansion of the form \[
\hat\tau-\tau_0
=
(\mathbb P_n-P)\varphi + o_p(n^{-1/2}).
\] Comparing with the display above, we identify \[
\varphi(W)
=
-\dot\Psi_\tau(\tau_0,\eta_0)^{-1}\psi(W;\tau_0,\eta_0).
\] In the functional / pathwise viewpoint, this same \(\varphi\) is the first-order derivative kernel that converts a small perturbation of the underlying law into a first-order change in the target. In the Hilbert space / tangent space viewpoint, this same object is the representer of that derivative in \(L_2^0(P)\). So in this centered estimating-equation setting, these earlier influence-function definitions all collapse to the same concrete formula: the score that defines the estimator, after Taylor linearization and normalization by the slope of the population moment map, becomes the influence function.
So this first term is not itself yet the influence function of the estimator. Rather, it is the centered empirical fluctuation term built from the true score, and after Taylor linearization of the population moment map in \(\tau\), that same score becomes the influence function up to the normalizing slope matrix \(\dot\Psi_\tau(\tau_0,\eta_0)^{-1}\).
The second term, \[
(\mathbb P_n-P)\big[\psi(W;\tau_0,\hat\eta)-\psi(W;\tau_0,\eta_0)\big],
\] is the empirical-process remainder induced by replacing the true nuisance functions with estimated ones. It corresponds to bias from overfitting and sample reuse.
The third term, \[
P\big[\psi(W;\tau_0,\hat\eta)-\psi(W;\tau_0,\eta_0)\big],
\] is the population plug-in bias. It measures how the population moment changes when \(\eta_0\) is replaced by \(\hat\eta\), and corresponds to bias from regularization or nuisance estimation.

When you evaluate the estimating equation at the true target \(\tau_0\) but with estimated nuisance \(\hat\eta\), the result differs from the ideal mean-zero empirical fluctuation by two extra error terms: one from the empirical process and one from plug-in bias. DML is built to control those last two terms separately: orthogonalization makes the plug-in bias second order, while sample splitting and cross-fitting control the empirical-process remainder. The first term remains and determines the first-order asymptotics.

title: Principles of Experimental Design
text:
Phase II vs. III
The simplest and most common phase II trials are nonrandomized one arm studies comparing a new therapy to a historical controls effectiveness; Phase III trials are overwhelmingly randomized with concurrent control.

We can find two-stage designs by iteration, using the following

We identify two-stage designs with the following iteration.
Given \((p_0, p_1, \alpha^\star, 1-\beta^\star)\)

Making a function for \(P(\text{Reject } H_0|p)\),

## reject iff X1 > a1 and X1 + X2 >= a
rej = function(p, a1, a, n1, n2) {
  acc = pbinom(a1, n1, p)
  lo = a1 + 1L; hi = n1
  if (lo <= hi) {
    i = lo:hi
    s1 = dbinom(i, n1, p)
    s2 = pbinom(a - i, n2, p)
    acc = acc + sum(s1*s2)
  }
  1 - acc
}

then we can use this to find \(\alpha,\beta\) for any specified design \((a_1,a,n_1,n_2)\) and using simple loops we can catalogue all designs that work with total sample size under some specific \(n=n_1+n_2\)


find_two_stage <- function(p0, p1,
                           alpha_star = 0.05, power_star = 0.85,
                           nmin = 10, nmax = 50) {
  out <- list(); k <- 1
  for (n in nmin:nmax) {
    for (n1 in 1:(n - 1)) {
      n2 <- n - n1
      for (a1 in 0:(n1 - 1)) {
        # here we start at (a1) to match clinfun
        # in general a1=a is one stage
        for (a in (a1):(n - 1)) {
          alpha <- rej(p0, a1, a, n1, n2)
          power <- rej(p1, a1, a, n1, n2)
          if (alpha <= alpha_star && power >= power_star) {
            pet0 <- pbinom(a1, n1, p0)       
            en0  <- n1 + (1 - pet0) * n2   
            out[[k]] <- data.frame(
              a1, a, n1, n2, n,
              alpha = as.numeric(alpha),
              power = as.numeric(power),
              PET_p0 = pet0,
              EN_p0  = en0
            )
            k <- k + 1L
          }}}}}
  do.call(rbind, out)
}

title: Principles of Experimental Design
text:
Phase II Trials: Binary Outcome
If our response is binary and we are interested in the population proportion of response under a new therapy \((p)\) then we usually want to establish that our treatment is better than some historical controls estimated proportion \((p_0)\)

Simon’s Two Stage Phase II Trial w/ Futility Stopping
If we know our targets \(\alpha^*, 1-\beta^*\) and specific alternative effectiveness \(p_1\) that we want to test, \[\boxed{H_0:p = p_0,\quad H_1: p = p_1}\] then noting that the counts in each stage are independent \(X_1 \perp\!\!\!\perp X_2\), finding a two stage regime with futility stopping is simply choosing sample sizes \((n_1,n_2)\) at each stage and cutoffs \((a_1,a)\) such that \[\begin{aligned}\alpha^* &\geq P(X_1>a_1,X_1+X_2>a|p_0)\\ 1-\beta^* &\leq P(X_1>a_1, X_1+X_2>a|p_1)
\end{aligned}\]

title: Themes of Mathematical Statistics
section: Numerical Optimization and the EM Algorithm
text:
Numerical Optimization and the EM Algorithm
In many statistical models the score equations are nonlinear or too complicated to solve explicitly.
EXAMPLE
In these types of more difficult settings, we use iterative numerical algorithms. The main idea is a difficult likelihood optimization problem can sometimes be replaced by a sequence of simpler optimization problems.
For example, Newton-Raphson uses a first-order Taylor approximation of the score around the current parameter estimate to move toward a stationary point of the log-likelihood,
\[
\theta^{(t+1)}
=
\theta^{(t)}
-
\left[
\nabla_\theta^2\ell(\theta^{(t)})
\right]^{-1}
U_n(\theta^{(t)}).
\]

EM Algorithm
The Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm is an iterative method for maximum likelihood estimation that is particularly useful when a model involves missing or latent variables.
Suppose \(Y\) denotes the observed data, \(Z\) denotes missing or latent data, and \(\theta\) is the unknown parameter. If we had access to both \(Y\) and \(Z\), we could construct the complete-data likelihood \(f(Y,Z;\theta)\), which may be relatively easy to maximize.
However, because \(Z\) is unobserved, we must instead work with the observed-data likelihood, obtained by integrating out the missing variables:
\[
L(\theta;Y)
=
f(Y;\theta)
=
\int f(Y,Z;\theta)\,dZ.
\]
Directly maximizing this likelihood may be difficult, even when maximizing the complete-data likelihood would be straightforward.
The key idea behind EM is to use the simpler complete-data likelihood to iteratively maximize the observed-data likelihood without directly optimizing the integral. To do this, we must specify a complete-data model \(f(Y,Z;\theta)\) whose marginal distribution for \(Y\) agrees with our observed-data model. The latent variables need not represent genuinely missing observations; they can also be introduced specifically to simplify the optimization problem.
Starting with an initial parameter estimate \(\theta^{(0)}\), the EM algorithm alternates between two steps:

Expectation (E-step). Given the observed data \(Y\) and our current parameter estimate \(\theta^{(t)}\), ask: What is the expected complete-data log-likelihood, averaging over the missing data given what we currently know?
We calculate
\[
Q(\theta\mid\theta^{(t)})
=
E_{\theta^{(t)}}[
\log f(Y,Z;\theta)\mid Y
],
\]
or equivalently,
\[
Q(\theta\mid\theta^{(t)})
=
\int
\log f(Y,z;\theta)
f(z\mid Y;\theta^{(t)})\,dz.
\]
Importantly, \(\theta^{(t)}\) is held fixed and determines the conditional distribution of the missing data, while \(\theta\) remains the argument of the log-likelihood. Thus, the E-step produces a function of \(\theta\) that averages over our uncertainty about \(Z\).
Maximization (M-step). Given the expected complete-data log-likelihood constructed in the E-step, ask: Which value of \(\theta\) maximizes this function?
We update the parameter estimate according to
\[
\theta^{(t+1)}
=
\arg\max_{\theta\in\Theta}
Q(\theta\mid\theta^{(t)}).
\]
This updated estimate is then used to calculate a new conditional distribution for the missing data in the next E-step.

We repeat these two steps until convergence. Under the usual EM construction, each iteration does not decrease the observed-data likelihood, even though we are maximizing the expected complete-data log-likelihood rather than the observed-data likelihood directly.
The important distinction is that the E-step does not generally replace missing observations with their expected values. Instead, it takes the conditional expectation of the entire complete-data log-likelihood, producing a function that is often easier to optimize.
EM is not guaranteed to find the global maximum, and convergence can be slow. Its usefulness depends on finding a complete-data representation for which both the E-step and M-step are computationally manageable.

Bayesian Likelihood-Based Inference

no matter the tack taken it boils down to axioms
So far, we have taken the frequentist perspective, treating \(\theta\) as an unknown but fixed parameter and using the observed data to construct an estimator \(\hat\theta\).
The Bayesian perspective instead places a probability distribution on the unknown parameter. Given a prior density \(\pi(\theta)\) and likelihood \(L(\theta)\), Bayes’ theorem gives the posterior distribution,
\[
\pi(\theta\mid x_1,\ldots,x_n)
=
\frac{
L(\theta)\pi(\theta)
}{
\int_\Theta L(t)\pi(t)\,dt
}.
\]
Thus the likelihood is central to both frequentist and Bayesian inference, but the inferential procedures differ.
Frequentist likelihood theory typically uses the likelihood to construct estimators, confidence regions, and hypothesis tests. Bayesian inference combines the likelihood with a prior distribution to obtain a posterior distribution, from which posterior summaries and credible regions can be calculated.
For example, a Bayesian may report the posterior mean
\[
E[\theta\mid X_1,\ldots,X_n],
\]
or the maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate,
\[
\hat\theta_{\mathrm{MAP}}
=
\arg\max_{\theta\in\Theta}
L(\theta)\pi(\theta).
\]
The MAP estimate resembles an MLE, except that it also incorporates the prior density.
Neither framework is uniformly easier or better. Bayesian hierarchical models can be particularly natural when many parameters share information through a common prior structure. Frequentist methods can be attractive when we want procedures with explicitly characterized repeated-sampling properties, often without specifying a prior.
Under suitable regularity conditions, frequentist and Bayesian procedures can also produce similar large-sample conclusions. For example, Bernstein-von Mises results establish circumstances under which a Bayesian posterior is approximately normal and closely related to the sampling distribution of the MLE.

title: Themes of Mathematical Statistics
section: Advanced (but useful) extension. estimating equation based information and The Sandwich Variance
text:
Advanced (but useful) extension. estimating equation based information and The Sandwich Variance
Maximum likelihood is an instance of M-estimation, because it optimizes a sample criterion. When the estimator solves a score equation, it can also be studied through Z-estimation. The latter perspective extends beyond likelihood scores to more general estimating equations.
Under suitable regularity conditions, the sandwich formula gives the asymptotic variance of an estimator around its population target without requiring a correctly specified likelihood.
This does not automatically make inference valid for the scientific estimand. Under misspecification, the estimator’s population target may differ from the quantity we want. Here, the Exponential estimator still targets \(\mu_0\), so correcting its variance is sufficient.
the key here is genearlizing the statitical model from one that is likleihood based to one that is more general and only moment based?






Correcting the Exponential Standard Error



The per-observation Exponential score is \[
\psi_m(Y)
=
\frac{\partial}{\partial m}\log f_m(Y)
=
\frac{Y-m}{m^2}.
\]
Under the true DGP, \[
E_0[\psi_m(Y)]
=
\frac{\mu_0-m}{m^2},
\] so the population estimating equation has the unique root \(m=\mu_0\).
Define \[
A
=
-E_0\left[
\left.
\frac{\partial\psi_m(Y)}{\partial m}
\right|_{m=\mu_0}
\right],
\qquad
B
=
E_0[\psi_{\mu_0}(Y)^2].
\]
Since \[
\frac{\partial\psi_m(Y)}{\partial m}
=
\frac1{m^2}-\frac{2Y}{m^3},
\] we obtain \[
A
=
-\frac1{\mu_0^2}
+\frac{2E_0[Y]}{\mu_0^3}
=
\frac1{\mu_0^2}.
\]
Also, \[
B
=
\frac{E_0[(Y-\mu_0)^2]}{\mu_0^4}
=
\frac{\operatorname{Var}_0(Y)}{\mu_0^4}
=
\frac1{k\mu_0^2}.
\]
Thus \(A\ne B\) when \(k\ne1\): the information equality fails.
The sandwich asymptotic variance is \[
\boxed{
A^{-1}BA^{-1}
=
\frac{B}{A^2}
=
\operatorname{Var}_0(Y)
=
\frac{\mu_0^2}{k}.
}
\]
This recovers the correct CLT variance.
We can estimate it without knowing the true distribution or its shape parameter. At \(\widehat m_E=\bar Y_n\), \[
\widehat A
=
-\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\left.
\frac{\partial\psi_m(Y_i)}{\partial m}
\right|_{m=\bar Y_n}
=
\frac1{\bar Y_n^2},
\] and \[
\widehat B
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\psi_{\bar Y_n}(Y_i)^2
=
\frac{n^{-1}\sum_i(Y_i-\bar Y_n)^2}{\bar Y_n^4}.
\]
Therefore, the estimated covariance of the unscaled estimator is \[
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}_{\mathrm{sand}}(\widehat m_E)
=
\frac1n\frac{\widehat B}{\widehat A^2}
=
\frac1{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^n(Y_i-\bar Y_n)^2.
\]
The corrected standard error and confidence interval are \[
\widehat{\operatorname{se}}_{E,\mathrm{sand}}
=
\sqrt{\frac1{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^n(Y_i-\bar Y_n)^2},
\] \[
\operatorname{CI}_{E,\mathrm{sand}}
=
\bar Y_n
\pm
z_{0.975}\widehat{\operatorname{se}}_{E,\mathrm{sand}}.
\]
This is exactly the same standard error obtained from the fitted Normal model. We have now justified it directly from the Exponential estimating equation, without assuming Normal observations.



Simulation: Exponential Model-Based Versus Sandwich Inference
We generate Gamma data repeatedly, fit the Exponential working model, and compare its model-based and sandwich confidence intervals.
The point estimate is the same in both analyses. Only the standard error changes.

set.seed(20261027)

mu0 <- 6
k <- 2
B <- 10000
sample_sizes <- c(30, 100, 500, 2000)
zcrit <- qnorm(0.975)

one_simulation <- function(n) {
  y <- rgamma(n, shape = k, scale = mu0 / k)

  # Exponential MLE
  m_hat <- mean(y)

  # Model-based standard error
  se_model <- m_hat / sqrt(n)

  # Sandwich standard error, with no finite-sample adjustment
  v_hat <- mean((y - m_hat)^2)
  se_sandwich <- sqrt(v_hat / n)

  c(
    estimate = m_hat,
    se_model = se_model,
    se_sandwich = se_sandwich,
    cover_model =
      abs(m_hat - mu0) <= zcrit * se_model,
    cover_sandwich =
      abs(m_hat - mu0) <= zcrit * se_sandwich
  )
}

title: Themes of Mathematical Statistics
text:
Proper Scoring Rules
An important distinction in statistical learning is the difference between estimating probabilities and making decisions. In much of applied machine learning, models are developed and evaluated for a predefined task, such as classification, with performance measured using accuracy, precision, recall, or F1. In statistical prediction and decision theory, the distinction is often made more explicitly: first estimate the conditional distribution of the outcome, then determine which action minimizes expected loss under the relevant decision problem.
For a binary outcome \(Y\in\{0,1\}\) and covariates \(X\), let
\[
p(x)=P(Y=1\mid X=x).
\]
Given an action space \(\mathcal A\) and loss function \(L(a,Y)\), the Bayes-optimal decision rule is
\[
a^*(x)=\arg\min_{a\in\mathcal A}E[L(a,Y)\mid X=x].
\]
For binary classification with false-positive cost \(c_{\mathrm{FP}}>0\) and false-negative cost \(c_{\mathrm{FN}}>0\), assuming correct classifications have zero cost, this becomes
\[
a^*(x)=\mathbb 1\left\{p(x)>\frac{c_{\mathrm{FP}}}{c_{\mathrm{FP}}+c_{\mathrm{FN}}}\right\},
\]
with either action optimal at equality. The familiar threshold of \(0.5\) is therefore optimal only under equal misclassification costs. Different applications, individuals, or populations may require different decisions even when the underlying event probability is identical.
Probability estimation and decision optimization are complementary, not competing objectives. Accurate conditional probabilities preserve information that can be used to construct different decision rules as the relevant costs and benefits change. A hard classification discards some of this information.
Nevertheless, estimating the entire conditional distribution is not always necessary. If the objective is a particular decision under a known loss function, a model can instead learn the decision rule directly. For example, classification algorithms may optimize surrogate losses that target accurate classifications without requiring calibrated probability estimates. Similarly, policy-learning methods may directly optimize expected utility. These approaches can be statistically justified, particularly when the model class is restricted or the available sample is small.
The distinction is therefore not that probability estimation is always preferable, but that the appropriate statistical objective depends on whether we seek a predictive distribution, a particular decision, or both.

Evaluating Probability Estimates
When the objective is probabilistic prediction, performance should be evaluated using a proper scoring rule. A scoring rule is proper if reporting the true probability distribution minimizes expected loss, and strictly proper if this minimizer is unique.
For binary outcomes, two common strictly proper scoring rules are:

Brier score:
\[
S_{\mathrm{Brier}}(p,y)=(y-p)^2.
\]
Logarithmic loss (log-loss):
\[
S_{\log}(p,y)=-y\log(p)-(1-y)\log(1-p).
\]

If the true conditional event probability is \(q\), both scoring rules satisfy
\[
E_q[S(q,Y)]\leq E_q[S(p,Y)],
\]
with equality if and only if \(p=q\).
In particular, the expected Brier score admits the decomposition
\[
\begin{aligned}
E_q[(Y-p)^2]
&=q(1-p)^2+(1-q)p^2\\
&=q(1-q)+(p-q)^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus, reporting \(p=q\) uniquely minimizes expected squared prediction error. Similarly, the expected excess log-loss is
\[
E_q[S_{\log}(p,Y)]-E_q[S_{\log}(q,Y)]
=
D_{\mathrm{KL}}\{\operatorname{Bern}(q)\Vert\operatorname{Bern}(p)\}\geq 0.
\]
These properties explain why proper scoring rules are useful: they reward accurate probability estimation without requiring an arbitrary classification threshold or a particular downstream utility function.
Unlike accuracy or F1, proper scoring rules evaluate the predicted probabilities themselves rather than first reducing them to binary decisions.






Misguided Critiques: Class Imbalance, Unbounded Log-Loss, and F1



Several common criticisms of proper scoring rules confuse probability estimation with decision optimization. For example, it is sometimes argued that log-loss is inappropriate because it is unbounded, or that the Brier score is only useful when misclassification costs are balanced. Others suggest that class imbalance makes metrics such as F1 or weighted F1 preferable.
These arguments require distinguishing the statistical properties of a scoring rule from the consequences of a particular decision.
1. Class imbalance and F1
For binary classification, the F1 score is
\[
F_1=\frac{2TP}{2TP+FP+FN},
\]
where \(TP\), \(FP\), and \(FN\) denote true positives, false positives, and false negatives.
Unlike proper scoring rules, F1 evaluates hard classifications and depends on the classification threshold. It discards information about the underlying probabilities and does not generally correspond to minimizing expected loss under specified false-positive and false-negative costs.
Weighted F1 and related metrics change the emphasis placed on different classification outcomes, but these weights should not be confused with a formally specified decision-theoretic utility function.
Consider a population in which every individual has the same \(1\%\) event probability, so covariates provide no additional predictive information. Using the population F1 score:

Classifying everyone as negative yields an F1 score of \(0\), under the usual convention.
Classifying everyone as positive yields an F1 score of approximately \(0.0198\).

Consequently, F1 favors classifying everyone as positive over classifying everyone as negative, even though the event occurs for only \(1\%\) of individuals.
This does not establish that predicting positive is always an inappropriate decision. Rather, it demonstrates that optimizing F1 is not equivalent to estimating probabilities or minimizing a specified misclassification cost.
Under the Brier score, by comparison,
\[
\begin{aligned}
E[S_{\mathrm{Brier}}(0.01,Y)]&=0.0099,\\
E[S_{\mathrm{Brier}}(0,Y)]&=0.01.
\end{aligned}
\]
Reporting the true probability minimizes expected loss, even when the event is rare.
Class imbalance does not invalidate proper scoring rules. However, rare events can make probability estimation and evaluation more difficult, and aggregate scores may obscure performance in clinically or operationally important subgroups. Comparisons with appropriate baseline models and supplementary diagnostic assessments remain important.
2. Unbounded log-loss
Log-loss is unbounded when a model assigns a probability approaching zero to an event that occurs:
\[
\lim_{p\to 0}S_{\log}(p,1)=\infty.
\]
This is not inherently a defect. Log-loss strongly penalizes confident but incorrect probability forecasts, and it remains strictly proper.
Nevertheless, unboundedness can create legitimate difficulties involving robustness, extreme predictions, numerical stability, and moment conditions required for certain theoretical guarantees. The bounded Brier score provides a strictly proper alternative when these considerations matter.
3. Unequal misclassification costs
Another misconception is that the Brier score is only appropriate when false-positive and false-negative costs are equal.
This confuses two different objectives. The true conditional probability \(P(Y=1\mid X=x)\) does not change merely because the costs of different decisions change. Rather, the optimal decision threshold changes.
For example, if false negatives cost nine times as much as false positives, the optimal classification threshold is \(0.1\), not \(0.5\).
A calibrated probability model can accommodate this change without necessarily being refitted. A classifier that outputs only hard labels generally cannot recover the information needed to adjust the threshold.
The central point is that proper scoring rules assess the quality of probability estimates, whereas classification metrics assess decisions made under a particular classification rule. Neither is a universal substitute for the other.




Calibration, Discrimination, and Predictive Performance
Two important aspects of probabilistic prediction are calibration and discrimination.

Calibration concerns agreement between predicted probabilities and observed event frequencies.
Discrimination concerns how well predictions distinguish observations with different outcomes.

Good discrimination does not imply good calibration. Conversely, a model that always predicts the marginal event probability may be calibrated in an aggregate sense while providing little individualized information.
Proper scoring rules provide an overall assessment of probabilistic predictive performance, rewarding both calibration and informative predictions. However, they should be supplemented by calibration diagnostics, comparisons against appropriate reference models, and out-of-sample evaluation.
Importantly, a model with a better average proper score need not yield better decisions under every possible loss function. Under model misspecification, restricted function classes, or finite samples, different scoring rules can favor different approximations to the true conditional distribution. A model optimized for a particular decision problem may outperform a globally better probability model for that specific decision.






Practical and Theoretical Limitations of Proper Scoring Rules



Although proper scoring rules have strong statistical foundations, several limitations are worth recognizing.

Some models output only decisions. Algorithms that produce hard class labels or directly learned policies may not provide meaningful probability estimates. A proper scoring rule cannot evaluate a full probabilistic forecast that the model does not produce. Classification-calibrated surrogate losses can nevertheless support consistent decision learning without requiring probability calibration.
Strict propriety is a population property. A strictly proper scoring rule is uniquely minimized by the true distribution when the prediction space is sufficiently rich. Under model misspecification or restricted model classes, minimizing different proper scores may yield different approximations.
Decision-specific performance may differ from predictive performance. When the action space and utility function are known, directly optimizing expected decision utility may be more efficient than estimating an entire predictive distribution. A lower Brier score or log-loss does not guarantee better performance for every downstream decision.
Rare events and distribution shifts complicate evaluation. Strict propriety does not eliminate finite-sample uncertainty, poor subgroup performance, model misspecification, or changes in the relationship between covariates and outcomes. Recalibration or model updating may be necessary when deploying predictions in a different population.
The target of prediction must be appropriate. Proper scoring rules evaluate predictions against observed outcomes. They do not establish causal identification, validate the scientific interpretation of predictors, or guarantee that observational predictions remain valid under interventions.

These limitations concern the choice of statistical target, model class, evaluation procedure, and decision problem, rather than undermining the mathematical justification for proper scoring rules.


Ultimately, a good probability model is not necessarily a good decision rule, and a good decision rule does not necessarily imply accurate probabilities. If the objective is probabilistic prediction, proper scoring rules provide a principled evaluation criterion. If the objective is a particular decision, performance should also be evaluated under the relevant loss or utility function.
The broader lesson is that statistical learning should begin by identifying what is being estimated or optimized. A benchmark metric is not automatically a scientifically meaningful estimand or a defensible decision objective merely because it is widely used.
Good predictive performance, moreover, does not establish that a model’s assumptions, interpretations, or causal conclusions are justified.
