title: Calculus
Calculus
Calculus
text:
Integration and Antiderivatives
Integration tells us how much of a function “accumulates” in a given area between the \(x\) axis and the function,



The area under \(f(x)=x^2\) from \(x=a\) to \(x=b\), the integral of \(f\) from \(a\) to \(b\)


The antiderivative (or indefinite integral) is the functional counterpart of this accumulation process, that is the integral is the actual area under the curve for a specified domain and the antiderivative/indefinite integral is the more general concept,






Definition (Indefinite Integral, Antiderivative)



Define \(A\) such that, \[
A(x) = \int_{a}^{x} f(t),\mathrm{d}t,
\] which by the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus satisfies, \[
A'(x) = f(x) \quad\text{and}\quad A(a)=0.
\] More generally, any function \(F\) whose derivative is \(f\) is called an antiderivative of \(f\), and we write \[
\int f(x),\mathrm{d}x = F(x) + C,
\] where \(C\) is an arbitrary constant. In this sense, integration “undoes” differentiation.


Integrals have several useful properties,






Theorem (Integration Rules)




Definite integral: for a continuous \(f\) on \([a,b]\), \[
\int_a^b f(x) \ dx
= F(b)-F(a),
\] where \(F'!=f\)
Antiderivative: \(F\) is any function with \(F'(x)=f(x)\).
Substitution rule: if \(u = g(x)\) is differentiable, \[\int f(g(x)),g'(x) \ dx
= \int f(u)du\]
Fundamental Theorem of Calculus: \[
\frac{d}{dx}\int_a^x f(t)dt = f(x),
\quad
\int_a^b f'(x) \ dx = f(b)-f(a).
\]









Example




Definite integral. Compute \[
\int_{0}^{2} 3x^2  \ dx
= \bigl[x^3\bigr]_{0}^{2}
= 8
\]
Antiderivative. For \(f(x)=\sin x\), an antiderivative is \[
F(x) = -\cos x + C,
\quad
F'(x)=\sin x
\]
Substitution rule. Evaluate \[
\int 2x,e^{x^2} \ dx
\] Let \(u = x^2\), so \(du = 2x \ dx\). Then \[
\int 2x,e^{x^2} \ dx
= \int e^udu
= e^u + C
= e^{x^2} + C
\]
Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.

Differentiation under the integral sign: \[
\frac{d}{dx}\int_{1}^{x} t^3dt
= x^3
\]
Definite integral of a derivative: \[
\int_{1}^{2} \frac{d}{dx}(x^3) \ dx
= \bigl[x^3\bigr]_{1}^{2}
= 8 - 1
= 7
\]










Remark



Unlike differentiation, integration is a global (non-local) operation and an inverse problem that need not admit an elementary closed-form. That is we may encounter integrals that are intractable analytically and instead must rely on numerical techniques to approximate them

title: Calculus
section: Function Approximation, Taylor’s Theorem, and Little-\(o\)/Big-\(O\) Notation
text:
Function Approximation, Taylor’s Theorem, and Little-\(o\)/Big-\(O\) Notation
A function may be difficult to work with directly, but near a chosen point we can often replace it by a simpler linear or quadratic expression. In statistics, this lets us approximate a transformed estimator or solve an estimating equation. We begin with an exact identity and then identify the approximation error.






Theorem (Exact Taylor representation)



Suppose \(f\) is continuously differentiable on an interval containing \(a\) and \(x\). The fundamental theorem of calculus gives
\[
f(x)-f(a)=\int_a^x f'(t)\,dt.
\]
For \(x\ne a\), dividing by \(x-a\),
\[
\frac{f(x)-f(a)}{x-a}
=
\frac{1}{x-a}\int_a^x f'(t)\,dt.
\]
The left-hand side is the secant slope between the points \((a,f(a))\) and \((x,f(x))\), while the right-hand side is the average of the tangent slopes \(f'(t)\) over the interval from \(a\) to \(x\). Thus,
\[
\boxed{
\text{secant slope}
=
\text{average tangent slope over the interval}.
}
\]
Equivalently, using the change of variables \(t=a+s(x-a)\) for \(s\in[0,1],\)
\[
f(x)
=
f(a)
+
(x-a)
\left[
\frac{1}{x-a}\int_a^x f'(t)\,dt
\right]=f(a)
+
(x-a)
\int_0^1
f'\bigl(a+s(x-a)\bigr)\,ds
\]
This is the exact Taylor representation of \(f(x)\) about \(x=a\), asserting the exact change in \(f\) is the distance \(x-a\) multiplied by the average derivative encountered while moving from \(a\) to \(x\).








Theorem (First-order Taylor approximation)



The first-order Taylor approximation is found by adding and subtracting \(f'(a)\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(x)
&=
f(a)
+
f'(a)(x-a)-f'(a)(x-a) +
(x-a)
\int_0^1
\left[
f'\bigl(a+s(x-a)\bigr)
\right]ds.
\\
&=f(a)
+
f'(a)(x-a)+
(x-a)
\int_0^1
\left[
f'\bigl(a+s(x-a)\bigr)-f'(a)
\right]ds.
\end{aligned}
\]
Hence
\[
f(x)
=
f(a)+f'(a)(x-a)+R(x,a),
\]
where the exact remainder is
\[
R(x,a)
=
(x-a)
\int_0^1
\left[
f'\bigl(a+s(x-a)\bigr)-f'(a)
\right]ds.
\]
If \(f'\) is continuous at \(a\), then as \(x\to a\),
\[
f'\bigl(a+s(x-a)\bigr)\to f'(a)
\]
uniformly over \(s\in[0,1]\). Therefore,
\[
\frac{R(x,a)}{|x-a|}
\to 0.
\]
This is written
\[
R(x,a)=o(|x-a|),
\]
so that
\[
\boxed{
f(x)
=
f(a)+f'(a)(x-a)+o(|x-a|).
}
\]
Thus the first-order Taylor approximation means that the error is negligible relative to the size of \(x-a\).








Theorem (Higher-order Taylor expansion)



More generally, if \(f\) has \(k\) continuous derivatives near \(a\), Taylor’s theorem gives
\[
f(x)
=
f(a)
+
f'(a)(x-a)
+
\frac{f''(a)}{2!}(x-a)^2
+\cdots+
\frac{f^{(k)}(a)}{k!}(x-a)^k
+
R_k(x,a).
\]
As \(x\to a\),
\[
R_k(x,a)=o(|x-a|^k).
\]
For example,
\[
f(x)
=
f(a)+f'(a)(x-a)+O((x-a)^2)
\]
when the second derivative is locally bounded.





xkcd #2605: Taylor Series


To describe how these errors shrink as the expansion point is approached, we use order notation.

Big-\(O\) notation






Definition (Big-O notation)



For deterministic functions \(r(x)\) and \(g(x)>0\), we write
\[
r(x)=O(g(x))
\qquad\text{as }x\to a
\]
if there exists a finite constant \(C\) such that, for all \(x\) sufficiently close to \(a\),
\[
|r(x)|\le C g(x).
\]
Thus \(O(g(x))\) means that \(r(x)\) is at most of the same order as \(g(x)\).
Equivalently,
\[
\frac{r(x)}{g(x)}
\]
remains bounded as \(x\to a\).








Example (A quadratic term is bounded by a linear rate)



For example,
\[
(x-a)^2=O(|x-a|)
\]
as \(x\to a\), because for \(x\) sufficiently close to \(a\),
\[
\frac{(x-a)^2}{|x-a|}
=
|x-a|
\]
is bounded.




Little-\(o\) notation






Definition (Little-o notation)



We write
\[
r(x)=o(g(x))
\qquad\text{as }x\to a
\]
if
\[
\frac{r(x)}{g(x)}\to0.
\]
Thus \(o(g(x))\) means that \(r(x)\) is asymptotically negligible relative to \(g(x)\).








Example (Negligible versus bounded error)



For example,
\[
(x-a)^2=o(|x-a|)
\]
because
\[
\frac{(x-a)^2}{|x-a|}
=
|x-a|
\to0.
\]
The distinction is therefore
\[
r(x)=O(g(x))
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\frac{r(x)}{g(x)}
\text{ is bounded},
\]
whereas
\[
r(x)=o(g(x))
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\frac{r(x)}{g(x)}
\to0.
\]
In particular,
\[
o(g(x))\subset O(g(x)),
\]
in the sense that every term that is little-\(o\) of \(g(x)\) is also big-\(O\) of \(g(x)\), but not conversely.


Taylor expansions are useful precisely because they separate a function into a leading term and a remainder whose order can be controlled. For example,
\[
f(x)-f(a)
=
f'(a)(x-a)
+
o(|x-a|)
\]
says that, when \(f'(a)\ne0\), the linear term gives the leading change in \(f\). If \(f'(a)=0\), a higher-order term may determine the leading behavior. Dividing through by \(x-a\),
\[
\frac{f(x)-f(a)}{x-a}
=
f'(a)+o(1),
\]
which recovers the statement that the secant slope converges to the tangent slope.

title: Calculus
text:
PErron frobenius and iteration
I NEED TO START THIS WITH DEFINING THE MULTIVARIABLE CHAIN RULE
The single-variable setup applies when we vary one scalar input or parameter. Many statistical problems involve several parameters, even when each response is univariate. When an observation has \(p\) characteristics/covariates, we arrange them into a vector
\[
\mathbf X_i
=\begin{bmatrix}
X_{i1},
X_{i2},
\cdots,
X_{ip}
\end{bmatrix}^\top
\in\mathbb R^p.
\]
In parametric statistics, the corresponding model parameters are arranged into the coefficient vector
\[
\boldsymbol\beta
=\begin{bmatrix}
\beta_1,
\beta_2,
\cdots,
\beta_p
\end{bmatrix}^\top
\in\mathbb R^p.
\]
Generally, parametric statistical estimation involves a scalar-valued criterion function indexed by a finite-dimensional parameter vector,
\[
Q:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R,
\]
where
\[
Q(\boldsymbol\beta)
=Q(\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_p),
\qquad
\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^p.
\]
The criterion function \(Q\) may represent a log-likelihood, negative log-likelihood, loss function, posterior log density, or another estimating criterion. Although \(Q(\boldsymbol\beta)\) returns a single scalar value, it may depend jointly on all components of \(\boldsymbol\beta\) and need not separate into coordinate-specific terms.
Statistical estimation then proceeds by optimizing \(Q(\boldsymbol\beta)\) with respect to the parameter vector \(\boldsymbol\beta\). The derivative becomes a vector because there is now one direction of change for each coordinate.






Definition (Gradient)



The gradient of \(Q\) is the vector of componentwise partial derivatives,
\[
\nabla_{\boldsymbol\beta}Q(\boldsymbol\beta)
=\begin{bmatrix}
\displaystyle \frac{\partial Q(\boldsymbol\beta)}{\partial\beta_1}\\
\displaystyle \frac{\partial Q(\boldsymbol\beta)}{\partial\beta_2}\\
\vdots\\
\displaystyle \frac{\partial Q(\boldsymbol\beta)}{\partial\beta_p}
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Each component gives the rate of change of \(Q\) as one parameter \(\beta_j\) varies while the remaining parameters are held fixed.








Example: linear functions



Consider the scalar-valued linear function
\[
Q(\mathbf X,\boldsymbol\beta)
=\mathbf X^\top\boldsymbol\beta
=X_1\beta_1+X_2\beta_2+\cdots+X_p\beta_p.
\]
The gradient with respect to \(\boldsymbol\beta\) is
\[
\nabla_{\boldsymbol\beta}
Q(\mathbf X,\boldsymbol\beta)
=\begin{bmatrix}
\displaystyle \frac{\partial Q}{\partial\beta_1}\\
\displaystyle \frac{\partial Q}{\partial\beta_2}\\
\vdots\\
\displaystyle \frac{\partial Q}{\partial\beta_p}
\end{bmatrix}
=\begin{bmatrix}
X_1\\
X_2\\
\vdots\\
X_p
\end{bmatrix}
=\mathbf X.
\]
Similarly, the gradient with respect to \(\mathbf X\) is
\[
\nabla_{\mathbf X}
Q(\mathbf X,\boldsymbol\beta)
=\begin{bmatrix}
\displaystyle \frac{\partial Q}{\partial X_1}\\
\displaystyle \frac{\partial Q}{\partial X_2}\\
\vdots\\
\displaystyle \frac{\partial Q}{\partial X_p}
\end{bmatrix}
=\begin{bmatrix}
\beta_1\\
\beta_2\\
\vdots\\
\beta_p
\end{bmatrix}
=\boldsymbol\beta.
\]
Thus, the derivative of \(\mathbf X^\top\boldsymbol\beta\) with respect to one vector is the other vector.








Theorem (First-order condition)



To estimate \(\boldsymbol\beta\), we generally solve for all components simultaneously. For an unconstrained interior optimum, the first-order condition is
\[
\nabla_{\boldsymbol\beta}Q(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})
=\mathbf 0
\]
This gives a system of \(p\) equations in the \(p\) unknown components of \(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}\).








Definition (Hessian)



As in single-variable optimization, the first-order condition identifies stationary points. Their local curvature is described by the Hessian,
\[
H_Q(\boldsymbol\beta)
=\nabla_{\boldsymbol\beta}^2Q(\boldsymbol\beta)
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\displaystyle \frac{\partial^2Q}{\partial\beta_1^2}
&
\cdots
&
\displaystyle \frac{\partial^2Q}{\partial\beta_1\partial\beta_p}
\\
\vdots
&
\ddots
&
\vdots
\\
\displaystyle \frac{\partial^2Q}{\partial\beta_p\partial\beta_1}
&
\cdots
&
\displaystyle \frac{\partial^2Q}{\partial\beta_p^2}
\end{bmatrix}.
\]








Theorem (Curvature and optimization)



Suppose \(Q\) is twice continuously differentiable near a stationary point \(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}\). Then,
\[
\begin{aligned}
H_Q(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})\text{ positive definite}
&\implies
\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}\text{ is a strict local minimum},\\
H_Q(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})\text{ negative definite}
&\implies
\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}\text{ is a strict local maximum},\\
H_Q(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})\text{ indefinite}
&\implies
\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}\text{ is a saddle point}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Here positive definiteness means \(\mathbf v^\top H_Q\mathbf v>0\) for every nonzero \(\mathbf v\); negative definiteness reverses the inequality. An indefinite Hessian gives positive curvature in some directions and negative curvature in others. A semidefinite Hessian alone does not settle the classification.
More globally, on an open convex domain, if \(Q\) is convex, any stationary point is a global minimum. If \(Q\) is strictly convex, that minimum is unique. Similarly, if \(Q\) is concave, any stationary point is a global maximum, and strict concavity gives uniqueness.








Example (Least-squares curvature)



For \(Q(\boldsymbol\beta)=\tfrac12\|\mathbf Y-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta\|^2\),
\[
\nabla Q(\boldsymbol\beta)=\mathbf X^\top(\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta-\mathbf Y),
\qquad H_Q(\boldsymbol\beta)=\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X.
\]
For any vector \(\mathbf v\),
\[
\mathbf v^\top H_Q\mathbf v=\|\mathbf X\mathbf v\|^2\ge0.
\]
Thus the criterion is convex. If \(\mathbf X\) has full column rank, the Hessian is positive definite and the least-squares solution is unique. This is the multivariable version of a bowl-shaped quadratic.


In statistics, whether we maximize or minimize depends on the criterion. We maximize a log-likelihood or log-posterior, for which negative curvature is desirable, and minimize a loss or negative log-likelihood, for which positive curvature is desirable.
Thus, in statistical applications, the usual sequence is
\[
\text{scalar log-likelihood}
\quad\longrightarrow\quad
\text{gradient or score vector}
\quad\longrightarrow\quad
\text{Jacobian of the score}
=\text{Hessian}.
\]
The score helps characterize the estimator through a first-order condition, while the Hessian describes the local curvature of the criterion function and, under standard likelihood regularity conditions, provides an approximation to the estimator’s uncertainty.
In many statistical models, the score equation
\[
\mathbf U_n(\boldsymbol\beta)
=\mathbf 0
\]
cannot be solved explicitly. We therefore use Taylor expansions to approximate the score or log-likelihood near a convenient point. In asymptotic statistics, this point is often the true parameter \(\boldsymbol\beta_0\).
As the number of observations \(n\) increases, the score and Hessian accumulate information across observations. In the usual fixed-dimensional parametric setting, the dimension \(p\) of \(\boldsymbol\beta\) remains fixed while \(n\to\infty\). Taylor’s theorem, together with probabilistic order notation, allows us to show that the approximation error becomes negligible relative to the leading terms.

title: Calculus
section: Function Approximation, Taylor’s Theorem, and Little-\(o\)/Big-\(O\) Notation
text:
Function Approximation, Taylor’s Theorem, and Little-\(o\)/Big-\(O\) Notation
Write \(\mathbf h\) for a small displacement in parameter space and \(\|\mathbf h\|=(\sum_{j=1}^p h_j^2)^{1/2}\) for its Euclidean length. The scalar displacement \(x-a\) is now replaced by this vector.






Theorem (Multivariable Taylor expansion)



For a differentiable scalar-valued function
\[
Q:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R,
\]
a first-order Taylor expansion around a point \(\boldsymbol\beta_0\) is
\[
Q(\boldsymbol\beta_0+\mathbf h)
=Q(\boldsymbol\beta_0)
+
\nabla Q(\boldsymbol\beta_0)^\top\mathbf h
+
r_1(\mathbf h),
\]
where the remainder satisfies
\[
r_1(\mathbf h)
=o(\|\mathbf h\|)
\]
as \(\|\mathbf h\|\to0\). Equivalently,
\[
\frac{r_1(\mathbf h)}{\|\mathbf h\|}
\to0.
\]
Thus, sufficiently close to \(\boldsymbol\beta_0\), the function is approximately linear:
\[
Q(\boldsymbol\beta_0+\mathbf h)
\approx
Q(\boldsymbol\beta_0)
+
\nabla Q(\boldsymbol\beta_0)^\top\mathbf h.
\]
If \(Q\) is twice continuously differentiable, then the second-order Taylor expansion is
\[
Q(\boldsymbol\beta_0+\mathbf h)
=Q(\boldsymbol\beta_0)
+
\nabla Q(\boldsymbol\beta_0)^\top\mathbf h
+
\frac{1}{2}
\mathbf h^\top
H_Q(\boldsymbol\beta_0)
\mathbf h
+
r_2(\mathbf h),
\]
where
\[
r_2(\mathbf h)
=o(\|\mathbf h\|^2).
\]
The linear term describes the local slope, while the quadratic term describes the local curvature.








Definition (Order notation for vector displacements)



The notation
\[
r(\mathbf h)=o(\|\mathbf h\|^k)
\]
means that the remainder is asymptotically negligible relative to \(\|\mathbf h\|^k\):
\[
\frac{r(\mathbf h)}{\|\mathbf h\|^k}
\to0.
\]
By contrast,
\[
r(\mathbf h)=O(\|\mathbf h\|^k)
\]
means that the remainder is bounded in magnitude by a constant multiple of \(\|\mathbf h\|^k\) sufficiently close to zero. That is, there exist constants \(C<\infty\) and \(\delta>0\) such that
\[
|r(\mathbf h)|
\le
C\|\mathbf h\|^k
\]
whenever \(\|\mathbf h\|<\delta\).
Thus, little-\(o\) indicates negligibility relative to a reference rate, whereas big-\(O\) indicates boundedness at that rate.


We now apply these derivatives to likelihood-based estimation.






Definition (Score and information)



For \(n\) independent observations, the log-likelihood can be written as
\[
\ell_n(\boldsymbol\beta)
=\sum_{i=1}^n
\ell_i(\boldsymbol\beta).
\]
Because \(\ell_n(\boldsymbol\beta)\) is scalar-valued, its gradient with respect to \(\boldsymbol\beta\) is the vector of first-order partial derivatives,
\[
\nabla_{\boldsymbol\beta}\ell_n(\boldsymbol\beta)
=\begin{bmatrix}
\displaystyle \frac{\partial\ell_n(\boldsymbol\beta)}{\partial\beta_1}\\
\displaystyle \frac{\partial\ell_n(\boldsymbol\beta)}{\partial\beta_2}\\
\vdots\\
\displaystyle \frac{\partial\ell_n(\boldsymbol\beta)}{\partial\beta_p}
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
In likelihood-based inference, this gradient is called the score vector,
\[
\mathbf U_n(\boldsymbol\beta)
=\nabla_{\boldsymbol\beta}\ell_n(\boldsymbol\beta).
\]
Each component of the score measures how the log-likelihood changes when one parameter varies while the remaining parameters are held fixed. The maximum likelihood estimator is often characterized by the first-order condition
\[
\mathbf U_n(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})
=\nabla_{\boldsymbol\beta}
\ell_n(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})
=\mathbf 0
\]
Since the score is a vector-valued function,
\[
\mathbf U_n:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R^p,
\]
it has a Jacobian. The Jacobian of the score is the Hessian of the log-likelihood:
\[
H_n(\boldsymbol\beta)
=\nabla_{\boldsymbol\beta}^2
\ell_n(\boldsymbol\beta)
=J_{\mathbf U_n}(\boldsymbol\beta).
\]
Its entries are the second-order partial derivatives,
\[
H_n(\boldsymbol\beta)
=\begin{bmatrix}
\displaystyle \frac{\partial^2\ell_n}{\partial\beta_1^2}
&
\displaystyle \frac{\partial^2\ell_n}{\partial\beta_1\partial\beta_2}
&
\cdots
&
\displaystyle \frac{\partial^2\ell_n}{\partial\beta_1\partial\beta_p}
\\
\displaystyle \frac{\partial^2\ell_n}{\partial\beta_2\partial\beta_1}
&
\displaystyle \frac{\partial^2\ell_n}{\partial\beta_2^2}
&
\cdots
&
\displaystyle \frac{\partial^2\ell_n}{\partial\beta_2\partial\beta_p}
\\
\vdots
&
\vdots
&
\ddots
&
\vdots
\\
\displaystyle \frac{\partial^2\ell_n}{\partial\beta_p\partial\beta_1}
&
\displaystyle \frac{\partial^2\ell_n}{\partial\beta_p\partial\beta_2}
&
\cdots
&
\displaystyle \frac{\partial^2\ell_n}{\partial\beta_p^2}
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
The Hessian describes the local curvature of the log-likelihood with respect to the parameter vector. For a perturbation \(\mathbf h\), the second-order Taylor expansion is
\[
\ell_n(\boldsymbol\beta+\mathbf h)
=\ell_n(\boldsymbol\beta)
+
\mathbf U_n(\boldsymbol\beta)^\top\mathbf h
+
\frac{1}{2}
\mathbf h^\top
H_n(\boldsymbol\beta)
\mathbf h
+
o(\|\mathbf h\|^2).
\]
Near a maximum likelihood estimator, the log-likelihood typically curves downward, so the Hessian is negative definite or negative semidefinite. Equivalently, the negative Hessian,
\[
-\nabla_{\boldsymbol\beta}^2
\ell_n(\boldsymbol\beta),
\]
is positive definite or positive semidefinite.
This negative curvature matrix is central to statistical inference. The observed information matrix is
\[
\mathcal J_n(\boldsymbol\beta)
=-\nabla_{\boldsymbol\beta}^2
\ell_n(\boldsymbol\beta),
\]
under the usual regularity conditions, the Fisher information matrix is
\[
\mathcal I_n(\boldsymbol\beta)
=-E_{\boldsymbol\beta}
\left[
\nabla_{\boldsymbol\beta}^2
\ell_n(\boldsymbol\beta)
\right].
\]


The score equation is vector-valued, so its exact expansion uses the Jacobian integrated along the line segment between the two parameter values. In general, there need not be a single intermediate point that works for every component.






Theorem (Exact score expansion and MLE approximation)



Suppose the log-likelihood is twice continuously differentiable along the segment from \(\boldsymbol\beta_0\) to an interior MLE \(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}\). Define
\[
\overline H_n
=\int_0^1 H_n\bigl(\boldsymbol\beta_0+t(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}-\boldsymbol\beta_0)\bigr)\,dt.
\]
Applying the exact Taylor representation componentwise to the score gives
\[
\mathbf 0=\mathbf U_n(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})
=\mathbf U_n(\boldsymbol\beta_0)
+\overline H_n(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}-\boldsymbol\beta_0).
\]
If \(\overline H_n\) is invertible, rearranging yields
\[
\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}-\boldsymbol\beta_0
=-\overline H_n^{-1}\mathbf U_n(\boldsymbol\beta_0).
\]
Multiplying by \(\sqrt n\) and rescaling gives
\[
\sqrt n(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}-\boldsymbol\beta_0)
=\left[-\frac{1}{n}\overline H_n\right]^{-1}
\frac{1}{\sqrt n}\mathbf U_n(\boldsymbol\beta_0).
\]
For a correctly specified, regular i.i.d. model with fixed parameter dimension, the two main asymptotic ingredients are
\[
\frac{1}{\sqrt n}\mathbf U_n(\boldsymbol\beta_0)
\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}
N\bigl(\mathbf 0,\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\beta_0)\bigr)
\]
and
\[
-\frac{1}{n}\overline H_n
\overset{p}{\longrightarrow}\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\beta_0),
\]
where \(\mathcal I\) is the information per observation and is assumed positive definite. The first convergence follows from a multivariate central limit theorem for the score; the second requires consistency and suitable local uniform control of the Hessian, not just a pointwise law of large numbers.
Slutsky’s theorem then gives
\[
\sqrt n
\left(
\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}
-\boldsymbol\beta_0
\right)
\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}
N\left(
\mathbf 0,
\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\beta_0)^{-1}
\right).
\]
Therefore,
\[
\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}
\approx
N\left(
\boldsymbol\beta_0,
\frac{1}{n}
\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\beta_0)^{-1}
\right)
\]
for large \(n\). With the additional moment conditions needed to approximate variances,
\[
\operatorname{Var}
\left(
\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}
\right)
\approx
\mathcal I_n(\boldsymbol\beta_0)^{-1}.
\]
Thus, Taylor expansion converts the nonlinear score equation into an approximately linear equation, while asymptotic arguments control the approximation error and determine the limiting distribution of the estimator.








Example (Normal mean: an exact score expansion)



Let \(X_i\) be i.i.d. \(N(\mu,\sigma^2)\) with known \(\sigma^2\). Then
\[
U_n(\mu)=\frac{n}{\sigma^2}(\bar X-\mu),
\qquad H_n(\mu)=-\frac{n}{\sigma^2}.
\]
The Hessian is constant, so the score expansion gives exactly
\[
\widehat\mu-\mu_0
=-\left(-\frac{n}{\sigma^2}\right)^{-1}
\frac{n}{\sigma^2}(\bar X-\mu_0)
=\bar X-\mu_0.
\]
Here \(\mathcal I_n=n/\sigma^2\), and its inverse \(\sigma^2/n\) is the exact variance of \(\widehat\mu=\bar X\).

title: Calculus
text:
Directional Derivatives
Suppose we wanted to describe the rate of change of a function in an arbitrary direction in its input or parameter space. Partial derivatives describe this rate along the coordinate directions: each varies one coordinate while holding the others fixed. A directional derivative allows several coordinates to change together, in proportions specified by a direction vector.
To define it, start at \(\boldsymbol\beta\) and move along a unit vector \(\mathbf v\). The perturbed input is \(\boldsymbol\beta+t\mathbf v\), where \(t\) is the signed distance moved. Applying the usual derivative definition to this one-dimensional path gives the directional derivative.






Definition (Directional derivative and gradient)



For a differentiable function \(Q:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R\) and a unit vector \(\mathbf v=(v_1,\ldots,v_p)^\top\), the directional derivative at \(\boldsymbol\beta\) is
\[
D_{\mathbf v}Q(\boldsymbol\beta)
\equiv
\lim_{t\to0}
\frac{Q(\boldsymbol\beta+t\mathbf v)-Q(\boldsymbol\beta)}{t}
=
\left.\frac{d}{dt}Q(\boldsymbol\beta+t\mathbf v)\right|_{t=0}.
\]
Along this path, coordinate \(j\) changes at rate \(v_j\). By the chain rule,
\[
D_{\mathbf v}Q(\boldsymbol\beta)
=
\sum_{j=1}^p
\frac{\partial Q(\boldsymbol\beta)}{\partial\beta_j}\,v_j.
\]
Thus, the directional derivative is a sum of partial derivatives, each multiplied by the rate at which its coordinate changes. Collecting the partial derivatives into a vector defines the gradient:
\[
\nabla Q(\boldsymbol\beta)
\equiv
\begin{pmatrix}
\frac{\partial Q(\boldsymbol\beta)}{\partial\beta_1}\\
\vdots\\
\frac{\partial Q(\boldsymbol\beta)}{\partial\beta_p}
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The directional derivative is therefore the inner product
\[
D_{\mathbf v}Q(\boldsymbol\beta)
=
\nabla Q(\boldsymbol\beta)^\top\mathbf v.
\]
Choosing \(\mathbf v=\mathbf e_j\), the \(j\)th coordinate unit vector, recovers the \(j\)th partial derivative. More generally, the gradient determines the slope in every direction. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality,
\[
D_{\mathbf v}Q(\boldsymbol\beta)
\leq
\|\nabla Q(\boldsymbol\beta)\|\,\|\mathbf v\|
=
\|\nabla Q(\boldsymbol\beta)\|.
\]
When the gradient is nonzero, equality holds for \(\mathbf v=\nabla Q(\boldsymbol\beta)/\|\nabla Q(\boldsymbol\beta)\|\). The gradient therefore points in the direction of greatest local increase, and its norm gives that maximum rate of increase.








Example (Normal Scores)



Suppose \[
X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2),
\] where \(\mu\) is the target and \(\sigma^2\) is the nuisance. Write \(v=\sigma^2\) to simplify the notation.
A path through this model is \[
\mu_t=\mu+ta,\qquad v_t=v+tb.
\] The vector \((a,b)\) specifies the direction: how quickly the mean and variance change. For sufficiently small \(|t|\), the variance remains positive.
The log density is \[
\log p_{\mu,v}(x)
=
-\frac12\log(2\pi v)-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2v}.
\]
Applying the directional-derivative formula gives \[
\begin{aligned}
s_{a,b}(x)
&=\left.\frac{d}{dt}\log p_{\mu+ta,v+tb}(x)\right|_{t=0}\\
&=a\frac{\partial\log p_{\mu,v}(x)}{\partial\mu}
+b\frac{\partial\log p_{\mu,v}(x)}{\partial v}\\
&=a\underbrace{\frac{x-\mu}{v}}_{\text{mean score}}
+b\underbrace{\frac{(x-\mu)^2-v}{2v^2}}_{\text{variance score}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
To recover the usual normal scores set either \((1,0)\) or \((0,1)\)

title: Calculus
section: A Statisticians Best Friend: Quadratic Forms, the “sandwich” pattern and going from a matrix toa shape

title: Calculus
text:
Optimization






Definition (Likelihood and maximum likelihood estimation)



In statistical inference, we typically assume we have observed data points \(x_1,\dots,x_n\) that are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) from a common probability density function \(f(x;\theta)\), where \(\theta\) is an unknown parameter (or vector of parameters). Under the i.i.d. assumption, the joint density of the sample is \[
L(\theta)
= \prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i;\theta),
\] which we refer to as the likelihood function. To estimate \(\theta\), we select the value \(\hat\theta\) that maximizes this joint density:
\[
\hat\theta
= \arg\max_{\theta} L(\theta),
\] or equivalently, since the logarithm is a strictly increasing function, \[
\hat\theta
= \arg\max_{\theta} \ell(\theta),
\quad
\ell(\theta)
= \sum_{i=1}^n \log f(x_i;\theta).
\] This procedure is known as the maximum likelihood estimator (MLE).








Remark



MLE is nothing more than the optimization from regular calculus, but now maximizing the above \(L(\theta)\), or equivalently \(\ell(\theta)\), with respect to \(\theta\). Therefore we must also check concavity and boundary behavior (if it exists)


R can make this maximization relatively easy using the optim function, (whose default is minimization so for maximum likelihood we equivalently minimize the negative log-likelihood,)

# normal one dim (in x) MLE through optim
ll = function(par, data){
  return(-(length(data)/2)*log(2*pi*par[2]^2) 
         - sum((data-par[1])^2)/(2*par[2]^2))}

nll = function(par,data){
  return(-ll(par,data))}

# simulate observed data from standard normal
dat_obs = rnorm(1000, mean=0,sd=1)

# optim
## initialization 
init_par = c(0,3)
## actual optimization
fit = optim(par = init_par, fn = nll, data = dat_obs)
stringr::str_c("MLE theta/mean: ", round(fit$par[1],4), 
               "  MLE sigma/sd: ", round(fit$par[2],4))

[1] "MLE theta/mean: -0.0486  MLE sigma/sd: 0.9849"



Closed-Form Maximum Likelihood Estimation
Some maximum likelihood estimators can be obtained directly by differentiating the log-likelihood, setting the resulting score equation equal to zero, and solving analytically for the unknown parameter.






Example (Normal regression and ordinary least squares)



For example, consider the normal linear regression model
\[
Y_i\mid X_i
\sim
N(X_i^\top\beta,\sigma^2),
\]
or, in matrix form,
\[
\mathbf Y\mid \mathbf X
\sim
N_n(\mathbf X\beta,\sigma^2\mathbf I_n),
\]
where \(\mathbf X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}\). The likelihood for \(\beta\) is
\[
L(\beta;\mathbf Y,\mathbf X)
=\prod_{i=1}^n
(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-1/2}
\exp\left\{
-\frac{(Y_i-X_i^\top\beta)^2}{2\sigma^2}
\right\},
\]
and the corresponding log-likelihood is
\[
\ell(\beta;\mathbf Y,\mathbf X)
=\sum_{i=1}^n
\left[
-\frac{1}{2}\log(2\pi\sigma^2)
-\frac{(Y_i-X_i^\top\beta)^2}{2\sigma^2}
\right]
\]
Equivalently, using matrix notation,
\[
\ell(\beta;\mathbf Y,\mathbf X)
=-\frac{n}{2}\log(2\pi\sigma^2)
-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}
(\mathbf Y-\mathbf X\beta)^\top
(\mathbf Y-\mathbf X\beta).
\]
Differentiating with respect to \(\beta\) gives the score vector
\[
s(\beta)
=\frac{\partial\ell(\beta)}{\partial\beta}
=\frac{1}{\sigma^2}
\mathbf X^\top
(\mathbf Y-\mathbf X\beta).
\]
Setting the score equal to zero yields the normal equations,
\[
\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X\beta
=\mathbf X^\top\mathbf Y.
\]
Provided that \(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X\) is invertible, the maximum likelihood estimator is therefore
\[
\widehat\beta_{\mathrm{OLS}}
=(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf X)^{-1}
\mathbf X^\top\mathbf Y.
\]








Example (Generalized least squares)



More generally, suppose the errors are correlated or have unequal variances, so that
\[
\mathbf Y\mid\mathbf X
\sim
N_n(\mathbf X\beta,\boldsymbol\Sigma),
\]
where \(\boldsymbol\Sigma\) is a known positive-definite covariance matrix that need not be diagonal. The log-likelihood is then, up to terms not involving \(\beta\),
\[
\ell(\beta)
=-\frac{1}{2}
(\mathbf Y-\mathbf X\beta)^\top
\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}
(\mathbf Y-\mathbf X\beta),
\]
with score vector
\[
s(\beta)=\nabla \ell(\beta)
=\mathbf X^\top
\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}
(\mathbf Y-\mathbf X\beta).
\]
Setting this score equal to zero gives the generalized least-squares estimator
\[
\widehat\beta_{\mathrm{GLS}}
=\left(
\mathbf X^\top
\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}
\mathbf X
\right)^{-1}
\mathbf X^\top
\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}
\mathbf Y.
\]
Ordinary least squares is the special case in which
\[
\boldsymbol\Sigma=\sigma^2\mathbf I_n.
\]


Thus, although these estimators require matrix calculations, they can be obtained in a single analytical step rather than through an iterative numerical optimization procedure.


Iterative Maximum Likelihood Estimation
Many likelihoods do not yield closed-form estimators and must instead be maximized iteratively. Logistic regression provides an important example.






Example (Logistic regression score)



Suppose
\[
Y_i\mid X_i
\sim
\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p_i),
\]
with the logit link
\[
\log\left(\frac{p_i}{1-p_i}\right)
=X_i^\top\beta.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
p_i(\beta)
=\frac{\exp(X_i^\top\beta)}
{1+\exp(X_i^\top\beta)}.
\]
The likelihood for \(\beta\) is therefore
\[
L(\beta)
=\prod_{i=1}^n
p_i(\beta)^{Y_i}
{1-p_i(\beta)}^{1-Y_i},
\]
and the corresponding log-likelihood is
\[
\ell(\beta)
=\sum_{i=1}^n
\left[
Y_iX_i^\top\beta
-\log\left\{
1+\exp(X_i^\top\beta)
\right\}
\right].
\]
Differentiating with respect to \(\beta\) gives the score vector,
\[
\begin{aligned}
s(\beta)
=\frac{\partial\ell(\beta)}{\partial\beta}
&=
\sum_{i=1}^n
\left[
Y_iX_i
-\frac{X_i\exp(X_i^\top\beta)}
{1+\exp(X_i^\top\beta)}
\right]
\\
&=
\sum_{i=1}^n
X_i{Y_i-p_i(\beta)}.
\end{aligned}
\]
In matrix notation, this is
\[
s(\beta)
=\mathbf X^\top
{\mathbf Y-\mathbf p(\beta)}.
\]
We want to choose \(\beta\) so that
\[
s(\beta)=0.
\]
Unlike the normal linear-model score equation, however, this equation is nonlinear in \(\beta\) because \(\mathbf p(\beta)\) depends nonlinearly on \(\beta\). It therefore cannot generally be rearranged to produce an explicit formula for \(\widehat\beta\).








Theorem (Newton–Raphson for logistic regression)



Instead, we begin with an initial estimate \(\beta^{(0)}\), approximate the score or log-likelihood locally, update the estimate, and repeat until the estimates stabilize. Newton–Raphson uses both the score and the Hessian. For logistic regression, the Hessian is
\[
H(\beta)
=\frac{\partial^2\ell(\beta)}
{\partial\beta\partial\beta^\top}
=-\mathbf X^\top
\mathbf W(\beta)
\mathbf X,
\]
where
\[
\mathbf W(\beta)
=\operatorname{diag}
\left\{
p_i(\beta)
\bigl[1-p_i(\beta)\bigr]
\right\}_{i=1}^n.
\]
The Newton–Raphson update is therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
\beta^{(t+1)}
&=
\beta^{(t)}
-H\left(\beta^{(t)}\right)^{-1}
s\left(\beta^{(t)}\right)
\\
&=
\beta^{(t)}
+
\left(
\mathbf X^\top
\mathbf W^{(t)}
\mathbf X
\right)^{-1}
\mathbf X^\top
\left(
\mathbf Y-\mathbf p^{(t)}
\right),
\end{aligned}
\]
where
\[
\mathbf p^{(t)}
=\mathbf p\left(\beta^{(t)}\right)
\]
and
\[
\mathbf W^{(t)}
=\mathbf W\left(\beta^{(t)}\right).
\]
For logistic regression, the negative Hessian is also the Fisher information matrix because it does not depend directly on the observed values of \(\mathbf Y\). Thus, Newton–Raphson and Fisher scoring produce the same update.








Remark (Iteratively reweighted least squares)



This update can be rewritten as a weighted least-squares problem. Define the current linear predictor
\[
\boldsymbol\eta^{(t)}
=\mathbf X\beta^{(t)}
\]
and the working response
\[
\mathbf z^{(t)}
=\boldsymbol\eta^{(t)}
+
\left(\mathbf W^{(t)}\right)^{-1}
\left(
\mathbf Y-\mathbf p^{(t)}
\right).
\]
Then the next estimate satisfies
\[
\beta^{(t+1)}
=\left(
\mathbf X^\top
\mathbf W^{(t)}
\mathbf X
\right)^{-1}
\mathbf X^\top
\mathbf W^{(t)}
\mathbf z^{(t)}.
\]
This has exactly the form of a weighted least-squares estimator. The procedure is therefore called iteratively reweighted least squares, or IRLS:

Use the current estimate \(\beta^{(t)}\) to calculate the fitted probabilities \(\mathbf p^{(t)}\).
Use those probabilities to calculate the weights \(\mathbf W^{(t)}\) and working response \(\mathbf z^{(t)}\).
Regress the working response on \(\mathbf X\) using weighted least squares.
Repeat until the estimates change negligibly.

The intuition is that logistic regression is nonlinear globally but can be approximated locally by a weighted linear regression. At each iteration, the algorithm constructs a temporary linear-regression problem around the current estimate. The weights are updated because the Bernoulli variance,
\[
p_i(\beta){1-p_i(\beta)},
\]
depends on the current fitted probability. Consequently, each iteration resembles the normal equations from linear regression, but both the working outcome and the observation weights change as the algorithm moves toward the maximum likelihood estimate.



# 1) Negative log-likelihood for logistic regression:
nll_logistic <- function(par, x, y) {
  b0 <- par[1]
  b1 <- par[2]
  eta <- b0 + b1 * x
  p   <- 1 / (1 + exp(-eta))
  # To avoid log(0), add a tiny epsilon:
  eps <- 1e-8
  loglik <- sum(y * log(p + eps) + (1 - y) * log(1 - p + eps))
  return(-loglik)
}

# 2) Simulate some data
set.seed(2025)
n <- 500
x <- runif(n, -2, 2)
# True parameters β0 = -0.5, β1 = 1.2
p_true <- 1 / (1 + exp(-(-0.5 + 1.2 * x)))
y      <- rbinom(n, size = 1, prob = p_true)

# 3) Initial guesses (you could use 0,0 or use a quick glm fit for starting values)
init_beta <- coef(glm(y ~ x, family = binomial))

# 4) optim() call
fit_logit <- optim(
  par    = init_beta,
  fn     = nll_logistic,
  x      = x,
  y      = y,
  method = "BFGS",
  hessian = TRUE
)

fit_logit$par       # MLE for (β0, β1)

(Intercept)           x 
    -0.4953      1.1677 

sqrt(diag(solve(fit_logit$hessian)))  # approximate standard errors

(Intercept)           x 
     0.1116      0.1088 

glm_fit <- glm(y ~ x, family = binomial)
coef(glm_fit)

(Intercept)           x 
    -0.4953      1.1677 


For logistic regression, IRLS is the Newton–Raphson algorithm and has local quadratic convergence under suitable smoothness and nonsingularity conditions. This is a local result, not a guarantee from every starting point; a finite MLE must also exist. The optim() example above uses BFGS, so it illustrates a different numerical route to the same likelihood maximization.

title: Calculus
text:
Asymptotics
Taylor expansions are the workhorses of asymptotic statistical inference,






Definition (Probabilistic order notation)



Thus, little-\(o_p\) means negligible relative to the reference rate in probability, while big-\(O_p\) means bounded at that rate in probability. These statements do not require a bound that holds for every possible sample.








Theorem (First-order delta method)



Suppose \(\widehat\theta\overset{p}{\longrightarrow}\theta_0\) and \(f\) is differentiable at \(\theta_0\). Differentiability gives
\[
f(\widehat\theta)
=f(\theta_0)+f'(\theta_0)(\widehat\theta-\theta_0)
+(\widehat\theta-\theta_0)\varepsilon_n,
\qquad \varepsilon_n=o_p(1).
\]
If \(\widehat\theta-\theta_0=O_p(n^{-1/2})\), then
\[
f(\widehat\theta)-f(\theta_0)
=f'(\theta_0)(\widehat\theta-\theta_0)+o_p(n^{-1/2}).
\]
In particular, if
\[
\sqrt n(\widehat\theta-\theta_0)\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}N(0,V),
\]
then
\[
\sqrt n\{f(\widehat\theta)-f(\theta_0)\}
\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}
N\bigl(0,[f'(\theta_0)]^2V\bigr).
\]
The remainder disappears on the \(\sqrt n\) scale. When \(f'(\theta_0)=0\), this limit is degenerate, and a higher-order expansion may be needed.








Example (Log odds of an estimated probability)



Let \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) be independent Bernoulli\((p)\) observations with \(0<p<1\) and \(\widehat p=\bar X\). The central limit theorem gives
\[
\sqrt n(\widehat p-p)\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}N\{0,p(1-p)\}.
\]
For \(f(p)=\log\{p/(1-p)\}\), the derivative is \(f'(p)=1/\{p(1-p)\}\). Therefore,
\[
\sqrt n\left\{
\log\frac{\widehat p}{1-\widehat p}
-\log\frac{p}{1-p}
\right\}
\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}
N\left(0,\frac{1}{p(1-p)}\right).
\]
For an interior estimate, the approximate standard error of the estimated log odds is \(\{n\widehat p(1-\widehat p)\}^{-1/2}\). The cases \(\widehat p=0\) or \(1\) have probability tending to zero; the log odds need a separate convention on those samples.


This separation into a linear term and a negligible remainder is the basic mechanism behind the delta method, asymptotic linearity, influence-function calculations, and many empirical-process arguments.

title: Calculus
text:
Examples






Example (Uniform\((0,\theta)\) maximization)



Let \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) be i.i.d. \(\mathrm{Uniform}(0,\theta)\) with \(\theta>0\). Then the joint density is \[
L(\theta)
= \prod_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{\theta}
= \theta^{-n},
\qquad \theta \ge X_{(n)} =\max_{1\le i\le n}X_i,
\] and \(L(\theta)=0\) for \(\theta<X_{(n)}\). The log‐likelihood is \[
\ell(\theta)
= -n\ln\theta,
\qquad \theta \ge X_{(n)}.
\] Differentiating, \[
\frac{d\ell}{d\theta}
= -\frac{n}{\theta}
<0
\quad\text{for }\theta>X_{(n)},
\] so there is no interior critical point in \((X_{(n)},\infty)\). Since \(\ell(\theta)\) is strictly decreasing on its domain, the maximum occurs at the boundary: \[
\hat\theta = X_{(n)}\quad \text{  (max observed data point)}
\] Thus the MLE lies on the boundary of the region where the likelihood is positive, and one must explicitly check the endpoint \(\theta = X_{(n)}\) to locate the maximum.








Example (Binomial likelihood maximization)



Suppose \(X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)\) and we observe \(0<x<n\) successes in \(n\) trials. The likelihood is \[
L(p)
= \Pr(X=x)
= \binom{n}{x} p^x (1-p)^{n-x},
\quad p\in(0,1).
\] The log-likelihood is \[
\ell(p)
= \log L(p)
= \log\binom{n}{x} + x\log p +(n-x)\log(1-p).
\] Differentiate and set to zero: \[
\frac{d\ell}{dp}
= \frac{x}{p} - \frac{n-x}{1-p}
=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\frac{x}{p} = \frac{n-x}{1-p}
\Longrightarrow
\hat p = \frac{x}{n}.
\] One checks \(\dfrac{d^2\ell}{dp^2}<0\) for \(p\in(0,1)\), so \(\hat p=x/n\) is the unique maximizer. If the parameter space includes \(0\) and \(1\), samples with \(x=0\) or \(x=n\) give boundary estimates \(0\) or \(1\), respectively.








Example (Poisson likelihood maximization)



Let \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) be i.i.d. \(\mathrm{Pois}(\lambda)\) and observe data \(x_1,\dots,x_n\). The joint likelihood is \[
L(\lambda)
= \prod_{i=1}^n \frac{\lambda^{x_i}e^{-\lambda}}{x_i!}
= \lambda^{\sum_i x_i} e^{-n\lambda}
\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{1}{x_i!}.
\] The log-likelihood (up to additive constant) is \[
\ell(\lambda)
= \Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\Bigr)\log\lambda - n\lambda.
\] Differentiate and set to zero: \[
\frac{d\ell}{d\lambda}
= \frac{\sum_i x_i}{\lambda} - n
=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\hat\lambda
= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i.
\] When \(\sum_i x_i>0\), \(\dfrac{d^2\ell}{d\lambda^2}<0\), so \(\hat\lambda=\bar X\) is the MLE. If all counts are zero and \(\lambda=0\) is allowed, the maximum occurs at that boundary.








Example (Normal likelihood maximization)



Let \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) be i.i.d. \(\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)\), with \(n\ge2\) and nonconstant observed data. The log-likelihood (up to constants) is \[
\ell(\mu,\sigma)
= -n\ln\sigma - \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\mu)^2.
\] Differentiating: \[
\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\mu}
= \frac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\mu)
\Longrightarrow
\hat\mu = \bar x,
\] \[
\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\sigma}
= -\frac{n}{\sigma} + \frac{1}{\sigma^3}\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\mu)^2
\Longrightarrow
\hat\sigma^2 = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar x)^2.
\]

title: Calculus
text:
Countable families and nested sets
A set is countable if it is finite or its elements can be listed in a sequence indexed by the positive integers. The integers are countable: start with \(0,1,-1,2,-2,\ldots\). The interval \([0,1]\) is uncountable. No such list contains every point in it. Indexed unions and intersections make sense in either case, but a sequence \((A_n)_{n\ge1}\) gives us a specific order in which to consider the sets.
If \(A_1\subset A_2\subset\cdots\) and \(A=\bigcup_{n\ge1}A_n\), we write \(A_n\uparrow A\). Once an outcome enters the sequence, it stays. If \(B_1\supseteq B_2\supseteq\cdots\) and \(B=\bigcap_{n\ge1}B_n\), we write \(B_n\downarrow B\). An outcome belongs to \(B\) precisely when it survives every step.
For example, take \(A_n\) to be the closed disk of radius \(n\) centered at the origin in the plane, and put \(A_0=\varnothing\). Then \(A_n\uparrow\mathbb R^2\). Each difference \(D_n=A_n\setminus A_{n-1}\) is the part added at step \(n\): first a disk, then successive rings. Those pieces are pairwise disjoint, and \[
A_n=\bigcup_{k=1}^n D_k,\qquad \mathbb R^2=\bigcup_{k=1}^{\infty} D_k.
\] For a decreasing example, \([-1/n,1/n]\downarrow\{0\}\). Every interval contains zero, and every nonzero point eventually falls outside. In the Advanced section we drop the nesting assumption and ask whether a point belongs to infinitely many sets or to every set from some point onward.

When membership can change more than once
Fix the sample space of a die. At odd indices let \(A_n=\{2,4,6\}\), and at even indices let \(A_n=\{4\}\). Follow the roll \(2\). However far out in the sequence you start, it belongs to some later set. Yet there is no point after which it belongs to every set. The roll \(4\), on the other hand, belongs to every set from the start.


Infinitely often and eventually always
Starting at index \(m\), the tail union \(\bigcup_{n\ge m}A_n\) contains outcomes that appear at least once from \(m\) onward. Requiring this for every starting index gives the upper limit: \[
\limsup_{n\to\infty} A_n
=\bigcap_{m=1}^{\infty}\bigcup_{n\ge m} A_n.
\] An outcome belongs to this set exactly when it belongs to \(A_n\) infinitely often.
The tail intersection \(\bigcap_{n\ge m}A_n\) contains outcomes that stay from \(m\) onward. Requiring this for some starting index gives the lower limit: \[
\liminf_{n\to\infty} A_n
=\bigcup_{m=1}^{\infty}\bigcap_{n\ge m} A_n.
\] An outcome belongs to this set exactly when it belongs to \(A_n\) eventually always. In the die example, the upper limit is \(\{2,4,6\}\) and the lower limit is \(\{4\}\).
An outcome that eventually stays must appear infinitely often, so \(\liminf_n A_n\subset\limsup_n A_n\). Their difference consists of outcomes that keep entering and leaving. When the two limits agree, we say the sets converge to their common limit. For an increasing sequence, both limits equal the union: once an outcome enters, it stays. For a decreasing sequence, both equal the intersection.


A donut argument
Return to the increasing disks from Essential. Let \(A_n\) be the closed disk of radius \(n\), put \(A_0=\varnothing\), and consider just the newly added ring \(D_n=A_n\setminus A_{n-1}\). Although the expanding disks cover the entire plane, each point belongs to exactly one ring. What is \(\limsup_n D_n\)?
Fix any point and let \(k\) be the index of its ring. The tail starting at \(k+1\) never contains that point. Since every point misses some tail union, \(\limsup_n D_n=\varnothing\). The disks and the rings have the same union, but very different upper limits. A union asks whether a point appears even once. An upper limit asks whether it appears however far out we start.

title: Essential Set Theory
Essential Set Theory
text:
A sample space, denoted \(\Omega\), is the set of all possible outcomes of a random process generating uncertain outcomes. We use \(\omega\) for an individual outcome. An event \(A\) is a subset of the sample space. It occurs when the observed outcome belongs to it, that is, when \(\omega\in A\). We can describe an event by listing its outcomes or by giving a condition for membership.
\[
A=\{\omega\in\Omega:\omega\text{ satisfies the condition}\}.
\]






Example: Drawing a card





If we draw one card and record only its rank, our sample space is
\[
\Omega=\{2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9,10,\text{Jack},\text{Queen},\text{King},\text{Ace}\}.
\]
That is, although a standard deck contains four twos, we list the rank only once in this set of ranks.

The element \(2\) is an outcome, so \(2\in\Omega\).
The singleton set \(\{2\}\) is an event so \(\{2\}\subset\Omega\).

We can specify a membership condition to define a (sub)set,
\[
\{\omega\in\Omega:\omega\text{ is a face-card}\}
=\{\text{Jack},\text{Queen},\text{King}, \text{Ace}\}.
\]
We can also choose elements and form a (sub)set directly, \[\{\text{Jack},9,\text{King},2,\text{Ace}\}\]

title: Essential Set Theory
Essential Set Theory
text:
Let \(P\) mean “\(\omega\in A\)” and \(Q\) mean “\(\omega\in B\).” Each way of combining these statements determines a set of outcomes.








Statement
Read it as
Outcomes where it is true




Negation \(\neg P\)
\(P\) is false.
\(A^c\)


Conjunction \(P\land Q\)
Both \(P\) and \(Q\) are true.
\(A\cap B\)


Disjunction \(P\lor Q\)
At least one of \(P\) and \(Q\) is true.
\(A\cup B\)


Implication \(P\Rightarrow Q\)
If \(P\) holds, then \(Q\) holds.
\(A^c\cup B\)


If and only if \(P\Leftrightarrow Q\)
\(P\) and \(Q\) are either both true or both false.
\((A\cap B)\cup(A^c\cap B^c)\)


Exclusive or \(P\oplus Q\)
Exactly one of \(P\) and \(Q\) is true.
\(A\triangle B\)



If and only if means that both implications hold: \(P\Rightarrow Q\) and \(Q\Rightarrow P\). If this is true for every outcome, then \(A=B\).






Remark: Logical Equivalence





Two statements are logically equivalent when they have the same truth value for every outcome. In terms of sets, this means they describe exactly the same subset of \(\Omega\).
For example, the conditional \(P\Rightarrow Q\) and its contrapositive \(\neg Q\Rightarrow\neg P\) are logically equivalent because both describe the set
\[
A^c\cup B=B\cup A^c.
\]
Similarly, the converse \(Q\Rightarrow P\) and inverse \(\neg P\Rightarrow\neg Q\) both describe \(B^c\cup A\).
Finally, \(P\Leftrightarrow Q\) holds for every outcome precisely when
\[
(A\cap B)\cup(A^c\cap B^c)=\Omega,
\]
which is equivalent to \(A=B\)









Example: Dice outcomes as sets





On a die, let \(P\) mean “the roll is a four” and \(Q\) mean “the roll is even.” Write \(A=\{4\}\) and \(B=\{2,4,6\}\). Each row below makes a claim about every possible roll and shows the sets don’t represent logically equivalent conditions,

Every even roll is a four.
\(B\subset A\)

Every roll other than four is odd.

No. Roll a two.

Every odd roll differs from four.

title: Essential Set Theory
text:
An index lets us refer to many sets at once. For a collection \((A_i)_{i\in I}\), membership in the union means at least one condition holds. Membership in the intersection means every condition holds:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\omega\in\bigcup_{i\in I}A_i &\iff \omega\in A_i\text{ for some }i\in I,\\
\omega\in\bigcap_{i\in I}A_i &\iff \omega\in A_i\text{ for every }i\in I.
\end{aligned}
\]






Remark: An index set need not be countable





An index is a label, and the index set \(I\) is the set of possible labels. It can be finite, countably infinite, or uncountable. We can specify \(I\) by describing which labels belong to it, even when we cannot list them in a sequence.
For example, consider the family of half-open intervals indexed by \(T=[0,1]\). For each \(t\in T\), define
\[
A_t=[0,t)=\{x\in\mathbb R:0\le x<t\}.
\]
Each point \(t\in T\) indexes a set. For \(t>0\), the interval contains \(0\) but excludes its upper endpoint \(t\). At \(t=0\), we have \(A_0=\varnothing\). Taking the union over all indices gives
\[
\bigcup_{t\in T}A_t=[0,1)
\]








Figure 1: Three members of the family of half-open intervals. A filled dot marks an included endpoint and an open dot marks an excluded endpoint.

title: Essential Set Theory
text:
Two sets are disjoint if \(A\cap B=\varnothing\). A collection of sets is pairwise disjoint if \(A_i\cap A_j=\varnothing\) whenever \(i\ne j\).






Remark: Pairwise disjointness, higher-order intersections and independent events






A family of events is mutually exclusive if its members are pairwise disjoint. For distinct indices \(i,j,k\), we have \(A_i\cap A_j\cap A_k\subseteq A_i\cap A_j\). Thus \[
\begin{aligned}
\text{every pairwise intersection is empty}
&\implies \text{every three-way intersection is empty}\\
&\implies \text{every four-way intersection is empty}.
\end{aligned}
\] The converses can fail. For example, the sets \(\{1,2\}\), \(\{2,3\}\), and \(\{1,3\}\) overlap in every pair, yet no element belongs to all three.
For independent events (described using probability), the implications run the other way. \[
\text{four-wise independence}
\implies \text{three-wise independence}
\implies \text{pairwise independence}.
\] Here too, the converses can fail.
Suppose \(A_1,\ldots,A_m\) are mutually exclusive events, each with positive probability, and \(m\ge 2\). For every pair \(i\ne j\), mutual exclusivity gives \(P(A_i\cap A_j)=0\), while independence would require \(P(A_i\cap A_j)=P(A_i)P(A_j)>0\). So every pair is dependent, and the collection cannot be mutually independent. Learning that any one event occurred rules out every other event in the collection.




A partition of \(\Omega\) is a collection of nonempty, pairwise disjoint sets whose union is \(\Omega\).






Remark: Why partitions matter





A partition puts each outcome in exactly one group. We can condition on each group, then combine the results across groups. That idea leads to regression and my favorite, and likely most often used, trio of theorems in statistics: the laws of total probability, total expectation, and total variance.

title: Essential Set Theory
text:
Suppose 13 people each tell us the month they were born. Even without knowing a single birthday, we know that at least two people share a birth month. The pigeonhole principle formalizes this intuition






Theorem: Pigeonhole principle



If more than \(k\) objects are placed into \(k\) groups, at least one group contains two or more objects. More generally, if \(n\) objects are placed into \(k\geq 1\) groups, at least one group contains at least \(\lceil n/k\rceil\) objects.

title: Essential Set Theory
text:
“Some infinities are bigger than other infinities.” — John Green, The Fault in Our Stars


So far, we have concerned ourselves with counting the elements of finite sets. The cardinality of a finite set \(A\), written \(|A|\), is simply the number of elements it contains. For example, \(|\{1,2,3\}|=3\). But what does it mean to count the elements of an infinite set? We cannot simply finish counting them! Instead, we compare the sizes of sets using bijections, or one-to-one correspondences between their elements. Two sets have the same cardinality if there exists a bijection between them.
For example, consider the natural numbers \(\mathbb N=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}\) and the positive even integers \(E=\{2,4,6,\ldots\}\). Although \(E\) is a proper subset of \(\mathbb N\), the function \(f(n)=2n\) establishes a bijection between them. Thus, they have the same cardinality.






Remark: Different sizes of infinity





The cardinality of the natural numbers is denoted by aleph-null, \(\aleph_0\). Sets that can be put into a one-to-one correspondence with \(\mathbb N\) are called countably infinite. Remarkably,
\[
\operatorname{card}(\mathbb N)
=\operatorname{card}(\mathbb Z)
=\operatorname{card}(\mathbb Q)
=\aleph_0.
\]
But not every infinite set has the same cardinality. Cantor’s diagonal argument establishes that the real numbers cannot be placed into a one-to-one correspondence with the natural numbers. In particular,
\[
\operatorname{card}([0,1])
=\operatorname{card}(\mathbb R)
=2^{\aleph_0}
>\aleph_0.
\]
This larger cardinality is called the cardinality of the continuum. Even the interval \([0,1]\) contains strictly more elements than the entire set of natural numbers.

title: Essential Set Theory
Essential Set Theory
text:
Intersection distributes over union, and union distributes over intersection. Both laws hold for any index set \(I\), even an uncountable one. \[
\begin{aligned}
C\cap\left(\bigcup_{i\in I} A_i\right)
&= \bigcup_{i\in I}(C\cap A_i),\\
C\cup\left(\bigcap_{i\in I} A_i\right)
&= \bigcap_{i\in I}(C\cup A_i).
\end{aligned}
\]

title: Essential Set Theory
text:
Theorem: De Morgan’s laws



For any collection \((A_i)_{i\in I}\) of subsets of the same space, \[
\left(\bigcup_{i\in I}A_i\right)^c=\bigcap_{i\in I}A_i^c,
\qquad
\left(\bigcap_{i\in I}A_i\right)^c=\bigcup_{i\in I}A_i^c.
\]






Proof





Fix an outcome \(\omega\). It lies outside the union exactly when it lies outside every \(A_i\). It lies outside the intersection exactly when it lies outside at least one \(A_i\).

title: Essential Set Theory
text:
The Cartesian product of two sets \(S\) and \(T\) is the set of ordered pairs \[
S\times T=\{(s,t):s\in S,\ t\in T\}.
\] If the sets are finite, each of the \(|S|\) choices for the first entry can be paired with any of the \(|T|\) choices for the second. Thus \(|S\times T|=|S||T|\). For two die rolls, this gives \(6^2=36\) ordered pairs.








Figure 2: The 36 possible outcomes of rolling two dice. Each cell gives the ordered pair (first roll, second roll).





The same idea extends to any finite number of sets. The Cartesian product \(S_1\times\cdots\times S_n\) consists of all ordered tuples \((s_1,\ldots,s_n)\) with \(s_i\in S_i\) for each \(i\). If the sets are finite, there are \(|S_i|\) choices for the \(i\)th entry, so
\[
|S_1\times\cdots\times S_n|=\prod_{i=1}^n |S_i|.
\]
When all \(n\) entries come from the same set \(S\), we write the product as \(S^n\). If \(|S|=m\), then \(|S^n|=m^n\).






Example: Binary representations and counting subsets





A binary representation writes a number \(x\) as a sum of powers of \(2\),
\[x = \sum_{i=1}^\infty x_i 2^i\]
with each coefficient \(x_i\) either \(0\) or \(1\). For example, \[
5=1\cdot 2^0 +0\cdot 2^1+1\cdot 2^2
\] so we write \(5\) in binary as \(101\). Allowing leading zeros, the strings in \(\{0,1\}^m\) represent the integers from \(0\) through \(2^m-1\) exactly once.
We can use the same strings to count subsets. List the elements of \(S=\{a,b,c\}\) in the order \(a,b,c\). Read \(1\) as “include” and \(0\) as “leave out.” Then \(101\) picks out \(\{a,c\}\), while \(000\) picks out the empty set. For a set with \(m\) elements, each subset corresponds to exactly one string in \(\{0,1\}^m\). Since there are two choices for each of the \(m\) elements, there are \(2^m\) subsets in all.

title: Essential Set Theory
text:
Indicators turn membership into arithmetic
The indicator of a set \(A\) records membership as a number: \[
\mathbf 1_A(\omega)=
\begin{cases}
1,&\omega\in A,\\
0,&\omega\notin A.
\end{cases}
\] Two identities follow by checking the possible values of the indicators: \[
\mathbf 1_{A^c}=1-\mathbf 1_A,
\qquad
\mathbf 1_{A\cap B}=\mathbf 1_A\mathbf 1_B.
\]
The distinction between how many and whether any is especially useful. For the visits above, \(\sum_{i=1}^m\mathbf 1_{A_i}\) counts the number of positive visits, while \(\mathbf 1_{\cup_{i=1}^m A_i}\) records whether the patient ever tested positive. A patient with three positive visits contributes \(3\) to the first quantity and \(1\) to the second.
Now fix one condition \(A\) and look across \(n\) observed outcomes \(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_n\). The proportion satisfying it is the average of their indicators: \[
\widehat p_A=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^n\mathbf 1_A(\omega_k).
\] This is why indicators show up everywhere in statistics. A sample proportion is a sample mean, and its population counterpart is \(E[\mathbf 1_A]=P(A)\).






Example: The birthday problem





Number the people in a group from \(1\) to \(n\). Ignoring leap day, record their birthdays as a vector in \(\{1,\ldots,365\}^n\). Let \(M_{ij}\) be the event that people \(i\) and \(j\) share a birthday. For \(n\ge 2\), \[
A=\bigcup_{1\le i<j\le n}M_{ij},
\qquad
A^c=\bigcap_{1\le i<j\le n}M_{ij}^c.
\] The union says at least one pair matches. Its complement says every pair differs. One matching pair establishes \(A\), but to establish \(A^c\) we must check all pairs. The second event is easier to count.
Assume birthdays are independent and uniform on the 365 days, so all \(365^n\) vectors are equally likely. For \(2\le n\le365\), the first person can have any birthday, the second has 364 choices that avoid a match, and the third has 363. Continuing this count gives \[
P(A)=1-P(A^c)=1-\frac{\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}(365-j)}{365^n}.
\] For two people, \(132{,}860\) of the \(133{,}225\) vectors have different birthdays. The other \(365\) have a match, giving \(P(A)=1/365\). For 23 people, the chance of at least one match is about \(0.507\). For more than 365 people, a match is certain.

title: Essential Set Theory
text:
Functions, images, and preimages
A function \(X:\Omega\to S\) assigns each outcome \(\omega\) a single value \(X(\omega)\). We can use the same function to ask questions in either direction.








Start with
Ask
Set




Outcomes \(A\subseteq\Omega\)
Which values do these outcomes produce?
Image \(X(A)=\{X(\omega):\omega\in A\}\)


Values \(B\subseteq S\)
Which outcomes produce one of these values?
Preimage \(X^{-1}(B)=\{\omega\in\Omega:X(\omega)\in B\}\)



For example, roll two dice and let \(X(i,j)=i+j\). The image of the full sample space is \(\{2,\ldots,12\}\). The preimage of \(\{4\}\) is \[
\{X=4\}=X^{-1}(\{4\})=\{(1,3),(2,2),(3,1)\}.
\] Several rolls give the same sum. A preimage collects all of them, so it makes sense even when there is no inverse function.
The shorthand \(\{X\leq x\}\) works the same way. It denotes the set \(X^{-1}((-\infty,x])\) of outcomes whose recorded value is at most \(x\). This is what sits inside the probability in \(P(X\leq x)\).
Preimages preserve unions, intersections, and complements. For instance, \[
\omega\in X^{-1}(B\cap C)
\iff X(\omega)\in B\text{ and }X(\omega)\in C
\iff \omega\in X^{-1}(B)\cap X^{-1}(C).
\] Once again, the proof amounts to picking one outcome and reading what each description says about it.

title: Essential Set Theory
section: advnaced inclusion exclusion and booles inequality
text:
advnaced inclusion exclusion and booles inequality






Theorem: Inclusion–exclusion for any finite number of sets





For finite sets \(A_1,\ldots,A_m\), \[
\left|\bigcup_{i=1}^m A_i\right|
=
\sum_{\varnothing\ne J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}}
(-1)^{|J|+1}
\left|\bigcap_{j\in J} A_j\right|.
\tag{1}\]
Add the individual counts, subtract all pairwise intersections, add all three-way intersections, and continue alternating signs.



Often we only need an upper bound. Adding the individual counts includes every outcome in the union at least once, so \[
\left|\bigcup_{i=1}^m A_i\right|\leq\sum_{i=1}^m |A_i|.
\] For finite sets, equality holds exactly when the sets are pairwise disjoint. The probability version is called the union bound, or Boole’s inequality: \[
P\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^m A_i\right)\leq\sum_{i=1}^m P(A_i).
\tag{2}\]
This is the idea behind the Bonferroni correction. If we conduct ten tests and each has probability at most \(0.005\) of a false rejection, then the probability of at least one false rejection is at most \(10(0.005)=0.05\). The bound holds even when the tests use the same data.
CHECK KOUROS NOTES, we need more davnced set theory to set up for measure theoretic probasility
More generally, for \(m\) finite sets,
\[
  \left|\bigcup_{i=1}^m A_i\right|
  =
  \sum_{\varnothing\neq J\subset\{1,\ldots,m\}}
  (-1)^{|J|+1}
  \left|\bigcap_{j\in J}A_j\right|
   \tag{3}\] and more generally we have subadditivity/Boole’s inequality \[
  \left|\bigcup_{i=1}^m A_i\right|
  \leq
  \sum_{i=1}^m
  \left|A_j\right|
   \tag{4}\] and equality holds when the sets are pairwise disjoint (for finite sets)
## Functions, images, and preimages
A function \(X:\Omega\to S\) assigns each outcome \(\omega\) a single value \(X(\omega)\) in \(S\). For \(A\subset\Omega\), its image is \(X(A)=\{X(\omega):\omega\in A\}\). We can also start with a set of values \(B\subset S\) and ask which outcomes produce them. This gives the preimage \[
X^{-1}(B)=\{\omega\in\Omega:X(\omega)\in B\}.
\] Several outcomes can give the same value, so taking a preimage requires no inverse function.
Return to the card example. Let \(X(\omega)=1\) for a face card and \(X(\omega)=0\) otherwise. Starting with the face cards gives the image \(X(F)=\{1\}\). Starting with the value \(1\) gives the preimage \[
\{X=1\}=X^{-1}(\{1\})=\{\text{Jack},\text{Queen},\text{King}\}=F.
\] The same shorthand appears throughout statistics. For a real-valued \(X\), the event \(\{X\le x\}\) is the preimage \(X^{-1}(( -\infty,x])\). That is how a condition on a measured value picks out a set of outcomes in the original sample space.
Preimages also let us carry a logical statement from one space to the other. If \(B,C\subset S\), then \[
\begin{aligned}
\omega\in X^{-1}(B\cap C)
&\iff X(\omega)\in B\text{ and }X(\omega)\in C\\
&\iff \omega\in X^{-1}(B)\cap X^{-1}(C).
\end{aligned}
\] That proves \(X^{-1}(B\cap C)=X^{-1}(B)\cap X^{-1}(C)\). Replacing “and” by “or” gives the corresponding identity for unions.

title: Essential Set Theory
section: Indexed families and De Morgan’s laws
text:
Indexed families and De Morgan’s laws






Theorem: De Morgan’s laws



Negating those sentences gives De Morgan’s laws: \[
\left(\bigcup_{i\in I}A_i\right)^c=\bigcap_{i\in I} A_i^c,
\qquad
\left(\bigcap_{i\in I}A_i\right)^c=\bigcup_{i\in I} A_i^c.
\]






Proof: De Morgan’s laws





To check the first identity, pick any \(\omega\). It lies outside the union precisely when it lies outside every \(A_i\). For the second, being outside the intersection only takes one failed condition.





For two conditions, these are the logical equivalences \(\neg(P\lor Q)\Leftrightarrow(\neg P\land\neg Q)\) and \(\neg(P\land Q)\Leftrightarrow(\neg P\lor\neg Q)\). For indexed families, the same idea exchanges “some” (\(\exists\)) and “every” (\(\forall\)). To disprove “every \(A_i\) contains \(\omega\),” it takes just one index \(i\) for which \(\omega\notin A_i\).

make_martingale_plots <- function(
  n_paths = 250,
  nW = 100,
  nB = 4000,
  T = 1,
  alpha_val = 0.01,
  cols = c(bm = "steelblue", mart = "firebrick", sub = "forestgreen", super = "purple"),
  seed = 489
) {
  stopifnot(length(cols) == 4)
  set.seed(seed)

  # ---- Brownian motion: n_paths on [0, T] ----
  dt <- T / nB
  bm_df <- purrr::map_dfr(1:n_paths, function(p) {
    dB <- rnorm(nB, mean = 0, sd = sqrt(dt))
    tibble(
      path = factor(p),
      t    = seq(0, T, length.out = nB + 1),
      B    = c(0, cumsum(dB))
    )
  })

  p_bm <- ggplot(bm_df, aes(x = t, y = B, group = path)) +
    geom_line(alpha = alpha_val, linewidth = 0.6, color = cols[["bm"]]) +
    labs(title = "(Continuous t) Brownian motion", x = "t", y = "B(t)") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(legend.position = "none")

  # ---- Wealth simulator (discrete time) ----
  simulate_wealth <- function(p, nW, n_paths) {
    purrr::map_dfr(1:n_paths, function(path_id) {
      X  <- ifelse(rbinom(nW, 1, p) == 1, 1, -1)  # ±1
      H  <- numeric(nW); H[1] <- 1
      for (k in 2:nW) H[k] <- 1 + 0.5 * (X[k-1] < 0)  # predictable stakes
      tibble(path = factor(path_id), n = 0:nW, W = c(0, cumsum(H * X)))
    })
  }

  wealth_mart_df  <- simulate_wealth(p = 0.5, nW = nW, n_paths = n_paths)
  wealth_sub_df   <- simulate_wealth(p = 0.6, nW = nW, n_paths = n_paths)
  wealth_super_df <- simulate_wealth(p = 0.4, nW = nW, n_paths = n_paths)

  p_mart <- ggplot(wealth_mart_df, aes(x = n, y = W, group = path)) +
    geom_line(alpha = alpha_val, linewidth = 0.6, color = cols[["mart"]]) +
    labs(title = "Fair game with predictable stakes, Wealth (p = 0.5)", x = "n", y = "W_n") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(legend.position = "none")

  p_sub <- ggplot(wealth_sub_df, aes(x = n, y = W, group = path)) +
    geom_line(alpha = alpha_val, linewidth = 0.6, color = cols[["sub"]]) +
    labs(title = "Favorable game with predictable stakes, Wealth (p = 0.6)", x = "n", y = "W_n") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(legend.position = "none")

  p_super <- ggplot(wealth_super_df, aes(x = n, y = W, group = path)) +
    geom_line(alpha = alpha_val, linewidth = 0.6, color = cols[["super"]]) +
    labs(title = "Unfavorable game with predictable stakes, Wealth (p = 0.4)", x = "n", y = "W_n") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(legend.position = "none")

  combo <- cowplot::plot_grid(p_bm, p_mart, p_sub, p_super, ncol = 2)

  list(
    data = list(
      brownian = bm_df,
      martingale = wealth_mart_df,
      submartingale = wealth_sub_df,
      supermartingale = wealth_super_df
    ),
    plots = list(
      brownian = p_bm,
      martingale = p_mart,
      submartingale = p_sub,
      supermartingale = p_super,
      combo = combo
    )
  )
}

path_qcov <- function(x, y) {
  dx <- diff(x); dy <- diff(y)
  sum(dx * dy)

qcov_mart_sub <- wealth_mart_df %>%

  group_by(path) %>%
  summarise(QCov = path_qcov(Wm, Wp), .groups = "drop") %>%

# ---- sub vs super quadratic covariation ----
qcov_sub_super <- wealth_sub_df %>%
  select(path, n, Ws = W) %>%
  inner_join(wealth_super_df %>% select(path, n, Wp = W), by = c("path","n")) %>%
  group_by(path) %>%
  summarise(QCov = path_qcov(Ws, Wp), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(pair = "sub vs super")

# bind all wealth qcov pairs
wealth_qcov <- bind_rows(qcov_mart_sub, qcov_mart_super, qcov_sub_super)

# updated summary
wealth_qcov_summary <- wealth_qcov %>%
  group_by(pair) %>%
  summarise(QCov_mean = mean(QCov), QCov_sd = sd(QCov), .groups = "drop")


# Brownian: cross-path covariation (independent paths; expect ~0)
n_paths <- n_distinct(bm_df$path)
bm_qcov_pairs <- tibble(path1 = 1:(n_paths-1), path2 = 2:n_paths)
bm_qcov <- purrr::pmap_dfr(bm_qcov_pairs, function(path1, path2) {
  X <- bm_df %>% filter(path == path1) %>% arrange(t) %>% pull(B)
  Y <- bm_df %>% filter(path == path2) %>% arrange(t) %>% pull(B)
  tibble(pair = paste0("B", path1, " vs B", path2), QCov = path_qcov(X, Y))
})
bm_qcov_summary <- summarise(bm_qcov, QCov_mean = mean(QCov), QCov_sd = sd(QCov))

# ---- Outputs ----------------------------------------------------------------

Suppose we observe a right continuous (kind of redundant in discrete but essential in continuous case) non-negative discrete time process \(Z(t)\)
\[\begin{aligned} A(0) &= 0\\ A(t) &= \sum_{k=0}^{t-1} E[\Delta Z_{k+1}|\mathcal F_k]\\
&= \sum_{k=0}^{t-1} E[Z(k+1) - Z(k)|\mathcal F_k]\\
\Delta A_{t+1} &= A(t+1) - A(t) = E[\Delta Z_{t}|\mathcal F_t]\end{aligned}\]
and \[\boxed{Z(t) = M(t) + A(t)}\]

This breakdown is relatively stragithforward to see in the discrete time case but harder in continuous time, first in discrete time we see 

More generally with continuous index we have the Doob Meyer Theorem, 









The martingale transform allows us to use the ,


Note that \(M^{(n)}(\tau)\) is often an average of individual martingales, \[\begin{aligned}
M^{(n)}(\tau)
  &= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n M_i(\tau)
   = \frac{1}{n} M(\tau),\\[4pt]
\langle M^{(n)}\rangle(\tau)
  &= \frac{1}{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^n \langle M_i\rangle(\tau)
   = \frac{1}{n^2}\langle M\rangle(\tau),
\end{aligned}\] Thus, at any fixed \(\tau\), \[\frac{M^{(n)}(\tau)}{\sqrt{\langle M^{(n)}\rangle(\tau)}}
  = \frac{M(\tau)/n}{\sqrt{\langle M\rangle(\tau)/n^2}}
  = \frac{M(\tau)}{\sqrt{\langle M\rangle(\tau)}}\]
Under the conditions of the martingale CLT (and using Slutsky’s theorem for plug-in estimation of the bracket), we obtain \[\frac{M^{(n)}(\tau)}{\sqrt{\langle M^{(n)}\rangle(\tau)}}
  = \frac{M(\tau)}{\sqrt{\langle M\rangle(\tau)}}
  \xrightarrow{d} N(0,1)\] exactly analogous to the classical CLT for the sample mean. In what follows we may omit the superscript \((n)\) when no confusion arises.

We now have all the building blocks we need to understand nonparametric survival straigthforwardly,

make_discrete_wealth_plots <- function(

  nW = 100,
  alpha_val = 0.25,
  p_mart = 0.5,
  p_sub  = 0.55,
  p_super = 0.45,
  cols = c(mart = "firebrick", sub = "forestgreen", super = "purple"),
  seed = 123
) {
  stopifnot(length(cols) == 3)
  suppressPackageStartupMessages({
    library(tidyverse)
    library(cowplot)
  })
  set.seed(seed)

  simulate_wealth <- function(p, nW, n_paths) {
    map_dfr(1:n_paths, function(path_id) {
      X  <- ifelse(rbinom(nW, 1, p) == 1, 1, -1)
      H <- numeric(nW); H[1] <- 1
      for (k in 2:nW) H[k] <- 1 + 0.5 * (X[k-1] < 0)

    })
  }

  # data

  df_sub   <- simulate_wealth(p = p_sub,   nW = nW, n_paths = n_paths)
  df_super <- simulate_wealth(p = p_super, nW = nW, n_paths = n_paths)

  # plots

    geom_line(alpha = alpha_val, linewidth = 0.6, color = cols[["mart"]]) +

    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(legend.position = "none")

title: Stochastic Processes
Stochastic Processes
text:
One sample log rank test
If we want to test the NA estimate against a fixed value (historical control) at a time \(\tau\), we can choose a predictable contrast \(H\), \[H(t) = \frac{1}{Y(t)}\,\mathbb 1\{t\le \tau\}\] so that the martingale transform directly targets the cumulative hazard. Then, \[\begin{aligned}
U^(\tau)
  &= \int_0^\tau H(s)\{dN(s) - Y(s)\,d\Lambda_0(s)\} \\
  &= \int_0^\tau \frac{1}{Y(s)}\{dN(s) - Y(s)\,d\Lambda_0(s)\} \\
  &= \big\{\hat\Lambda(\tau) - \Lambda_0(\tau)\big\},
\end{aligned}\]

Under a null hypothesis based on a historical control, \[H_0:\ \Lambda_0(\tau) = \Lambda^*(\tau)\] we have \[U(\tau) = \big\{\hat\Lambda(\tau) - \Lambda^*(\tau)\big\}\] as a mean–zero martingale transform under \(H_0\).

Its predictable quadratic variation is \[\langle U\rangle(\tau)
  = \int_0^\tau H^2(s)Y(s)\,d\Lambda_0(s)
  = \int_0^\tau \frac{1}{Y(s)}\,d\Lambda_0(s)\] which we estimate by plugging in \(d\hat\Lambda(s)=Y(s)^{-1}dN(s)\): \[\widehat{\langle U\rangle}(\tau)
= \int_0^\tau \frac{1}{Y(s)^2}\,dN(s)
= \sum_{j:\,t_j\le\tau} \frac{D_j}{Y(t_j)^2}\] where the sum runs over distinct event times \(t_j\) with \(D_j\) events at risk set size \(Y(t_j)\).

By the MCLT and Slutsky we have the , \[Z(\tau)
:= \frac{U(\tau)}{\sqrt{\widehat{\langle U\rangle}(\tau)}}
= \frac{\hat\Lambda(\tau) - \Lambda^*(\tau)}{\sqrt{\sum_{j:\,t_j\le\tau} D_j/Y(t_j)^2}}
\ \xrightarrow{d}\ N(0,1)\quad\text{under }H_0\]
Where this test statistic takes the familiar pearson statistic form \[Z(\tau) = \frac{O-E}{\sqrt{Var(O)}}\]


n         <- 30
rate_true <- 0.10
rate_cens <- 0.05

Ttrue <- rexp(n, rate_true)
Ctrue <- rexp(n, rate_cens)

time   <- pmin(Ttrue, Ctrue)
status <- as.integer(Ttrue <= Ctrue)

one_sample_logrank_NA <- function(time, status, rate_hist, tau = max(time)) {
  et <- sort(unique(time[status == 1 & time <= tau]))
  Yj <- sapply(et, function(t) sum(time >= t))
  dj <- sapply(et, function(t) sum(time == t & status == 1))
  
  Lam_hat  <- sum(dj / Yj)
  Var_Lam  <- sum(dj / (Yj^2))
  Lam_star <- rate_hist * tau
  
  Z <- (Lam_hat - Lam_star) / sqrt(Var_Lam)
  p <- 2 * (1 - pnorm(abs(Z)))
  c(Z_hand = Z, p_hand = p)
}

title: Stochastic Processes
text:
Two sample log rank test
To test two survival curves against one another assume each subject \(i\) has a group indicator \(Z_i\in\{0,1\}\) (e.g. \(Z_i=1\) = treatment, \(Z_i=0\) = control) and define group–specific counting and at–risk processes \[N_g(t) = \sum_{i:Z_i=g} N_i(t),\qquad
Y_g(t) = \sum_{i:Z_i=g} Y_i(t),\qquad g=0,1\] and total processes \(N(t)=N_0(t)+N_1(t)\), \(Y(t)=Y_0(t)+Y_1(t)\).
Under the null of equal hazards, \[H_0:\ \lambda_0(t\mid Z_i=0) = \lambda_0(t\mid Z_i=1) = \lambda_0(t)\]

We choose the predictable contrast \[H_i(t) = Z_i - \frac{Y_1(t)}{Y(t)}\] which compares group membership to the risk–set proportion in group 1. The martingale transform is \[\begin{aligned}
U(\tau)
&= \sum_{i=1}^n \int_0^\tau H_i(t)\,dM_i(t) \\
&= \sum_{i=1}^n \int_0^\tau \left(Z_i - \frac{Y_1(t)}{Y(t)}\right)\,dN_i(t)
      \quad\text{(drift cancels under }H_0\text{)} \\
&= \int_0^\tau \left\{dN_1(t) - \frac{Y_1(t)}{Y(t)}\,dN(t)\right\}
\end{aligned}\]

At distinct event times \(t_j\), \[D_j = \Delta N(t_j),\quad
D_{1j} = \Delta N_1(t_j),\quad
Y_j = Y(t_j),\quad
Y_{1j} = Y_1(t_j)\] and using the counting measure \(U(\tau)\) can be written as \[U(\tau) = \sum_{t_j\le\tau} \left\{D_{1j} - \frac{Y_{1j}}{Y_j}D_j\right\}\] i.e. “observed minus expected” events in group 1.

The predictable quadratic variation is then, \[d\langle U\rangle(t)
= \sum_{i=1}^n H_i(t)^2 Y_i(t)\lambda_0(t)\,dt
= \frac{Y_1(t)Y_0(t)}{Y(t)}\,\lambda_0(t)\,dt\]
Estiamted using the NA plug and integrating up to (\(\tau\)), \[\begin{aligned}\widehat{\langle U\rangle}(\tau)
= \int_0^\tau \frac{Y_1(t)Y_0(t)}{Y(t)^2}dN(t)\end{aligned}\]
In discrete form at distinct event times (\(t_j\)) with total events (\(D_j\)), risk set size (\(Y_j\)), and group \(1\) at risk \((Y_{1j}\)), group \(0\) at risk (\(Y_{0j}\)), \[\widehat{\langle U\rangle}(\tau)
= \sum_{t_j\le\tau} \frac{Y_{1j}Y_{0j}}{Y_j^2}D_j\]

But we use a finite sample correction
\[\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}\left({U(\tau)}\right)
= \sum_{t_j\le\tau}
\frac{Y_{1j}Y_{0j}}{Y_j^2}
\left(\frac{Y_j - D_j}{Y_j - 1}\right)
D_j\] which is what you then use in the denominator of the two–sample log-rank statistic

Thus, by the MCLT and Slutsky, the statistic is, \[Z(\tau)
= \frac{U(\tau)}{\sqrt{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}\{U(\tau)\}}}
= \frac{\displaystyle \sum_{t_j\le\tau} \left\{D_{1j} - \frac{Y_{1j}}{Y_j}D_j\right\}}
       {\displaystyle \sqrt{\sum_{t_j\le\tau}
         \frac{Y_{1j}Y_{0j}}{Y_j^2}\,\frac{Y_j-D_j}{Y_j-1}\,D_j}}
\ \xrightarrow{d}\ N(0,1)\quad\text{under }H_0\]


## simulate simple 2-sample survival data
n1 <- 30; n0 <- 30
rate1 <- 0.12  # group 1 hazard
rate0 <- 0.10  # group 0 hazard
rateC <- 0.05  # censoring hazard

T1 <- rexp(n1, rate1); C1 <- rexp(n1, rateC)
T0 <- rexp(n0, rate0); C0 <- rexp(n0, rateC)

time   <- c(pmin(T1, C1), pmin(T0, C0))
status <- c(as.integer(T1 <= C1), as.integer(T0 <= C0))
group  <- c(rep(1, n1), rep(0, n0))  # 1 = trt, 0 = ctrl

two_sample_logrank <- function(time, status, group, tau = max(time)) {
  et  <- sort(unique(time[status == 1 & time <= tau]))
  Dj  <- sapply(et, function(t) sum(time == t & status == 1))
  Yj  <- sapply(et, function(t) sum(time >= t))
  Y1j <- sapply(et, function(t) sum(time >= t & group == 1))
  Y0j <- Yj - Y1j
  D1j <- sapply(et, function(t) sum(time == t & status == 1 & group == 1))
  
  O <- sum(D1j)
  E <- sum(Y1j / Yj * Dj)
  V <- sum((Y1j * Y0j / Yj^2) * ((Yj - Dj) / (Yj - 1)) * Dj)
  
  Z <- (O - E) / sqrt(V)
  p <- 2 * (1 - pnorm(abs(Z)))
  c(Z_hand = Z, p_hand = p)
}

title: Stochastic Processes
section: Two stage, one-sample log-rank test (Futility Stop)
text:
Two stage, one-sample log-rank test (Futility Stop)
We separate first and second stages in notation and plan our study to run up to calendar time \(t\).

Suppose we want an interim futility test at \(\tau\in(0,t)\)



It is common to suppress \(u\) and write \(\int_0^\infty\) with the understanding that the processes are stopped at the proper analysis time,
\[\begin{aligned}  W_1 &= n_1^{-\frac{1}{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_1}\int_0^\infty \{dN_{1i}(s) - Y_{1i}(s)d\Lambda_0(s)\},\quad \hat \sigma_1^2 = n_1^{-1} \sum_{i=1}^{n_1} \int_{0}^\infty Y_{1i}(s)d\Lambda_0(s)\\ W &= n^{-\frac{1}{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\int_0^\infty \{dN_{i}(s) - Y_{i}(s)d\Lambda_0(s)\},\quad \hat \sigma^2 = n^{-1} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \int_{0}^\infty Y_{i}(s)d\Lambda_0(s)\end{aligned}\]


For a particular design and hypothesis, \[\left(n_1, n, \alpha, \Lambda_0\right),
\qquad
\begin{array}{ll}
n_1 :     & \text{stage-1 sample size},\\
n   :     & \text{total sample size},\\
\alpha :  & \text{common one-sided type I error},\\
\Lambda_0 : & \text{historical cumulative hazard}
\end{array}\]
are prespecified and \[(c_1, c)\] are chosen to guarantee
\[\alpha = P(\text{reject } H_0 | H_0) = P\left(\underbrace{\frac{W_1}{\hat \sigma_1}}_{Z_1} \leq c_1, \underbrace{\frac{W}{\hat \sigma}}_{Z} \leq c | H_0\right)\]

which can be solved via numerical methods. Because \(c_1 = \Phi^{-1}(\alpha)\) and solve for \(c\)


alpha_two_stage <- function(c1, c, rho) {
  integrand <- function(z) {
    dnorm(z) * pnorm((c1 - rho * z) / sqrt(1 - rho^2))
  }
  integrate(integrand, lower = -Inf, upper = c)$value
}

## solve for c given c1, alpha, rho
solve_c_given_c1 <- function(c1, alpha, rho) {
  f <- function(c) alpha_two_stage(c1, c, rho) - alpha
  uniroot(f, interval = c(-5, 5))$root
}

# joint solver
solve_c1_c <- function(alpha, rho, alpha1_stage) {
  c1 <- qnorm(alpha1_stage)
  c  <- solve_c_given_c1(c1, alpha, rho)
  c(c1 = c1, c = c)
}
