title: Essential Combinatorics
Essential Combinatorics
text:
A simple way to count outcomes is to picture a row of empty slots, one for each choice. Ask how many options you have for the first slot, then for the second, and so on. Replacement determines whether you can use an item again if it was used earlier. Order determines whether the slot order matters or arrangements like \(AB\) and \(BA\) count as two outcomes or one.





Each of the \(K\) slots represents one choice.




The Product Rule (or the Multiplication Rule) helps determine the total number of ways to fill our slots/number of total choices, if there are \(n\) ways to perform one action and \(m\) ways to perform a second independent action, then there are \[n(m)\] ways to perform both actions. This can be envisioned as simply filling two slots,






Example: Two slots, three letters





Choose two letters from \(\{A,B,C\}\) without replacement and record them in order. There are three choices for the first slot. Whichever letter we use, exactly two choices remain for the second slot. If the first letter is \(A\), the second can be \(B\) or \(C\). Starting with \(B\) or \(C\) also gives two possibilities, so we get \(3\times 2=6\) ordered outcomes: \[
\underbrace{AB,\ AC}_{A\text{ first}},\qquad
\underbrace{BA,\ BC}_{B\text{ first}},\qquad
\underbrace{CA,\ CB}_{C\text{ first}}.
\]



To fill these two slots we can further envision counting spots in a grid with the \(n\) options representing slot \(1\) along the horizontal axis and \(m\) options representing slot \(2\) along the vertical axis,





Each of the n(m) boxes represents one choice










Theorem: The Generalized Product Rule [Thm 1.2, Rozanov]



Given \(n_1\) elements \(a_1,\ldots,a_{n_1}\) and \(n_2\) elements \(b_1,\ldots,b_{n_2}\) etc. up to \(n_r\) elements \(x_1,\ldots,x_{n_r}\) there are precisely \(n_1n_2\ldots n_r\) r-tuples \((a_{i_1},b_{i_2},\ldots,x_{i_r})\) containing one element of each kind

title: Essential Combinatorics
text:
The product rule gives us a way to count choices slot by slot. Start with the case where order matters and we choose without replacement.






Definition: Permutation



An \(m\)-permutation of \(n\) distinct items is an ordered selection of \(m\) of those items without replacement. For \(1\le m\le n\), there are \(n\) choices for the first slot, \(n-1\) for the second, and \(n-m+1\) for the last. By the product rule, \[
    P(n,m)
\coloneqq \underbrace{n(n-1)\cdots(n-m+1)}_{m\text{ factors}}
=\frac{n!}{(n-m)!}.
\tag{1}\]
The formula also gives \(P(n,0)=1\), since there is exactly one empty selection. When \(m=n\), we arrange all \(n\) items and get \(P(n,n)=n!\).








Example: First and second prize





Ann (A), Bob (B), Carla (C), and Dave (D) are competing for first and second prize. Write each outcome as an ordered pair \((\text{first},\text{second})\). For example, \((A,B)\) means Ann wins first prize and Bob wins second. Reversing the pair changes who wins each prize.
There are four choices for first prize. Whoever wins it, three contestants remain eligible for second prize. Grouping the outcomes by the first-prize winner makes the count easy to see: \[
    \begin{aligned}
    (A,B),\quad (A,C),\quad (A,D)\\
    (B,A),\quad (B,C),\quad (B,D)\\
    (C,A),\quad (C,B),\quad (C,D)\\
    (D,A),\quad (D,B),\quad (D,C).
    \end{aligned}
    \] So \(P(4,2)=4\cdot 3=12\).









Theorem: Properties of Factorials and Permutations





Factorials and permutations satisfy several useful identities and approximations that simplify counting problems and connect combinatorics to probability theory,

Sequential permutation identity. Suppose we fill \(i\) slots and then fill another \(j\) slots, all without replacement. For nonnegative integers \(i,j\) with \(i+j\le n\),
\[
P(n,i+j)=P(n,i)\,P(n-i,j).
\tag{2}\]






Proof





There are \(P(n,i)\) ways to fill the first \(i\) slots. Whichever items we use, exactly \(n-i\) remain, so there are \(P(n-i,j)\) ways to fill the next \(j\) slots. Every ordered list of \(i+j\) items arises exactly once this way. The product rule gives the result.



Derangements. A derangement is a permutation in which no item stays in its original position. Let \(D_n\) denote the number of derangements of \(n\) distinct items. If we choose \(i\) items to stay in place, the remaining \(n-i\) items can be arranged in \((n-i)!\) ways. Applying inclusion–exclusion gives \[
D_n
=\sum_{i=0}^n(-1)^i\binom{n}{i}(n-i)!
=n!\sum_{i=0}^n\frac{(-1)^i}{i!}.
\tag{3}\]
If all \(n!\) permutations are equally likely, then \[
P(\text{no item stays in place})
=\frac{D_n}{n!}
=\sum_{i=0}^n\frac{(-1)^i}{i!}
\longrightarrow e^{-1}\approx 0.368.
\] The limit follows from the power series for \(e^x\) evaluated at \(x=-1\).
Stirling’s approximation. For large \(n\), we can approximate \(n!\) by \[
n!\sim\sqrt{2\pi n}\left(\frac{n}{e}\right)^n,
\qquad n\to\infty,
\tag{4}\]
where \(\sim\) means the ratio of the two sides approaches \(1\). Taking logarithms gives \[
\log(n!)=n\log n-n+\tfrac12\log(2\pi n)+o(1),
\] where \(o(1)\) is a term that approaches zero. This form is useful when factorials appear in a log-likelihood, as they do for the Poisson and multinomial distributions.

title: Essential Combinatorics
text:
Definition: Combination



Combinations address scenarios where order does not matter and selections are made without replacement. Here, only the set of chosen items is important, not the sequence in which they are selected. The number of ways to choose \(m\) items from \(n\) items is written as \(C(n, m)\) or \(\binom{n}{m}\) by: \[C(n,m) \coloneqq \frac{n!}{m!(n-m)!} \tag{5}\]








Example: Combination





If you are forming a committee from a larger group and the order in which members are chosen is irrelevant, then combinations are used. That is suppose we are forming a committee of 2 members from 3 possibilities: Ann (A), Bob (B) and Carla (C).
Here there are three possible committees, \[(A \ \& \ B),(A \ \& \ C),(B \ \& \ C)\] \[\frac{3!}{(3-2)!(2)!} = 3\]









Example: XKCD 3015, Dungeons and Dragons








xkcd #3015


If 5 of 10 arrows are cursed, the probability of selecting two uncursed arrows without replacement is
\[
P(\text{neither cursed})
=\frac{\binom{5}{2}}{\binom{10}{2}}
=\frac{2}{9}\approx0.2222.
\]
The dungeon master claims that rolling three six-sided dice and one four-sided die, using a total of at least 16 as the cutoff, gives the same probability of \(2/9\). Since the dice rolls are independent, there are \(6^3(4)=864\) equally likely outcomes. We can count the favorable outcomes using the following table:



Four-sided die
Required sum of 3d6
Favorable outcomes




1
\(\geq 15\)
20


2
\(\geq 14\)
35


3
\(\geq 13\)
56


4
\(\geq 12\)
81


Total

192



Thus,
\[
P(\text{sum}\geq16)=\frac{192}{864}=\frac29.
\]
and as always, the dungeon master is correct









Remark: Intuition on why we divide by \((n-m)!\) and \(m!\)





When computing the number of arrangements (or permutations) for \(m\) items out of \(n\) distinct items without replacement, a useful approach is to start by considering how many ways there are to arrange all \(n\) items. This total is \(n!\), but we are only interested in the order of the first \(m\) items.
Notice that in each complete ordering of \(n\) items, the last \((n-m)\) positions (positions \((m+1)\) through \(n\)) can be arranged in any order. There are exactly \((n-m)!\) ways to arrange these remaining items. In other words, if we view the first \(m\) items in a full ordering as our permutation of interest, then different orderings of the remaining \((n-m)\) items do not alter this selected permutation.
For example, suppose \(n=4\) and \(m=2\). The full orderings \([1,2,3,4]\) and \([1,2,4,3]\) both yield the same permutation \([1,2]\) when only the first two items are considered.
We can represent a full ordering as, \[
\underbrace{[x_1,\ldots,x_m}_{\text{Permutation of Interest}}, \underbrace{x_{m+1},\ldots,x_n}_{\text{Extra Portion}}].
\]
Since each distinct permutation of the \(m\) items appears \((n-m)!\) times in the \(n!\) full orderings, we divide \(n!\) by \((n-m)!\) to account for the repeated arrangements of the extra portion. This gives the number of unique permutations of \(m\) items from \(n\) items as \(\frac{n!}{(n-m)!}\) a similar argument yields the formula for combinations.









Remark: Pascal’s Triangle













Figure 1: Pascal’s triangle. Each interior number is the sum of the two numbers touching it from above.





Pascal’s triangle starts with a single \(1\). Each row begins and ends with \(1\), and each interior entry is the sum of the two entries immediately above it. Every row is symmetric from left to right.








Figure 2: The two middle entries of the row \(1,3,3,1\) give the middle entry of the next row: \(3+3=6\).





The entry in row \(n\), position \(i\) is \(\binom{n}{i}\), the number of ways to choose \(i\) items from \(n\) distinct items.









Theorem: Properties of Combinations





Combinations, permutations, and factorials satisfy many useful identities that simplify counting problems. Many of these identities can be visualized with Pascal’s triangle above,

Symmetry of Combinations. \[\binom{n}{i}=\binom{n}{n-i}\] {#eq-symm},
Relationship between permutations and combinations. For \(0\le i\le n\), \[
P(n,i)=i!\binom{n}{i}=\frac{n!}{(n-i)!}.
\tag{6}\]






Proof





First choose the \(i\) items that will appear. There are \(\binom{n}{i}\) ways to do this. Once the items are chosen, there are \(i!\) ways to arrange them. Every ordered selection arises exactly once, so the product rule gives \(P(n,i)=i!\binom{n}{i}\).



Row sums. The entries in row \(n\) sum to \(2^n\). \[
\sum_{i=0}^n\binom{n}{i}=2^n.
\tag{7}\]






Proof





Count the subsets of a set with \(n\) items. Each item can be included or excluded, giving \(2^n\) subsets. Alternatively, group the subsets by size. There are \(\binom{n}{i}\) subsets of size \(i\), and summing over all sizes counts every subset exactly once.



Sum of squared combinations. The sum of the squares of the entries in row \(n\) equals the middle entry of row \(2n\). \[
\sum_{i=0}^n\binom{n}{i}^2=\binom{2n}{n}.
\]






Proof





Split \(2n\) distinct items into two groups of \(n\) and choose \(n\) items in total. If we choose \(i\) from the first group, we must choose \(n-i\) from the second. Choosing \(n-i\) items to include is equivalent to choosing \(i\) items to leave out, so \(\binom{n}{n-i}=\binom{n}{i}\). Summing over \(i\) gives \[
\binom{2n}{n}
=\sum_{i=0}^n\binom{n}{i}\binom{n}{n-i}
=\sum_{i=0}^n\binom{n}{i}^2.
\]



Square of a row sum. Squaring the sum of row \(n\) gives the sum of row \(2n\). \[
\left(\sum_{i=0}^n\binom{n}{i}\right)^2
=4^n
=\sum_{k=0}^{2n}\binom{2n}{k}.
\]






Proof





By the row-sum identity, row \(n\) sums to \(2^n\). Squaring gives \((2^n)^2=2^{2n}\), which is the sum of row \(2n\) by the same identity.



Addition identity (Pascal’s rule). Each interior entry is the sum of the two entries directly above it. For \(1\le i\le n-1\), \[
\binom{n}{i}
=\binom{n-1}{i-1}+\binom{n-1}{i}.
\tag{8}\]






Proof





Mark one of the \(n\) items. Every selection of \(i\) items falls into exactly one of two cases.

It includes the marked item. Choose the remaining \(i-1\) items from the other \(n-1\), giving \(\binom{n-1}{i-1}\) selections.
It excludes the marked item. Choose all \(i\) items from the other \(n-1\), giving \(\binom{n-1}{i}\) selections.

Adding the two counts gives \(\binom{n}{i}\). We can also see the identity directly by putting the two terms over a common denominator: \[
\begin{aligned}
\binom{n-1}{i-1}+\binom{n-1}{i}
&=\frac{i(n-1)!+(n-i)(n-1)!}{i!(n-i)!}\\
&=\frac{n!}{i!(n-i)!}
=\binom{n}{i}.
\end{aligned}
\]



Hockey-stick identity. For integers \(n\ge i\ge0\), \[
\sum_{j=i}^{n}\binom{j}{i}=\binom{n+1}{i+1}.
\tag{9}\]






Proof





Choose \(i+1\) numbers from \(\{1,\ldots,n+1\}\) and group the selections by their largest number. If the largest is \(j+1\), the remaining \(i\) numbers must come from \(\{1,\ldots,j\}\), giving \(\binom{j}{i}\) possibilities. Every selection has exactly one largest number, and its possible values run from \(i+1\) to \(n+1\). Summing over \(j=i,\ldots,n\) counts every selection once.



Vandermonde’s identity. For integers \(0\le i,m\le n\), \[
\binom{n}{i}
=\sum_{j=0}^{i}\binom{m}{j}\binom{n-m}{i-j}.
\tag{10}\]






Proof





Split \(n\) items into two groups of sizes \(m\) and \(n-m\). To choose \(i\) items with exactly \(j\) from the first group, we must choose the other \(i-j\) from the second. The product rule gives \(\binom{m}{j}\binom{n-m}{i-j}\) such selections. Summing over \(j\) counts every selection of \(i\) items once. If either group is too small for a proposed selection, its binomial coefficient is zero.
The sum-of-squares identity is the special case where both groups have the same size and we choose half the items.



Alternating row sums. For \(n\ge1\), the entries in even positions and the entries in odd positions have the same sum. Equivalently, \[
\sum_{i=0}^n(-1)^i\binom{n}{i}=0.
\tag{11}\]






Proof





Fix one of the \(n\) items. Pair each subset with the subset obtained by toggling that item: add it if it is absent and remove it if it is present. Toggling twice returns us to the original subset, so every subset belongs to exactly one pair. Each pair contains one even-sized subset and one odd-sized subset. Their contributions to the alternating sum cancel.



Binomial theorem. The entries of Pascal’s triangle are called binomial coefficients because they are the coefficients in the expansion of \((a+b)^n\). For every nonnegative integer \(n\), \[
(a+b)^n
=\sum_{i=0}^n\binom{n}{i}a^i b^{n-i}
=\sum_{i=0}^n\binom{n}{i}a^{n-i}b^i.
\tag{12}\]






Proof





For \(n=0\), both sides equal \(1\). Now suppose the expansion holds for \(n-1\). Multiplying by \(a+b\) gives \[
\begin{aligned}
(a+b)^n
&=a\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\binom{n-1}{i}a^i b^{n-1-i}
  +b\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\binom{n-1}{i}a^i b^{n-1-i}\\
&=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\binom{n-1}{i-1}a^i b^{n-i}
  +\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\binom{n-1}{i}a^i b^{n-i}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The first sum supplies the endpoint \(a^n\), and the second supplies \(b^n\). For each interior power \(a^i b^{n-i}\), both sums contribute. Adding their coefficients gives \(\binom{n-1}{i-1}+\binom{n-1}{i}=\binom{n}{i}\) by Pascal’s rule. This proves the first expansion. Replacing \(i\) by \(n-i\) and using \(\binom{n}{n-i}=\binom{n}{i}\) gives the second.



Binomial coefficient moment identities. Weighting the entries of row \(n\) by \(i\) or by \(i(i-1)\) gives \[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i=0}^n i\binom{n}{i} &= n2^{n-1},\\
\sum_{i=0}^n i(i-1)\binom{n}{i} &= n(n-1)2^{n-2}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{13}\]






Proof





Differentiate the binomial expansion with respect to \(a\), holding \(b\) fixed. The sum is finite, so we can differentiate term by term. For \(n\ge2\), \[
\begin{aligned}
n(a+b)^{n-1}
&=\sum_{i=1}^n i\binom{n}{i}a^{i-1}b^{n-i},\\
n(n-1)(a+b)^{n-2}
&=\sum_{i=2}^n i(i-1)\binom{n}{i}a^{i-2}b^{n-i}.
\end{aligned}
\] Set \(a=b=1\) to obtain both identities. The cases \(n=0,1\) follow directly from the first two rows of the triangle.









Example: Mean and variance of the binomial distribution





Let \(X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,p)\), so \(P(X=i)=\binom{n}{i}p^i(1-p)^{n-i}\). Setting \(a=p\) and \(b=1-p\) in the binomial theorem shows that these probabilities sum to \((p+1-p)^n=1\).
Now make the same substitution after differentiating. Multiplying the first derivative identity by \(p\) and the second by \(p^2\) restores the factor \(p^i\) in each probability. This gives \[
\begin{aligned}
E(X)
&=\sum_{i=0}^n i\,P(X=i)=np,\\
E\{X(X-1)\}
&=\sum_{i=0}^n i(i-1)\,P(X=i)=n(n-1)p^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(X^2=X(X-1)+X\), we get the variance without calculating a new sum: \[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}(X)
&=E\{X(X-1)\}+E(X)-[E(X)]^2\\
&=n(n-1)p^2+np-n^2p^2\\
&=np(1-p).
\end{aligned}
\]

title: Essential Combinatorics
Essential Combinatorics
text:
When selecting \(i\) items from \(n\) distinct items without replacement and without regard to order, we can assign each item one of two labels: selected or not selected. There are \(i\) repetitions of the first label and \(n-i\) repetitions of the second. Counting the distinct arrangements of these labels gives
\[
\binom{n}{i}
=
\frac{n!}{i!(n-i)!}
=
\binom{n}{i,n-i}.
\]
The multinomial coefficient generalizes this idea from two categories to \(K\) categories.






Theorem: Multinomial Coefficient (Thm. 1.4, Rozanov)



Suppose we have \(n\) distinct elements and \(K\) labeled categories. Let \(n_1,\ldots,n_K\) be nonnegative integers satisfying \(\sum_{i=1}^K n_i=n\). The number of ways to partition the elements into these categories, with exactly \(n_i\) elements in category \(i\), is
\[
P(n;n_1,\ldots,n_K)
\coloneqq
\binom{n}{n_1,\ldots,n_K}
=
\frac{n!}{n_1!\cdots n_K!}.
\tag{15}\]

title: Probability and Set Theory
text:
“Probability is the most important concept in modern science, especially as nobody has the slightest notion what it means.” — Bertrand Russell


Probability assigns values to events in a sample space. Starting with set theory we can define probability using Kolomogorov’s axioms on a collection of measurable subsets called a sigma algebra, denoted by \(\mathcal F\). This collection contains \(\Omega\) and is closed under complements and countable unions. Probability is defined on the events in \(\mathcal F\).






Kolmogorov Axiom and Defining Probability Measure



A probability measure \(\mathbb P\) is a set function that assigns each event a number in \([0,1]\): \[
\mathbb P:\mathcal F\longrightarrow[0,1].
\]
It satisfies the conditions of the kolmogorov axiom,

Nonnegativity: Already included in the requirement that \(\mathbb P\) takes values in \([0,1]\)
Normalization: \(\mathbb P(\Omega)=1\)
Countable additivity: For any sequence of pairwise disjoint events \(A_1,A_2,\ldots\), \[
\mathbb P\left(\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}A_n\right)
=
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\mathbb P(A_n).
\]



The triple \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) is called a probability space. We use \(Prob(A)\) and \(\mathbb P(A)\) interchangeably below, (though \(Prob(\cdot)\) is often reserved for the pushforward-measure, which is expalined in more detail in the measure-theoretic probability section)
The finer details of this framework belong to measure-theoretic probability. For many introductory applications, we work primarily with the following consequences, (which can be proven using them)






Kolmogorov Axiom Consequences: Properties of Probability




Complement rule: \[
Prob(A^c)=1-Prob(A).
\]
Empty event: \[
Prob(\emptyset)=0.
\]
Addition rule: \[
Prob(A\cup B)
=
Prob(A)+Prob(B)-Prob(A\cap B).
\]
Monotonicity: If \(A_1\subseteq A_2\), then \[
Prob(A_1)\leq Prob(A_2).
\]
Countable subadditivity (union bound): For any sequence of events \(A_1,A_2,\ldots\), \[
Prob\left(\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}A_n\right)
\leq
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}Prob(A_n).
\]



Below, we introduce key ideas in probability theory, leaving detailed treatments of particular distributions to other references and practical applications (though I can not stress enough how important becoming confrtable with different distributions is to a thorough understanding of probability theory). We introduce both standard frequentist and Bayesian viewpoints and emphasize both satisfy Kolmogorov’s axioms, but differ in how probability is interpreted and used for inference

title: Probability and Set Theory
text:
Conditional Probability


“Conditioning is the soul of statistics, every probability is conditional… Everything is conditional” — Joseph Blitzstein


What about when we care about a specific subset of random variables or have some type of prior information we want to incorporate into the probability? In that case we need a notion of probability that is dependent upon or conditional with respect to specific events,






Definition: Conditional Probability



The of event \(A\) \(B\) is, \[Prob(A\mid B)=\frac{Prob(A\cap B)}{Prob(B)}\]



Conditional Probability is for most purposes simply a more granular probability, its covering your eyes and pretending what you are conditioning on \(B\) is the new \(\Omega\) in a sense







Remark



Think of conditioning on an event \(B\) as “zooming in” on the piece of your probability space that lives inside \(B\).


The relevant probability depends on what we condition on. A small population-wide probability does not necessarily imply a small probability within a subgroup facing substantially greater exposure.



xkcd #795: Conditional Risk








rv vs set conditioning



conditioing is not an operation on an rv it is a set and set function operation so for example in consitsnecy we wouldnt write \(Y(a)=Y|A=a\) we woudll write \(A=a\implies Y=Y(a)\) or \(Y=Y(A)\)








Definition: Joint and Marginal Distributions



Let \((X,Y)\) be a pair of random variables on the same probability space.

Joint PDF (continuous case)
If \((X,Y)\) has a joint probability density function \(f_{X,Y}(x,y)\), then \[
Prob\bigl((X,Y)\in A\times B\bigr)
=
\int_A\int_B f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dy\,dx
\] for all measurable sets \(A,B\). The joint density is nonnegative and satisfies \[
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dy\,dx
=
1.
\]
A density is not itself a probability; probabilities are obtained by integrating the density over a region.
Marginal PDF
The marginal density of \(X\) “forgets” \(Y\) by integrating over its possible values, and similarly for \(Y\): \[
f_X(x)
=
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dy,
\] \[
f_Y(y)
=
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dx.
\]
Joint PMF (discrete case)
If \(X\) and \(Y\) take values in countable sets \(\mathcal S_X\) and \(\mathcal S_Y\), their joint probability mass function is \[
p_{X,Y}(x,y)
=
Prob(X=x,Y=y).
\]
It is nonnegative and satisfies \[
\sum_{x\in\mathcal S_X}\sum_{y\in\mathcal S_Y}
p_{X,Y}(x,y)
=
1.
\]
Some pairs in \(\mathcal S_X\times\mathcal S_Y\) may have probability zero.
Marginal PMF
The marginal mass functions are obtained by summing over the other variable: \[
p_X(x)
=
\sum_{y\in\mathcal S_Y}p_{X,Y}(x,y),
\] \[
p_Y(y)
=
\sum_{x\in\mathcal S_X}p_{X,Y}(x,y).
\]



This allows us to find conditional probabilities via contingency tables,






Example: Contingency Table



Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be two discrete random variables taking values in \(\{0,1\}\) with joint PMF
\[
p_{X,Y}(x,y)=
\begin{cases}
0.10,&(x,y)=(0,0),\\
0.40,&(x,y)=(0,1),\\
0.20,&(x,y)=(1,0),\\
0.30,&(x,y)=(1,1),\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\] The corresponding contingency table is
\[
\begin{array}{c|cc|c}
       & Y=0 & Y=1 & Prob(X=x) \\ \hline
X=0    & 0.10 & 0.40 & 0.50 \\
X=1    & 0.20 & 0.30 & 0.50 \\ \hline
Prob(Y=y) & 0.30 & 0.70 & 1.00
\end{array}
\] where
\[
Prob_X(0)=0.10+0.40=0.50,\quad
Prob_X(1)=0.20+0.30=0.50,
\] \[
Prob_Y(0)=0.10+0.20=0.30,\quad
Prob_Y(1)=0.40+0.30=0.70.
\] We can also compute conditional probabilities, for instance
\[\begin{aligned}
Prob(Y=1\mid X=0)
&=\frac{Prob(X=0,Y=1)}{Prob(X=0)}
=\frac{0.40}{0.50}=0.80\\
Prob(X=1\mid Y=0)
&=\frac{Prob(X=1,Y=0)}{Prob(Y=0)}
=\frac{0.20}{0.30}\approx0.67\end{aligned}\]


Conditional PDF are defined similarly to conditional probabilities via dividing joint and marginal PDF, and going back to \(Prob\) vs \(\mathbb{P}\) we see there is really no difference and we define,






Definition: Conditional density



Let \((X,Y)\) have joint density \(f_{X,Y}(x,y)\) and marginal density \[
f_Y(y)=\int_{-\infty}^\infty f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dx,
\] and assume \(f_Y(y)>0\). Then the of \(X\) given \(Y=y\) is \[
f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)
\;=\;
\frac{f_{X,Y}(x,y)}{f_Y(y)},
\] which satisfies \(\int_{-\infty}^\infty f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)\,dx = 1\)








Example: COnditional Probability



Let \((X,Y)\) have joint density \[
f_{X,Y}(x,y)
=\begin{cases}
2, & 0 \le x \le y \le 1,\\
0, & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\] First compute the marginal of \(Y\): \[
f_Y(y)
=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dx
=\int_{0}^{y} 2\,dx
=2y,
\quad 0\le y\le1.
\] Since \(f_Y(y)>0\) on \([0,1]\), the conditional density of \(X\) given \(Y=y\) is \[
f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)
=\frac{f_{X,Y}(x,y)}{f_Y(y)}
=\frac{2}{2y}
=\frac{1}{y},
\quad 0\le x\le y.
\] One checks \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)\,dx
=\int_{0}^{y}\frac{1}{y}\,dx
=1\), as required









Properties of Conditional Probability



Given a large joint probability or density we can factor it using conditionals,
\[\begin{aligned}f(x_1,\ldots,x_n) &= f(x_n \vert x_1,\ldots,x_{n-1})f(x_1,\ldots,x_{n-1})\\
&= f(x_n \vert x_1,\ldots,x_{n-1})f(x_{n-1}|x_1,\ldots,x_{n-2})f(x_1,\ldots,x_{n-2})\end{aligned}\]
and so on until
\[f(x_1,\ldots,x_n) = f(x_1)f(x_2 | x_1)f(x_3|x_1,x_2)\ldots f(x_n|x_1,\ldots,x_{n-1})\]
This is especially helpful as it helps us marginalize/integrate out dimensions/RV. Once you’ve factorized the joint via the chain rule, marginalization becomes a matter of “peeling off” one factor at a time by summing or integrating out the unwanted variables.








Marginalization



Suppose we had two RV with density \(f_{X_1,X_2}(x_1,x_2)\) and we want \(f_{X_1}(x1)\), using the factorization above \[
f_{X_1}(x_1)
=\int f_{X_1,X_2}(x_1,x_2)\,dx_2
=\int f_{X_1\mid X_2}(x_1\mid x_2)\,f_{X_2}(x_2)\,dx_2
\] Generally with \(n\) RV, \[
f_{X_1}(x_1)
=\int\cdots\int
\Bigl[\prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i\mid x_{i+1},\dots,x_n)\Bigr]
\,dx_2dx_3\cdots dx_n
\]








Example



Let \((X_1,X_2)\) be uniformly distributed on the unit square \([0,1]\times[0,1]\), so its joint density is \[
f_{X_1,X_2}(x_1,x_2)
=\begin{cases}
1,&0\le x_1\le1,\;0\le x_2\le1,\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\] The marginal density of \(X_1\) is obtained by integrating out \(x_2\): \[
f_{X_1}(x_1)
=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f_{X_1,X_2}(x_1,x_2)\,dx_2
=\int_{0}^{1}1\,dx_2
=\begin{cases}
1,&0\le x_1\le1,\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]








Example: de Montmort’s Matching Problem



Suppose we have \(n\) cards numbered \(1,\ldots,n\). We shuffle them uniformly at random and place them in \(n\) positions. What is the probability that at least one card occupies its correctly numbered position?
Let \(A_i\) denote the event that card \(i\) is in position \(i\). We want
\[
P\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^n A_i\right).
\]
There are \(n!\) equally likely permutations. If a particular card \(i\) must occupy its correct position, the remaining \(n-1\) cards can be arranged in \((n-1)!\) ways. Therefore,
\[
P(A_i)=\frac{(n-1)!}{n!}=\frac1n.
\]
More generally, if \(k\) specified cards must occupy their correct positions, the remaining \(n-k\) cards can be arranged in \((n-k)!\) ways. Thus, for distinct indices \(i_1,\ldots,i_k\),
\[
P(A_{i_1}\cap\cdots\cap A_{i_k})
=
\frac{(n-k)!}{n!}.
\]
By the inclusion–exclusion principle,
\[
\begin{aligned}
P\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^n A_i\right)
&=
\sum_{k=1}^n
(-1)^{k+1}
\sum_{\substack{S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\\|S|=k}}
P\left(\bigcap_{i\in S}A_i\right)\\
&=
\sum_{k=1}^n
(-1)^{k+1}
\binom nk\frac{(n-k)!}{n!}\\
&=
\sum_{k=1}^n
\frac{(-1)^{k+1}}{k!}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The final simplification follows from
\[
\binom nk\frac{(n-k)!}{n!}=\frac1{k!}.
\]
Recall the Taylor series
\[
e^{-1}=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^k}{k!}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\boxed{
\lim_{n\to\infty}
P(\text{at least one match})
=
1-\frac1e
\approx 0.6321.
}
\]
Equivalently, the probability that no cards occupy their correct positions approaches \(1/e\approx0.3679\).
A permutation with no fixed points is called a derangement. The number of derangements of \(n\) objects, commonly denoted \(!n\), is therefore
\[
\boxed{
!n=n!\sum_{k=0}^n\frac{(-1)^k}{k!}.
}
\]
This example illustrates how inclusion–exclusion allows us to calculate the probability of a union of dependent events, even when directly counting the desired outcomes is difficult.
See Blitzstein’s Statistics 110, Lecture 3 for a discussion of the problem.








Example:Newton pepys problem



pepys strongly belived (c) is the best but (a) is the best via binomial theorem but this is not obvious



Laws of Total Probability, Expectation and Variation
Conditioning also helps establish the law of total probability,






Theorem: Law of Total Probability



Let \(\{A_1, A_2, \dots, A_n\}\) be a partition of the sample space (so \(Prob(A_i)>0\) for all \(i\) and \(\sum_{i=1}^nProb(A_i)=1\)), and let \(B\) be any event with \(Prob(B)>0\) then \[
Prob(B)
=\sum_{i=1}^n Prob(B\mid A_i)\,Prob(A_i) = \sum_{i=1}^n \,Prob(A_i\cap B)
\]


Again this law can be written in terms of PDF and more generally \(\mathbb{P}\) as well.






Example: Law of Total Probability



Suppose bulbs are produced by two factories. Factory \(A\) produces 60% of all bulbs with a 5% defect rate, and Factory \(B\) produces 40% of all bulbs with a 10% defect rate. Let \[
A_1 = \{\text{bulb from Factory }A\},\quad
A_2 = \{\text{bulb from Factory }B\},
\] so \(\{A_1,A_2\}\) is a partition with \(P(A_1)=0.6\) and \(P(A_2)=0.4\). Let \(D\) be the event “bulb is defective.” Then by the law of total probability, \[\begin{aligned}
Prob(D)
&= Prob(D\mid A_1)\,Prob(A_1) \;+\; Prob(D\mid A_2)\,Prob(A_2)\\
&= (0.05)(0.6) + (0.10)(0.4)\\
&= 0.03 + 0.04\\
&= 0.07\end{aligned}
\] Thus the overall defect rate is 7%.


Generalizing the law of total probability leads to the law of total expectation: we can compute an overall expectation by first computing conditional expectations and then averaging them over the distribution of the conditioning variable.






Theorem: Law of Total Expectation



Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be random variables with \(E[|Y|]<\infty\). Then \[
E[Y]=E\bigl[E[Y\mid X]\bigr].
\]
If \(X\) is discrete, \[
E[Y]
=
\sum_{x:\,Prob(X=x)>0} E[Y\mid X=x]\,Prob(X=x).
\]
If \(X\) has a density \(f_X\), \[
E[Y]
=
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} E[Y\mid X=x]\,f_X(x)\,dx.
\]


Here \(E[Y\mid X]\) is itself a random variable: its value depends on \(X\). The outer expectation averages these conditional means over the distribution of \(X\), recovering the unconditional mean of \(Y\).






Example: Averaging Group Means



Suppose \(X\) indicates treatment group, with \(Prob(X=1)=0.4\) and \(Prob(X=0)=0.6\). If the mean outcome in each group is \[
E[Y\mid X=1]=10,
\qquad
E[Y\mid X=0]=5,
\] then the overall mean is \[
E[Y]
=
10(0.4)+5(0.6)
=
7.
\]
Thus, the overall mean is the weighted average of the group means, with weights given by the proportions in each group.


The law of total probability is a special case: take \(Y=\mathbf{1}_B\), the indicator of an event \(B\). Since expectations of indicators are probabilities, \[
Prob(B)
=
E[\mathbf{1}_B]
=
E\bigl[E[\mathbf{1}_B\mid X]\bigr]
=
E\bigl[Prob(B\mid X)\bigr].
\]
This helps establish the law of total variation
\[Var(Y) = E(Var(Y|X)) + Var(E(Y|X))\]
Finally conditional probabilities are directional \(Prob(A|B) \neq Prob(B|A)\) but they are related via Baye’s Theorem






Theorem: Bayes’ Theorem



Let \(A\) and \(B\) be events with \(Prob(A)>0\) and \(Prob(B)>0\). Then \[
Prob(A\mid B)
=
\frac{Prob(B\mid A)\,Prob(A)}{Prob(B)}.
\]
More generally, let \(\{A_1,A_2,\dots,A_n\}\) be a partition of the sample space, with \(Prob(A_i)>0\) for every \(i\), and let \(B\) be an event with \(Prob(B)>0\). Then, for each \(k=1,\dots,n\), \[
Prob(A_k\mid B)
=
\frac{Prob(B\mid A_k)\,Prob(A_k)}
{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n Prob(B\mid A_i)\,Prob(A_i)}.
\]
The denominator is obtained from the law of total probability: \[
Prob(B)
=
\sum_{i=1}^n Prob(B\mid A_i)\,Prob(A_i).
\]





xkcd #1236: Seashell


Bayes’ theorem allows us to reverse the direction of conditioning. In general, \(P(A\mid B)\) and \(P(B\mid A)\) are not equal: observing evidence changes our probability assessment according to both its likelihood and the prior probability of the event.






Example: Bayes’ Theorem in diagnostic testing



Let \(D\) be the event “patient has the disease” and \(T^+\) be the event “test is positive.” Let \(T^-\) denote a negative result. Suppose \[
Prob(D)=0.01,
\qquad
Prob(T^+\mid D)=0.99,
\qquad
Prob(T^-\mid D^c)=0.95.
\]
Thus, the disease prevalence is \(1\%\), the test sensitivity is \(99\%\), and its specificity is \(95\%\).
By the complement rule, \[
Prob(T^+\mid D^c)
=
1-Prob(T^-\mid D^c)
=
0.05.
\]
Applying Bayes’ theorem and the law of total probability, \[
\begin{aligned}
Prob(D\mid T^+)
&=
\frac{Prob(T^+\mid D)\,Prob(D)}
{Prob(T^+\mid D)\,Prob(D)
+Prob(T^+\mid D^c)\,Prob(D^c)}
\\[6pt]
&=
\frac{0.99\cdot0.01}
{0.99\cdot0.01+0.05\cdot0.99}
\\[6pt]
&=
\frac{0.0099}{0.0099+0.0495}
\\[6pt]
&\approx 0.167.
\end{aligned}
\]
Hence, even with a highly sensitive and reasonably specific test, the probability that a person has the disease given a positive result is only about \(16.7\%\) in this population. Because the disease is uncommon, false positives among people without the disease outnumber true positives among those with it.

title: Probability and Set Theory
text:
Independence






Definition: Independent RV



Two random variables \(X\) and \(Y\) are said to be if knowledge of one provides information about the other. They are if knowing one gives no information about the other. Equivalently, \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent if and only if their joint distribution factorizes into the product of the marginals: \[
\begin{cases}
p_{X,Y}(x,y)
= p_X(x)\,p_Y(y),
&\text{(discrete case),}\$6pt]
f_{X,Y}(x,y)
= f_X(x)\,f_Y(y),
&\text{(continuous case),}
\end{cases}
\quad\text{for all }x,y.
\] Equivalently in terms of events and probabilities, for all measurable A and B, \[
\mathbb{P}\bigl(X\in A,\,Y\in B\bigr)
= \mathbb{P}\bigl(X\in A\bigr)\,\mathbb{P}\bigl(Y\in B\bigr)
\]


If this factorization fails, then \(X\) and \(Y\) are . In practice, independence is sometimes assumed, other times it is assessed which amounts to verifying one of these equivalent factorization criteria.






Example: XKCD #1985, marginal probabilities alone do not determine joint probabilities






xkcd #1985: Meteorologist


Suppose a weather forecast reports a 20% chance of rain during each of the next five hours. What is the probability that it rains at least once?
Let \(A_i\) denote the event that it rains during hour \(i\), with \(P(A_i)=0.2\) for \(i=1,\ldots,5\). We want to calculate
\[
P\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^5 A_i\right).
\]
If the hourly events are mutually independent, the complement rule gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
P\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^5 A_i\right)
&=1-P\left(\bigcap_{i=1}^5 A_i^c\right)\\
&=1-\prod_{i=1}^5 P(A_i^c)\\
&=1-(0.8)^5\\
&\approx0.6723.
\end{aligned}
\]
However, if rain occurs during all five hours together or not at all, the probability is only \(0.2\). Alternatively, if the five events are mutually exclusive, the probability is \(5(0.2)=1\).
Thus, the same five marginal probabilities can yield dramatically different probabilities for their union, depending on the dependence structure.
Independence is an assumption about the joint distribution, not a consequence of knowing the marginal distributions.








Example



Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be two independent fair coin flips, each taking values in \(\{H,T\}\) with \[
Prob(X=H)=Prob(X=T)=\tfrac12,
\quad
Prob(Y=H)=Prob(Y=T)=\tfrac12.
\] Then \[
Prob(X=H,\,Y=H)=\tfrac12\times\tfrac12=\tfrac14
= Prob(X=H)\,Prob(Y=H),
\] and similarly for all other outcomes, so \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent.
 Now define \(Z = X\). Clearly
\[Prob(X=H,\,Z=H)=Prob(X=H)=\tfrac12\] but \[Prob(X=H)\,Prob(Z=H)=\tfrac12\times\tfrac12=\tfrac14\]
Since \(Prob(X=H,Z=H)\neq Prob(X=H)Prob(Z=H)\), \(X\) and \(Z\) are dependent.


Independence has nice effects on Mean and Cov






Effects of Independence on Expectation and Covariance



Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be independent random variables with finite second moments.
Then: - \(\displaystyle \mathbb{E}[X+Y] = \mathbb{E}[X] + \mathbb{E}[Y].\)

\(\displaystyle \mathbb{E}[XY] = \mathbb{E}[X]\,\mathbb{E}[Y].\)
\(\displaystyle Cov(X,Y) = \mathbb{E}[XY] - \mathbb{E}[X]\mathbb{E}[Y] = 0.\)
\(\displaystyle Var(X+Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y)\)



Having an independent set of possibilities is not the same thing as having a mutually exclusive set of possibilities, in fact being mutually exclusive implies dependence,






Mutually Exclusive Implies Dependence



Mutually exclusive events with positive probability are dependent








Proof



Mutual exclusivity means \[Prob(A\cap B)=0.\] Independence would require \[Prob(A\cap B)=Prob(A)\,Prob(B).\] Combining these gives \[0 = Prob(A)\,Prob(B),\] which contradicts \(Prob(A)>0\) and \(Prob(B)>0\). Hence mutually exclusive events with positive probability are necessarily dependent.








Example



Roll a fair six-sided die once. Let \[A = \{\,\text{roll is even}\} = \{2,4,6\},
\quad
B = \{\,\text{roll is odd}\} = \{1,3,5\}.\] Then \[Prob(A)=\tfrac{3}{6}=\tfrac12,\quad
Prob(B)=\tfrac{3}{6}=\tfrac12,\quad
Prob(A\cap B)=0,\] but \[Prob(A)\,Prob(B)=\tfrac12\times\tfrac12=\tfrac14\neq 0.\] Thus \(A\) and \(B\) are mutually exclusive yet not independent.



Independence and Conditional Probability
Another way of thinking of independence is that conditioning has no effect on the probabilities of events (or on distributions of random variables).






Independence via Conditional PDF



Two random variables \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent if and only if \[
\begin{cases}
p_{X}(x)
= p_{X|Y}(x|y),\text{ or }\quad p_{Y}(y)
= p_{Y|X}(y|x)
&\text{(discrete case),}\\
f_{X}(x)
= f_{X|Y}(x|y),\text{ or }\quad f_{Y}(y)
= f_{Y|X}(y|x)
&\text{(continuous case),}
\end{cases}
\quad\text{for all }x,y.
\] Equivalently in terms of events and probabilities, for all measurable A and B,
\[\mathbb{P}\bigl(X\in A\bigr)
= \mathbb{P}\bigl(X\in A \vert Y \in B\bigr), \quad \mathbb{P}\bigl(Y\in B\bigr)
= \mathbb{P}\bigl(Y\in B \vert X \in A\bigr)\]


By bayes rule we know \(P(AB) = P(A|B)P(B)\) if \(P(A|B) = P(A)\) we arrive at our previous definition of independence, therefore the two definitions are independent.
Going through the same coin flip example,






Example



Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be two independent fair coin flips, each taking values in \(\{H,T\}\) with \[
Prob(X=H)=Prob(X=T)=\tfrac12,
\quad
Prob(Y=H)=Prob(Y=T)=\tfrac12.
\] To show independence by conditioning, observe for example \[
Prob\bigl(X=H\mid Y=H\bigr)
=\frac{Prob(X=H,Y=H)}{Prob(Y=H)}
=\frac{\tfrac14}{\tfrac12}
=\tfrac12
=Prob(X=H).
\] Since conditioning on \(Y=H\) does not change the probability of \(X=H\), and similarly for all other combinations, \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent








Remark: Mutual Exclusivity and \(r\)-Wise Independence



A collection of events \(\{A_1,\ldots,A_n\}\), where \(A_i\subseteq\Omega\), is pairwise mutually exclusive if
\[
A_i\cap A_j=\emptyset
\qquad\text{for all }i\neq j.
\]
This is usually referred to simply as mutual exclusivity. More generally, we can define \(r\)-wise exclusivity by requiring that the intersection of every \(r\) distinct events is empty. Consequently,
\[
\boxed{
\text{Pairwise exclusivity}
\implies
\text{3-wise exclusivity}
\implies
\cdots
\implies
\text{$n$-wise exclusivity}.
}
\]
The reverse implications do not generally hold. For example, three events can have an empty three-way intersection while having nonempty pairwise intersections.
Statistical independence has the opposite hierarchy. A collection of events is called \(r\)-wise independent if every subcollection of at most \(r\) events is independent. In particular, pairwise independence requires
\[
P(A_i\cap A_j)=P(A_i)P(A_j)
\qquad\text{for all }i\neq j,
\]
whereas mutual independence requires, for every nonempty subset \(S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\),
\[
P\left(\bigcap_{i\in S}A_i\right)
=
\prod_{i\in S}P(A_i).
\]
Thus,
\[
\boxed{
\text{$n$-wise independence}
\implies
\cdots
\implies
\text{3-wise independence}
\implies
\text{Pairwise independence}.
}
\]
Again, the reverse implications do not generally hold. Pairwise independence alone does not imply that three or more events are jointly independent.
Finally, mutual exclusivity and independence are distinct properties. If \(A\) and \(B\) are mutually exclusive and both have positive probability, then
\[
P(A\cap B)=0
\neq
P(A)P(B)>0,
\]
so they cannot be independent.

title: Probability and Set Theory
text:
Random Variables


“Random variables are a lot like Guinea pigs, neither a pig, nor from Guinea” — A conversation I overheard as an undergrad


Random variables are actually measurable functions \(X:\Omega \to \mathbb{R}\) on the sample space. We use these functions to evaluate randomly selecte Random variables are the “mechanisms” assigning values to events and subsequently allowing us to assign probability to events, most genrally A random function is a probability distribution on a space of functions, i.e. a function-valued random variable. Very confusing!






Definition: Random Variable [RV]



Given a sample space \(\Omega\) a assigns a real value to any outcome \(\omega \in \Omega\),
\[X:\Omega \to \mathbb{R}\]


When \(\Omega\) is small and obvious (say, the set of poker hands) it’s just as easy to reason on \(\Omega\) itself. But in more elaborate experiments, \(\Omega\) can be huge or hard to describe, so we summarize everything by the distribution of the random variable \(X\). The collection of possible values of \(X\) (together with their probabilities) then completely characterizes the underlying random process.






Definition: Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF)



Let \(X\) be a real-valued random variable. Its is the function \[F_X(x)= Prob\bigl(X \le x\bigr)= \mathbb{P}\bigl(\{\omega\in\Omega: X(\omega)\le x\}\bigr),\quad x\in\mathbb{R}\] It satisfies the following properties:

\(F_X\) is nondecreasing/monotonically increasing: if \(x_1<x_2\) then \(F_X(x_1)\le F_X(x_2)\).
Right-continuous: \(\displaystyle \lim_{h\downarrow0}F_X(x+h)=F_X(x)\) for all \(x\).
Boundary limits at 0 and 1: \(\displaystyle \lim_{x\to-\infty}F_X(x)=0\) and \(\displaystyle \lim_{x\to+\infty}F_X(x)=1\).



CDF \(F_X\) uniquely determine the map/law of \(X\) but they must satisfy the above properties to be a valid CDF, that is if two RV have the same valid CDF they are indistinguishable probabilistically even if they are describing the same situations!






Example



Suppose we have two piecewise functions, which is a CDF and which is not?

\[\begin{align*}
  F(x)&=
  \begin{cases}
    0,     & x<0,\\
    a,     & x=0,\\
    a + (1-a)\,\dfrac{x}{2}, & 0<x<2,\\
    1,     & x\ge2,
  \end{cases}\\
  G(x)&=
  \begin{cases}
    0,     & x<0,\\
    b,     & x=0,\\
    a + (1-a)\,\dfrac{x}{2}, & 0<x<2,\\
    1,     & x\ge2,
  \end{cases}
\end{align*}\]
We check the CDF axiom above systematically,

Non decreasing: Both \(F\) and \(G\) are non-decreasing
Right continuity: \(F\) is right continuous but \(G\) is not (at \(x=0\))
Limits at \(\pm\infty\): \[\lim_{x\to-\infty}F(x)=0,\;
   \lim_{x\to+\infty}F(x)=1\] and similarly for \(G\)

Conclusion: \(F\) is a valid CDF, while \(G\) is not.


In statistical modeling, we specify a collection of candidate distributions \(\mathcal P\) and use observed data to infer which distribution, or which features of that distribution, best describe the data-generating process. Before exploring those applications, however, it is crucial to distinguish between discrete and continuous random variables, since the techniques and interpretations differ for each case.






Definition: Support



The \(\mathcal{S}\) of a RV is the set of real values that have nonzero probability - the ranomd variable “puts” probability on the support. This corresponds to the possible set of elementary events in the discrete case and in the continuous case it is the set the PDF is strictly positive on.



Distributions of Random Variables


Important Distriubtions
bernoulli, binomial, poisson,, normal ,gamma
Adjust the number of trials and success probability to explore a binomial distribution.

viewof binom_n = Inputs.range([1, 50], {

  step: 1,
  label: "Number of trials (n)"
})
viewof binom_p = Inputs.range([0.05, 0.95], {
  value: 0.5,
  step: 0.05,
  label: "Success probability (p)"
})
























Plot.plot({
  width: 680,
  height: 320,
  marginBottom: 45,
  x: {label: "Number of successes", domain: [-0.5, binom_n + 0.5]},
  y: {label: "Probability", grid: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.rectY(binom_data, {
      x1: d => d.k - 0.42,
      x2: d => d.k + 0.42,
      y: "prob",
      fill: "#506c83",
      tip: true
    }),
    Plot.ruleY([0])
  ]
})







html`<p><strong>Mean:</strong> ${(binom_n * binom_p).toFixed(2)}
  |  
<strong>Variance:</strong> ${(binom_n * binom_p * (1 - binom_p)).toFixed(2)}</p>`












Discrete Random Variable and Probability Mass Function (PMF)



A random variable \(X\) is called discrete if its distribution is concentrated on an at most countable set of points. Its support may be written as
\[
\mathcal S_X
=
\{x\in\mathbb R:Prob(X=x)>0\}.
\]
The probability mass function (PMF) is defined by
\[
p_X(x)
=
Prob(X=x),
\qquad
x\in\mathcal S_X,
\]
and satisfies
\[
\sum_{x\in\mathcal S_X}p_X(x)=1.
\]
Thus, a discrete distribution assigns positive probability mass directly to individual points








Example: Bernoulli Random Variable



Suppose \(X=1\) represents success and \(X=0\) represents failure. Then \(X\) is a discrete random variable with a Bernoulli distribution. If \(Prob(X=1)=p\), then \(Prob(X=0)=1-p\).


What matters to a random variable is its probability distribution, not whether its realized values appear random or equally likely.






Example: XKCD #221 — Degenerate Distributions






xkcd #221: Random Number


Although the function in the comic always returns 4, it still defines a valid random variable, albeit one with a degenerate distribution. If \(X=4\) with probability one, its distribution is a Dirac point mass at 4, denoted by
\[
P_X=\delta_4,
\]
where the Dirac measure is defined by
\[
\delta_4(A)=
\begin{cases}
1, & 4\in A,\\
0, & 4\notin A.
\end{cases}
\]
Equivalently, its PMF is \(p_X(x)=\mathbf{1}_{\{4\}}(x)\). We can also formally express its generalized density using the Dirac delta function,
\[
f_X(x)=\delta(x-4),
\]
although this is not an ordinary density with respect to Lebesgue measure.
Thus, \(P(X=4)=1\), \(E[X]=4\), and \(Var(X)=0\). The function does not generate new random outcomes; it simply returns the same value every time.








Example: XKCD #1277 — Randomness and the Principle of Indifference






xkcd #1277: Ayn Random


The comic satirizes Ayn Rand’s philosophical system of Objectivism, joking that a random number generator favoring certain numbers might be justified because those numbers are intrinsically better.
This illustrates a distinction between randomness and uniformity. A random variable need not assign equal probabilities to all possible outcomes. For example,
\[
p_X(x)=
\begin{cases}
0.2, & x=1,\\
0.3, & x=2,\\
0.5, & x=3,\\
0, & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\]
defines a perfectly valid, albeit nonuniform, discrete distribution.
This connects to the philosophical principle of indifference, also known as the principle of insufficient reason. Roughly, the principle suggests assigning equal probabilities to alternatives when there is no reason to favor one over another. However, lack of information does not mathematically imply equal probabilities, and the choice of how to partition the outcomes matters.
For example, two independent fair six-sided dice produce 36 equally likely ordered outcomes, but only 11 possible sums. Assuming these sums are equally likely would incorrectly give
\[
P(X_1+X_2=7)=\frac{1}{11},
\]
whereas counting the underlying outcomes gives
\[
P(X_1+X_2=7)=\frac{6}{36}=\frac16.
\]
Thus, uniformity must be justified by the probability model, rather than assumed merely because the outcome is random. A biased random number generator is not inherently invalid; it is problematic when it claims to sample from a different distribution.


The examples above illustrate that discrete random variables assign probability to individual outcomes, whether those probabilities are uniform, unequal, or concentrated entirely at a single point. However, many quantities of interest, such as time, height, or temperature, are naturally modeled as taking values along a continuum. This motivates continuous random variables, for which individual points have probability zero and probabilities are instead assigned to intervals or other measurable sets.






Continuous Random Variables



A random variable \(X\) is called continuous if its distribution has no point masses. Equivalently,
\[
Prob(X=x)=0
\]
for every \(x\in\mathbb R\). This is equivalent to the CDF \(F_X\) being continuous.
Thus, unlike a discrete random variable, a continuous random variable does not assign positive probability to individual points. Probability is instead spread across subsets of \(\mathbb R\).
It is important, however, that a continuous random variable does not necessarily possess a probability density function. A continuous CDF may fail to be representable as the integral of a density. The Cantor distribution is the standard example.
The continuous distributions most commonly encountered in statistical modeling belong to the stronger class of absolutely continuous distributions, for which a PDF does exist.








Example: Normal Random Variable



A random variable with distribution \(N(\mu,\sigma^2)\) is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure and has support over all of \(\mathbb R\). Individual points have probability zero, while probabilities of intervals are obtained by integrating the normal density across the input axis (not the vertical output axis as the image below)

Example: Computing Expectations



 Let \(X\) be the outcome of a fair six‐sided die, so \[
Prob(X=i)=\frac{1}{6},\quad i=1,2,\dots,6.
\] Then \[
\mathbb{E}[X]
=\sum_{i=1}^{6} i\;Prob(X=i)
=\sum_{i=1}^{6} i\;\frac{1}{6}
=\frac{1+2+3+4+5+6}{6}
=\frac{21}{6}
=3.5.
\]
 Let \(Y\sim Uniform(0,1)\), so its density is \[
f_Y(y)=
\begin{cases}
1,&0\le y\le1,\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\] Then \[
\mathbb{E}[Y]
=\int_{0}^{1} y\,f_Y(y)\,dy
=\int_{0}^{1} y\,dy
=\Bigl[\tfrac{y^2}{2}\Bigr]_{0}^{1}
=\tfrac12.
\]








Variance



The of a random variable \(X\) is the expected square distance from the population mean. We write given \(X\) continuous and discrete respectively, with \(\mu\) denoting the population mean,
\[\boxed{Var(X) = \int_{x\in\mathcal{S}}(x-\mu)^2f_X(x)dx,\quad\mathbb{E}(X) = \sum_{x\in\mathcal{S}}(x-\mu)^2f_X(x)}\]
Standard Deviation is the square root of the variance








Example: Computing Variance



 Let \(X\) be the outcome of a fair coin coded as \[
Prob(X=1)=Prob(X=0)=\tfrac12.
\] Then \(\mu = \mathbb{E}[X] = \tfrac12\) and \[
Var(X)
= \sum_{x\in\{0,1\}} (x-\mu)^2\,Prob(X=x)
= (0-\tfrac12)^2\cdot\tfrac12 + (1-\tfrac12)^2\cdot\tfrac12
= \tfrac{1}{4}\cdot\tfrac12 + \tfrac{1}{4}\cdot\tfrac12
= \tfrac{1}{4}.
\]
 Let \(Y\sim Uniform(0,1)\), so \(f_Y(y)=1\) for \(0\le y\le1\). Then \(\mu=\mathbb{E}[Y]=\tfrac12\) and \[
Var(Y)
= \int_{0}^{1} (y-\tfrac12)^2\,dy
= \int_{0}^{1} \bigl(y^2 - y + \tfrac14\bigr)\,dy
= \Bigl[\tfrac{y^3}{3} - \tfrac{y^2}{2} + \tfrac{y}{4}\Bigr]_0^1
= \tfrac{1}{3} - \tfrac{1}{2} + \tfrac{1}{4}
= \tfrac{1}{12}.
\]

Covariance



Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be random variables with means \(\mu_X\) and \(\mu_Y\) \[\boxed{\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y) \;=\; \mathbb{E}\bigl[(X - \mu_X)\,(Y - \mu_Y)\bigr]}\]








Example: Computing Covariance



 Let \((X,Y)\) have the joint distribution \[
Prob(X=0,Y=0)=\tfrac12,
\quad
Prob(X=1,Y=2)=\tfrac12,
\] and zero otherwise. Then \[
\mathbb{E}[X]
=0\cdot\tfrac12 +1\cdot\tfrac12
=\tfrac12,
\qquad
\mathbb{E}[Y]
=0\cdot\tfrac12 +2\cdot\tfrac12
=1.
\] Now compute \[\begin{aligned}
Cov(X,Y)
&=\mathbb{E}\bigl[(X-\tfrac12)(Y-1)\bigr]\\
&=\tfrac12\bigl[(0-\tfrac12)(0-1)+(1-\tfrac12)(2-1)\bigr]\\
&=\tfrac12\bigl[(\!-\,\tfrac12)(\!-1)+(\tfrac12)(1)\bigr]\\
&=\tfrac12(\tfrac12+\tfrac12)\\
&=\tfrac12\end{aligned}
\] Hence \(Cov(X,Y)=\tfrac12\)
 Let \(X\sim Uniform(0,1)\) with density \(f_X(x)=1\) for \(0\le x\le1\), and define \(Y=2X\). Then \[
\mu_X = \mathbb{E}[X] = \int_0^1 x\,dx = \frac12,
\qquad
\mu_Y = \mathbb{E}[Y] = 2\,\mathbb{E}[X] = 1.
\] Next, \[
\mathbb{E}[XY] = \mathbb{E}[2X^2] = 2\int_0^1 x^2\,dx = \frac{2}{3}.
\] Hence \[
Cov(X,Y) = \mathbb{E}[XY] - \mathbb{E}[X]\,\mathbb{E}[Y]
= \frac{2}{3} - \Bigl(\frac12\cdot 1\Bigr)
= \frac{2}{3} - \frac{1}{2}
= \frac{1}{6}.
\]


The mean and variance of a random variable \(\mathbb{E}(X), var(X)\) actually describe characteristics of the sampling distribution of \(X\) and our sample based estimators seek to infer these characteristics. Definition: Raw and Central Moments



Let \(X\) be a random variable with finite moments, and let \(\mu = \mathbb{E}[X]\) denote its first (raw) moment. For any integer \(r \geq 1\):

The \(r\)th of \(X\) is \[
\mu'_r \;=\; \mathbb{E}\bigl[X^r\bigr].
\]
The \(r\)th of \(X\) is \[
\mu_r \;=\; \mathbb{E}\bigl[\,(X - \mu)^r\bigr].
\] In particular, \(\mu_1 = 0\) and \(\mu_2 = Var(X)\).









Example: Raw and Central Moments



Let \(X\sim Uniform(0,1)\). Then its \(r\)th raw moment is \[
\mu'_r = \mathbb{E}[X^r] = \int_{0}^{1} x^r \,dx = \frac{1}{r+1}.
\] In particular, \[\mu'_1 = \frac{1}{2},
\quad
\mu'_2 = \frac{1}{3},
\quad
\mu'_3 = \frac{1}{4},\;\ldots\] The mean is \(\mu = \mu'_1 = \tfrac12\), and the central moments are \[\mu_r = \mathbb{E}\bigl[(X - \mu)^r\bigr]
= \int_{0}^{1}\Bigl(x - \tfrac12\Bigr)^r\,dx.\] Hence \[\mu_1 = 0,
\quad
\mu_2 = \int_{0}^{1}\Bigl(x-\tfrac12\Bigr)^2 dx = \frac{1}{12}\]


Importantly when we do not have access to \(\mu\) we must estimate it in the central moments.

Intuition on Moments
Moments and their definition seem unmotivated and odd at first, but they are actually the same thing as the moment of inertia from newton’s mechanics. Specifically the moment of inertia measures an object’s resistance to change in angular momentum and it changes depending on the distribution of weights in the object. Moments of a distribution similarly describe the shape and characteristics of a distribution.
Newton’s second law gives us the relationship between mass, force and acceleration of objects in a straight line, \[F = ma\]
essentially, in order to accelerate different objects in the same manner we must use force that is proportional to the of the object. Through this lens, mass is a measure of resistance to linear acceleration. Similarly, when we wish to accelerate an object rotationally (rotate it about some axis) we have some resistance to this acceleration - we call this resistance the , \(I\), and it is dependent on the with respect to the center of rotation, if the center of rotation is \(\textbf{c} = (c_1,c_2,\cdots, c_n)\) and we denote our object as \(\textbf{O}\), \[I = \int r^2 dm\]where \(r\) is the distance from the point in the object with differential mass \(dm\) to the center of rotation \(\textbf{c}\) if we describe the points in the object as \(\textbf{x} \in \textbf{O}\) we have an equivalent formula for the moment of inertia as,
\[\begin{align*}
    I &= \int_{\textbf{x} \in \textbf{O}} (dist(\textbf{x}, \textbf{c}))^2 dm\\
    &= \int_{\textbf{x} \in \textbf{O}} \left(\sqrt{\sum_{k \leq n}{(x_k - c_k)^2}}\right)^2 dm\\
    &= \int_{\textbf{x} \in \textbf{O}} \left(\sum_{k \leq n}{(x_k - c_k)^2}\right)dm
\end{align*}\]
if our object is some mass distributed across one dimension we have the moment of inertia as,
\[\begin{equation*}
    I =\int_{x \in \textbf{O}} \left(x-c\right)^2 dm
\end{equation*}\]
Notice this is a very similar formula to the one we use for calculating the second central moment of a probability distribution (variance) where the c, center of rotation, is equivalent to the mean centering. We solidify this connection through two examples, one inertia calculation and one probability density calculation.

    I &= \int_{0}^{1} (x-\frac{1}{2})^2 dx\\

Remark on central moments



 Central moments describe the shape relative to a central point. Generally this implies the mean of a statistical distribution or the “balancing point” of a physical object with distributed mass.








Remark on moments and random variables



Interestingly, although the CDF uniquely determines a random variable’s distribution, equality of all moments—even when every moment exists—is not generally sufficient to establish equality in distribution. Additional conditions are needed for moments to determine a distribution uniquely. In contrast, the characteristic function always exists and uniquely determines the distribution, just as the CDF does.




Relationships Among Moments
Except in special families (like the normal), the only universal link between raw moments and central moments is \[
      \boxed{Var(X) = \mathbb{E}[(X-\mathbb{E}[X])^2] = \mathbb{E}[(X-\mu)^2] = \mathbb{E}[X^2] - \bigl(\mathbb{E}[X]\bigr)^2 = \mathbb{E}[X^2] - (\mu)^2}
    \] or more generally, \[\boxed{Cov(X,Y) = E(XY) - E(X)E(Y)}\]and the identity \(E(X^2) = E(X(X-1)) + E(X)\) implies \(Var(X) = E(X(X-1)) + E(X) - (E(X))^2\) The above implies that zero variance means the RV is a constant (a.s.): \[
      Var(X) = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; X = \mathbb{E}[X]\quad \text{(a.s.)}
    \] and there is no general recurrence for higher raw moments. However, cumulants satisfy a binomial recurrence, \[
      \kappa_1 = \mu_1,
      \qquad
      \kappa_n
      = \mu_n
        - \sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\binom{n-1}{k-1}\,\kappa_k\,\mu_{n-k},
      \quad n\ge2.
    \] Since \[
      M_X(t) = \mathbb{E}\bigl[e^{tX}\bigr] = \exp\bigl(K_X(t)\bigr),
      \quad
      K_X(t) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \kappa_n\,\frac{t^n}{n!},
    \] we can then recover all raw moments by exponentiating the cumulant‐generating function.






Cumulant Recurrence for a Bernoulli\((p)\) Random Variable



Let \(X\sim Bern(p)\), so \[
\mu'_r = \mathbb{E}[X^r] = p\quad (r\ge1).
\] Hence \(\mu'_1 = p,\;\mu'_2 = p,\;\mu'_3 = p.\)
The central moments are \[
\mu_2 = Var(X) = p(1-p),
\quad
\mu_3 = \mathbb{E}[(X-p)^3] = p(1-p)(1-2p).
\]
Now use the cumulant recurrence \[
\kappa_1 = \mu'_1 = p,
\qquad
\kappa_n
= \mu'_n
  - \sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\binom{n-1}{k-1}\,\kappa_k\,\mu'_{\,n-k},
\quad n\ge2.
\] \[\begin{align*}
\kappa_2
&= \mu'_2 \;-\;\binom{1}{0}\,\kappa_1\,\mu'_1
= p \;-\; (1)\,p\cdot p
= p - p^2
= p(1-p),\\
\kappa_3
&= \mu'_3- \Bigl[\binom{2}{0}\,\kappa_1\,\mu'_2 + \binom{2}{1}\,\kappa_2\,\mu'_1\Bigr]\\
&= p- \bigl[1\cdot p\cdot p \;+\;2\cdot p(1-p)\cdot p\bigr]\\
&= p \;-\;(p^2 + 2p^2 -2p^3)
= p -3p^2 +2p^3
= p(1-p)(1-2p)
\end{align*}\]






Transformations of Random Variables
Suppose we have a random variable \(X\) for which we have the moments and associated distribution. If we apply a transformation to \(X\) to yield a new random variable \(g(X)\) how then do we find the moments and distribution of this new \(g(X)\)?
Fortunately, the moments are relatively easy to find for general \(g\),






Law of the Unconscious Statistician, LOTUS



Let \(X\) be a random variable with cumulative distribution function \(F_X\). For any function \(g\) (not necessarily monotone or invertible) we have, \[\begin{aligned}
\text{(continuous case)}\quad
E[g(X)]
&=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(x)\,f_X(x)\,dx\\
\text{(discrete case)}\quad
E[g(X)]
&=\sum_{x} g(x)\,p_X(x)\end{aligned}\]








Example: LOTUS



 Let \(X\sim U(0,1)\) with density \(f_X(x)=1\) for \(0\le x\le1\). Take \(g(x)=x^2\). Then by LOTUS, \[
E[g(X)]
=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x^2\,f_X(x)\,dx
=\int_{0}^{1} x^2\,dx
=\frac{1}{3}.
\]
 Let \(X\) be the roll of a fair six-sided die, so \(p_X(x)=1/6\) for \(x\in\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}\). Take \(g(x)=2^x\). Then by LOTUS, \[
E[g(X)]
=\sum_{x=1}^{6} 2^x\,p_X(x)
=\frac{1}{6}\,(2 + 4 + 8 + 16 + 32 + 64)
=\frac{126}{6}
=21.
\]


The linearity of integrals give us convenient rules for linear transformations,






Properties of Linear Transformations



Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be random variables with finite first and second moments, and let \(a,b,c,d\in\mathbb{R}\) be constants. Then \[
\boxed{E[aX + b] = a\,E[X] + b,
\quad
Var(aX + b) = a^2\,Var(X)}
\] \[\begin{aligned}
Cov(aX + bY,\;cZ + dW)
&= Cov(aX,cZ+dW) + Cov(bY, cZ+dW)\\ &= Cov(aX,cZ) + Cov(aX,dW) + Cov(bY,cZ) + Cov(bY, dW)\\
&= (ac)Cov(X,Z) + (ad)Cov(X,W) + (bc)Cov(Y,Z) + (bd)Cov(Y,W)
\end{aligned}\] \[\boxed{Var(aX+bY) = a^2Var(X) + b^2Var(Y) + 2abCov(X,y)}\] If \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent then \(Cov(X,Y) = 0\) and \[Var(aX+bY) = a^2Var(X) + b^2Var(Y)\]








Remark



In particular \(E\) is linear and \(Cov\) is bilinear but \(Var\) is not


Unfortunately the corresponding distributions for these easier to find moments of transformations can be rather difficult to find, and except in relatively simple cases they are analytically intractable,






Example: Analytically Intractable Transformation



Let \(X\sim Exp(1)\) with density \[
f_X(x)=e^{-x},\quad x\ge0.
\] Define \[
Y=\sin(X).
\] Although \(f_X\) is simple, to find the density \(f_Y\) one must solve \(\sin(x)=y\), whose solutions on \([0,\infty)\) are \[
x_k = (-1)^k\arcsin(y) + \pi k,\quad k=0,1,2,\dots.
\] Thus \[
f_Y(y)
=\sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{f_X(x_k)}{\bigl|\cos(x_k)\bigr|}
=\sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{e^{-x_k}}{\bigl|\cos(x_k)\bigr|},
\qquad -1<y<1,
\] and no finite closed-form expression exists for this infinite series. Hence the distribution of \(Y\) is analytically intractable, despite \(X\) having a simple exponential law.


In the case when \(g\) is invertible and monotone we can find the distribution analytically however,






Definition: Monotone Transformations



Let \(X\) be a continuous random variable with density \(f_X(x)\), and let \(Y = g(X)\) where \(g\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) is a strictly monotone, differentiable function with inverse \(g^{-1}\). Then \(Y\) has density \[
\boxed{f_Y(y)
=
f_X\bigl(g^{-1}(y)\bigr)
\;\biggl|\frac{d}{dy}\,g^{-1}(y)\biggr|}
\] supported on \(g(\mathcal{X})\), where \(\mathcal{X}\) is the support of \(X\).








Proof



Let \(F_Y(y)=P\bigl(Y\le y\bigr)=P\bigl(g(X)\le y\bigr)\).
First suppose \(g\) is monotone increasing (the decreasing case is analogous, with an absolute-value correction), we have \[
g(X)\le y
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
X \le g^{-1}(y).
\] Hence \[
F_Y(y)
= P\bigl(X \le g^{-1}(y)\bigr)
= F_X\bigl(g^{-1}(y)\bigr).
\] Differentiating both sides with respect to \(y\) and applying the chain rule gives \[
f_Y(y)
= \frac{d}{dy}\,F_Y(y)
= \frac{d}{dy}\,F_X\bigl(g^{-1}(y)\bigr)
= f_X\bigl(g^{-1}(y)\bigr)\,\frac{d}{dy}\bigl[g^{-1}(y)\bigr].
\]
Now suppose \(g\) is monotone decreasing then \(g^{-1}\) is as well and
\[
g(X)\le y
\;\Longleftrightarrow\;
X \ge g^{-1}(y),
\] so \[
F_Y(y)
= P\bigl(g(X)\le y\bigr)
= P\bigl(X \ge g^{-1}(y)\bigr)
=1 - F_X\bigl(g^{-1}(y)\bigr).
\] Differentiating with respect to \(y\) gives \[
f_Y(y)
=\frac{d}{dy}F_Y(y)
=-\frac{d}{dy}\,F_X\bigl(g^{-1}(y)\bigr)
=-f_X\bigl(g^{-1}(y)\bigr)\,\bigl(g^{-1}\bigr)'(y).
\] Since \(\bigl(g^{-1}\bigr)'(y)\le0\), we may take absolute values to obtain the unified formula
Taking absolute values of the derivative of the inverse encapsulates both situations, \[
f_Y(y)
= f_X\bigl(g^{-1}(y)\bigr)\;\Bigl|\tfrac{d}{dy}\,g^{-1}(y)\Bigr|.
\]

Theorem: Change of Variables for Piecewise Monotone Transformations



Let \(X\) be a continuous random variable with density \(f_X\) supported on \(\mathcal{X}\). Suppose \(g\colon\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}\) is differentiable and can be partitioned into \(k\) regions \(\mathcal{X}_1,\dots,\mathcal{X}_k\) on each of which \(g\) is strictly monotone with inverse \(g_i^{-1}\) on \(g(\mathcal{X}_i)\). Then the density of \(Y=g(X)\) is \[
\boxed{f_Y(y)
=\sum_{i=1}^k
f_X\bigl(g_i^{-1}(y)\bigr)\;\Bigl|\bigl(g_i^{-1}\bigr)'(y)\Bigr|,
\quad y\in\mathcal{Y}}
\] and \(f_Y(y)=0\) otherwise.








Cubing a Uniform\((-1,1)\) Variable



Let \(X\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(-1,1)\), so \[
f_X(x)=
\begin{cases}
\tfrac12, & -1\le x\le1,\\
0, & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\] Define \(Y = g(X) = X^3\). On \([-1,1]\), \(g\) is strictly increasing with inverse \(g^{-1}(y)=y^{1/3}\). By the change-of-variables formula, \[
f_Y(y)
= f_X\bigl(y^{1/3}\bigr)\;\Bigl|\tfrac{d}{dy}\bigl(y^{1/3}\bigr)\Bigr|
= \frac12 \times \frac{1}{3\,|y|^{2/3}}
= \frac{1}{6\,|y|^{2/3}},
\quad -1<y<1,
\] and \(f_Y(y)=0\) otherwise. One checks \(\displaystyle \int_{-1}^{1}\frac{1}{6\,|y|^{2/3}}\,dy
=2\int_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{6\,y^{2/3}}\,dy
=\frac{1}{3}\int_{0}^{1}y^{-2/3}\,dy
=1.\)


What do we do if we do not have an monotone and invertible \(g\), or we can not split our function into monotone intervals? We have to rely on approximations!






Example: Monte Carlo Approximation when \(g\) Is Intractable



Let \(X\sim Exp(1)\) with density \(f_X(x)=e^{-x}\) for \(x\ge0\), and define the transformed variable $ Y = (X),. $ As shown earlier, the exact density $ f_Y(y) =_{k=0}^, x_k = (-1)^k(y)+k, $ is an infinite series and not available in closed form. To approximate \(f_Y\) (or moments of \(Y\)) numerically, we can run a monte carlo simulation drawing a 100000 samples from \(Exp(1)\) and plot the histogram as an approximate density

We can also use a numerical integration and grid approximation as an alternative approach but this proves to be rather difficult in most cases.
Alternatively, we can rely on asymptotic approximations. If the original estimator is asymptotically normal, we can use a first-order Taylor expansion to approximate the transformation locally around the true parameter. This is the basis of the delta method, which allows us to derive an asymptotically normal distribution for the transformed estimator, provided the derivative of the transformation is nonzero at the true parameter.






Theorem: Univariate Delta Method



Let \(\hat\theta_n\) be an estimator of a parameter \(\theta\) such that \[
\boxed{\sqrt{n}\,(\hat\theta_n - \theta)\;\xrightarrow{d}\;N(0,\sigma^2)}
\] and let \(g\) be a function that is differentiable in a neighborhood of \(\theta\) with \(g'(\theta)\neq0\). Then \[
\sqrt{n}\,\bigl(g(\hat\theta_n) - g(\theta)\bigr)
\;\xrightarrow{d}\;
N\!\bigl(0,\,[g'(\theta)]^2\,\sigma^2\bigr).
\] Equivalently, for large \(n\), \[
\boxed{g(\hat\theta_n)\approx N\!\Bigl(g(\theta),\,\tfrac{[g'(\theta)]^2\sigma^2}{n}\Bigr)}
\]








Proof



The taylor expansion of \(g(\hat\theta_n)\) around \(\hat\theta_n = \theta\) is \[g(\hat\theta_n) = g(\theta) + g'(\theta)(\hat\theta_n-\theta) + o(\hat\theta_n - \theta)\]
Then as \(\hat\theta_n \to \theta\) \(o(\hat\theta_n - \theta) \to 0\) then rearranging and applying slutsky’s theorem yields, \[\sqrt{n}(g(\hat\theta_n) - g(\theta)) = g'(\theta)\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta_n - \theta) \;\xrightarrow{d}\;
N\!\bigl(0,\,[g'(\theta)]^2\,\sigma^2\bigr)\]








Example: Exponential Transformation; Delta Method and Direct



Suppose \(X_1,\dots,X_n\) are i.i.d. \(N(\theta,1)\). Then the sample mean \(\hat\theta_n = \bar X\) satisfies \[
\sqrt{n}\,(\bar X - \theta)\;\xrightarrow{d}\;N(0,1).
\] Take \(g(x)=e^x\), we can actually use simple monotone change of variables formula here because \(\bar X\sim N\bigl(\theta,\tfrac1n\bigr)\) exactly for any \(n\), and \(g(x)=e^x\) is strictly increasing with inverse \(g^{-1}(y)=\ln y\), the change–of–variables formula gives for \(y>0\): \[
f_Y(y)
= f_{\bar X}\bigl(\ln y\bigr)\;\Bigl|\frac{d}{dy}\ln y\Bigr|
= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\,(1/n)}}\exp\!\Bigl\{-\frac{(\ln y-\theta)^2}{2(1/n)}\Bigr\}\,\frac1y,
\] i.e. \[
Y = e^{\bar X}\;\sim\;\mathrm{Lognormal}\!\Bigl(\mu=\theta,\;\sigma^2=\tfrac1n\Bigr).
\] Hence the exact moments are
\[
E[Y]
= \exp\!\Bigl(\theta + \tfrac{1}{2n}\Bigr),
\qquad
Var(Y)
= \bigl(e^{1/n}-1\bigr)\,\exp\!\Bigl(2\theta + \tfrac{1}{n}\Bigr)
\]
but \(e^{1/n} = \left(1+\frac{1}{n} + \frac{1}{2n^2} + o(n^{-2})\right)\) then
\[
\begin{aligned}
Var(Y)
&= e^{2\theta}\,
   \Bigl(\underbrace{\tfrac{1}{n}}_{A}
         +\underbrace{\tfrac{1}{2n^2}}_{B}
         +o(n^{-2})\Bigr)\,
   \Bigl(\underbrace{1}_{C}
         +\underbrace{\tfrac{1}{n}}_{D}
         +\underbrace{\tfrac{1}{2n^2}}_{E}
         +o(n^{-2})\Bigr)\$6pt]
&= e^{2\theta}\,\Bigl[
     A\cdot C
   + A\cdot D
   + A\cdot E \$-2pt]
&\qquad\quad
   + B\cdot C
   + B\cdot D
   + C\cdot E
   +o(n^{-2})
  \Bigr]\$6pt]
&= e^{2\theta}\,\Bigl[
     \tfrac{1}{n}\cdot 1
   + \tfrac{1}{n}\cdot \tfrac{1}{n}
   + \tfrac{1}{n}\cdot \tfrac{1}{2n^2}
   + \tfrac{1}{2n^2}\cdot 1 \$-2pt]
&\qquad\quad
   + \tfrac{1}{2n^2}\cdot \tfrac{1}{n}
   + 1\cdot \tfrac{1}{2n^2}
   +o(n^{-2})
  \Bigr]\$6pt]
&= e^{2\theta}\,\Bigl[
     \tfrac{1}{n}
   + \tfrac{1}{n^2}
   + \tfrac{1}{2n^3}
   + \tfrac{1}{2n^2}
   + \tfrac{1}{2n^3}
   + \tfrac{1}{2n^2}
   +o(n^{-2})
  \Bigr].
\end{aligned}
\] Notice that the terms of order \(n^{-3}\) (i.e. \(\tfrac1{2n^3}\)) are absorbed into \(o(n^{-2})\). Combining the \(n^{-2}\) terms, \[
\tfrac{1}{n^2} + \tfrac{1}{2n^2} + \tfrac{1}{2n^2}
= \frac{1 + \tfrac12 + \tfrac12}{n^2}
= \frac{2}{n^2}
= \frac{3}{2n^2},
\] we obtain the final expansion \[
Var(Y)
= e^{2\theta}\,\Bigl(\tfrac{1}{n} + \tfrac{3}{2n^2} + o(n^{-2})\Bigr).
\]
We can also use the univariate delta method, \[
\sqrt{n}\,\bigl(e^{\bar X} - e^{\theta}\bigr)
\;\xrightarrow{d}\;
N\!\bigl(0,\,(e^\theta)^2\bigr)
\;=\;
N\!\bigl(0,\;e^{2\theta}\bigr).
\] Equivalently, for large \(n\), \[
Y = e^{\bar X}
\approx
N\!\Bigl(e^{\theta},\;\tfrac{e^{2\theta}}{n}\Bigr).
\]








Remark



Notice the delta method is an asymptotically linear approximation and in the above example it misses the \(e^{1/2n}\) term in the expectation and \(\frac{3e^{2\theta}}{2n^2}\) in variance but is valid as a linear/first order approximation in limit. We can expand it to higher orders if desired to capture these HOT but this is not usually done


We also have the Delta Method for multiple parameters but need access to their covariance matrix,






Theorem: Multivariate Delta Method



Let \(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n\in\mathbb{R}^k\) be an estimator of \(\boldsymbol\theta\in\mathbb{R}^k\) such that \[\boxed{\sqrt{n}\,\bigl(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n - \boldsymbol\theta\bigr)
\;\xrightarrow{d}\;
N_k\bigl(\mathbf{0},\,\Sigma\bigr)}\] and let \(g:\mathbb{R}^k\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be differentiable in a neighborhood of \(\boldsymbol\theta\) with Jacobian matrix \(Dg(\boldsymbol\theta)\) (an \(m\times k\) matrix). Then \[\sqrt{n}\,\bigl(g(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n) - g(\boldsymbol\theta)\bigr)
\;\xrightarrow{d}\;
N_m\!\bigl(\mathbf{0},\,Dg(\boldsymbol\theta)\,\Sigma\,Dg(\boldsymbol\theta)^\top\bigr).\] Equivalently, for large \(n\), \[\boxed{g(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}_n)\approx
N_m\!\Bigl(g(\boldsymbol\theta),\,\tfrac{1}{n}\,Dg(\boldsymbol\theta)\,\Sigma\,Dg(\boldsymbol\theta)^\top\Bigr)}\]








Example: Multivariate Delta Method, Clinical Trial Overall Success - Raw



Successful clinical trials involve passing three distinct phases. Suppose the probability of success in each stage is \(p_1,p_2,p_3\) respectively and the success are independent. Suppose we are interested in the overall probability of success \(p_1p_2p_3\), we can use the delta method to approximate this.
\[\hat p_i = \text{observed success rate in phase }i,\quad i=1,2,3,\] with \(E[\hat p_i]=p_i\) and \(Var(\hat p_i)=\frac{p_i(1-p_i)}{n_i}\) for large sample sizes \(n_i\). We are interested in the overall success probability \[g(p_1,p_2,p_3) \;=\; p_1\,p_2\,p_3\]
By the multivariate delta method, define the vector \(\widehat{\boldsymbol p}=(\hat p_1,\hat p_2,\hat p_3)\) and compute the gradient \[\nabla g(p_1,p_2,p_3)
=\begin{pmatrix}
\frac{\partial}{\partial p_1}(p_1p_2p_3)\$6pt]
\frac{\partial}{\partial p_2}(p_1p_2p_3)\$6pt]
\frac{\partial}{\partial p_3}(p_1p_2p_3)
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
p_2\,p_3\$3pt]
p_1\,p_3\$3pt]
p_1\,p_2
\end{pmatrix}\] Assuming the \(\hat p_i\) are independent, their covariance matrix is diagonal with entries \(Var(\hat p_i)\). Hence \[\begin{aligned}
Var\bigl(g(\widehat{\boldsymbol p})\bigr)
&\approx
\nabla g^\top
\begin{pmatrix}
\frac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n_1} & & \$3pt]
& \frac{p_2(1-p_2)}{n_2} & \$3pt]
& & \frac{p_3(1-p_3)}{n_3}
\end{pmatrix}\\
\nabla g
&=
(p_2p_3)^2\frac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n_1}
+
(p_1p_3)^2\frac{p_2(1-p_2)}{n_2}
+
(p_1p_2)^2\frac{p_3(1-p_3)}{n_3}\end{aligned}\] Thus, for large \(n_i\), \[\widehat p_1\,\widehat p_2\,\widehat p_3
\;\approx\;
N\!\Bigl(p_1p_2p_3,\;
(p_2p_3)^2\tfrac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n_1}
+(p_1p_3)^2\tfrac{p_2(1-p_2)}{n_2}
+(p_1p_2)^2\tfrac{p_3(1-p_3)}{n_3}
\Bigr).\]


Sometimes applying an invertible transform then unapplying it in the end can be helpful, consider the above example but applying \(log\) first,






Multivariate Delta Method, Clinical Trial Overall Success - Log Transformed



Instead of applying the multivariate delta method directly to \(\;g(p_1,p_2,p_3)=p_1p_2p_3\), we can work on the more convenient scale \[
h(p_1,p_2,p_3)
=\log g(p_1,p_2,p_3)
=\log p_1 + \log p_2 + \log p_3.
\] Since \(\hat p_i\approx N(p_i,\;p_i(1-p_i)/n_i)\), by the (univariate) delta method, \[
\log\hat p_i
\approx N\!\Bigl(\log p_i,\;\frac{1}{p_i^2}\,\frac{p_i(1-p_i)}{n_i}\Bigr)
= N\!\Bigl(\log p_i,\;\frac{1-p_i}{p_i\,n_i}\Bigr).
\] Because the \(\hat p_i\) are independent, the sum \(\sum_{i=1}^3\log\hat p_i\) is approximately normal with \[
E\Bigl[\sum\log\hat p_i\Bigr]
=\sum\log p_i,
\quad
Var\Bigl[\sum\log\hat p_i\Bigr]
=\sum\frac{1-p_i}{p_i\,n_i}.
\] Hence on the original scale, \[
\hat p_1\,\hat p_2\,\hat p_3
=\exp\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^3\log\hat p_i\Bigr)
\approx\text{Log-Normal}\!\Bigl(\mu=\sum\log p_i,\;\sigma^2=\sum\frac{1-p_i}{p_i\,n_i}\Bigr).
\] In particular, \[
E[\hat p_1\hat p_2\hat p_3]\approx
\exp\Bigl(\sum\log p_i + \tfrac12\sum\frac{1-p_i}{p_i\,n_i}\Bigr),
\quad
Var(\hat p_1\hat p_2\hat p_3)\approx
\bigl(e^{\sigma^2}-1\bigr)\,e^{2\sum\log p_i+\sigma^2}.
\] Compared to the direct delta method approximation (which gives a Normal law on the product scale), the log transform approach yields a Log-Normal approximation that automatically respects positivity

Finally applying a convex or concave transformation to a random variable \(X\) systmeatically raises or lowers the expectation, this is Jensen’s inequality
::: {.callout-important title = “Theorem: Jensen’s Inequality”} Let \(X\) be a random variable with \(E[|X|]<\infty\), and let \(\varphi\colon I\to\mathbb{R}\) be a convex function on an interval \(I\) containing the support of \(X\). Then \[
\varphi\bigl(E[X]\bigr)\;\le\;E\bigl[\varphi(X)\bigr].
\] If \(\varphi\) is instead concave on \(I\), the inequality reverses: \[
\varphi\bigl(E[X]\bigr)\;\ge\;E\bigl[\varphi(X)\bigr].
\] :::

title: Probability and Set Theory
section: Intro: The DGP and Statistical Models
text:
Intro: The DGP and Statistical Models
A statistical model is a collection of probability distributions for the observed data, intended to represent the data-generating mechanisms (DGPs) we consider plausible. We may write \[
\mathcal P
=
\{P:P\text{ satisfies the assumptions of the model}\}.
\]
This is more general than choosing a specific distributional family. We can instead describe the DGP through moment conditions, such as restrictions on means or variances, without specifying its entire distribution.
We do not usually know the true DGP \(P_0\). Assuming \(P_0\in\mathcal P\), we use the observed data and the restrictions defining \(\mathcal P\) to infer properties of \(P_0\).

title: What is Causal Inference?
text:
“Far better an approximate answer to the right question than an exact answer to the wrong question” — John Tukey
Causality is the broader study of causes, effects, and causal relationships, including philosophical questions about what causation means, how it operates, and what constitutes a causal explanation. Causal inference concerns estimating the effects of causes in contrast to causal structure discovery or causal model elicitation and causes of effects.

title: What is Causal Inference?
text: Associational vs causal (interventions)

title: What is Causal Inference?
text:
Identification comes before estimation
Causal inference forces us to understand the differences in defining, identifying, and estimating a effect.

Definition: What quantity are we interested in? For example, the average treatment effect, \(E[Y(1)-Y(0)]\).
Identification: Under what assumptions can we express this causal quantity in terms of the observed-data distribution?
Estimation: Given that expression, how can we estimate it from a finite sample?

These distinctions are there for simple associational estimands as well but they are rarely talked about outside construct validity and measruement errors. An estimator can have excellent statistical properties while estimating something that does not answer our causal question. More data, better prediction, or more sophisticated machine learning cannot resolve a failure of identification on their own.
