title: What is Causal Inference?
section: three striaghtforwards ways to estimate the total causal effect: randomziation, Outcome modeling, weighting
text:
three striaghtforwards ways to estimate the total causal effect: randomziation, Outcome modeling, weighting
Two especially important approaches to estimating causal effects are outcome modeling and weighting.
For a binary treatment, let
\[
m_a(x)=E[Y\mid A=a,X=x],
\qquad
e(x)=P(A=1\mid X=x).
\]
Under consistency, conditional exchangeability, and positivity, the ATE can be identified through the outcome regression:
\[
ATE=E_X[m_1(X)-m_0(X)].
\]
This is the basis of standardization, or outcome-regression-based estimation. We estimate the expected outcome under each treatment and average over the target population’s covariate distribution.
Alternatively, the same effect can be identified through inverse probability weighting (IPW):
\[
ATE=E\left[
\frac{AY}{e(X)}
-
\frac{(1-A)Y}{1-e(X)}
\right].
\]
Rather than modeling the outcome directly, IPW reweights observations according to their probability of receiving the treatment they actually received.
The important point is that these are different statistical representations of the same causal estimand, not different definitions of a causal effect.
Much of observational causal inference can be understood as trying to recover some of the inferential advantages of randomized experiments.
In a properly randomized trial, treatment assignment is independent of the potential outcomes by design. In observational studies, we generally do not have that luxury.
Methods such as matching, weighting, and standardization attempt to make comparisons between treatment groups meaningful under assumptions about the treatment assignment mechanism.
The target trial framework makes this connection particularly explicit: specify the hypothetical randomized experiment we would ideally conduct, then ask whether and how observational data can emulate it.
However, not all causal inference methods attempt to reproduce a conventional randomized trial. Instrumental variables, regression discontinuity, and difference-in-differences can exploit other sources of identifying variation, each with its own assumptions and often its own target estimand.
Randomization is a useful benchmark, but the larger principle is identifying what makes a comparison causally interpretable.
We also need to remember that a treatment effect belongs to a particular intervention, comparator, outcome, time horizon, and target population. Changing any of these can change the causal question itself.

title: What is Causal Inference?
text:
Negative controls and falsification
Negative controls provide a useful gut check on causal analyses.
A negative control outcome is an outcome that the treatment is assumed not to affect. A negative control exposure is an exposure that is assumed not to affect the outcome of interest.
If an analysis suggests an effect where we believe none should exist, that raises questions about residual confounding, selection bias, measurement problems, or other failures of our assumptions.
For example, suppose we believe a treatment affects a particular health outcome but should have no effect on some unrelated outcome. Finding an association with that negative control outcome might suggest that the treatment and outcome groups differ in ways our analysis has not adequately addressed.
There are two important qualifications.
First, passing a negative-control check does not establish that our causal assumptions are correct. An analysis can fail to detect bias even when substantial bias remains.
Second, negative controls are not merely informal diagnostics. Under additional assumptions, they can help identify and adjust for otherwise unmeasured confounding, as in proximal causal inference.
The usefulness of a negative control therefore depends on why we believe the relevant causal effect is absent and what other relationships the control is expected to share with the variables of interest.

title: What is Causal Inference?
section: Causal uncertainty extends beyond sampling uncertainty to estimand uncertainty
text:
Causal uncertainty extends beyond sampling uncertainty to estimand uncertainty
Statistical inference typically quantifies uncertainty arising from the fact that we observe a finite sample rather than the entire population.
For example, a confidence interval may have valid frequentist coverage for an identified statistical functional under the assumed data-generating process and regularity conditions.
But statistical precision does not guarantee causal validity.
If exchangeability fails because of unmeasured confounding, a confidence interval can become arbitrarily narrow around a quantity that differs substantially from the causal effect we wanted.
Similarly, violations of positivity, inconsistently defined interventions, selection bias, and measurement error can all compromise causal conclusions in ways that ordinary standard errors do not capture.
This is why sensitivity analyses, falsification tests, alternative identification strategies, and partial identification are important complements to conventional statistical inference.
The distinction is simple: uncertainty about how well we estimated an identified quantity is not the same as uncertainty about whether that quantity has the causal interpretation we intended.

These ideas point to a common theme: causal inference requires us to separate what we want to know, what the data and assumptions allow us to know, and how precisely we can estimate it. Statistical methods address the last problem, but they cannot substitute for the first two.

title: What is Causal Inference?
text:
Confounding, Collision and Mediation
In a DAG conditioning determines which conditional independence are implied and which dependencies are possible. There are three basic substructures in DAG,

Chain (mediation): \(X\rightarrow M\rightarrow Y\). Conditioning on \(M\) blocks this path between \(X\) and \(Y\)
Fork (common cause, confounder if not blocked): \(X\leftarrow C\rightarrow Y\). Conditioning on \(C\) blocks this path between \(X\) and \(Y\)
Collider (common effect): \(X\rightarrow C\leftarrow Y\). This path is blocked by default, but conditioning on \(C\) or one of its descendants opens it







Remark: Collider Bias vs. Selection Bias





Collider bias can be identified by a DAG but selection bias occurs whenever the process determining which observations enter a sample distorts estimation. Selection bias can arise through collider bias, but the two are not identical, and neither is necessarily a subset of the other.

title: What is Causal Inference?
section: How it Works: Conditional Independence from DAGs

title: What is Causal Inference?
text:
Markov Equivalence
Conditional independence relationships generally do not uniquely determine a DAG.
\[\begin{aligned}
(X\rightarrow M\rightarrow Y) &\implies X\perp\!\!\!\perp Y \mid M\\
(X\leftarrow M\rightarrow Y) &\implies X\perp\!\!\!\perp Y \mid M
\end{aligned}\]
Thus, even if we could perfectly recover all conditional independence relationships from observed data, we generally could only identify a Markov equivalence class: a collection of DAGs that imply exactly the same conditional independencies. From my limited understanding of causal structure learning, however, this is only the beginning of the difficulties. We rarely know which variables belong in the DAG in the first place. Important variables may be unmeasured, and in high-dimensional settings there can be an enormous number of possible relationships and conditioning sets to investigate. Moreover, conditional independences must be inferred from finite samples, introducing statistical uncertainty. No thanks! But more power to those who pursue such a tough problem…

title: What is Causal Inference?
section: Encoding More Complicated Situations in DAGs
text:
Encoding More Complicated Situations in DAGs
DAGs can represent more than simple confounding, mediation, and colliders. By introducing additional nodes, we can describe features of real studies such as treatment noncompliance, exogenous shocks, and measurement error.






Example: Treatment Noncompliance





In a randomized trial, the treatment participants are assigned may differ from the treatment they actually receive. We can represent these as separate variables:

\(Z\): Randomized treatment assignment
\(A\): Treatment actually received
\(Y\): Outcome
\(U\): Unmeasured common causes of treatment received and outcome

A possible DAG contains
\[
Z\rightarrow A\rightarrow Y,
\qquad
A\leftarrow U\rightarrow Y.
\]
Randomization removes common causes of \(Z\) and the other pre-treatment variables, but does not necessarily remove confounding between \(A\) and \(Y\). Under additional assumptions, including no direct effect of \(Z\) on \(Y\) except through \(A\), treatment assignment can serve as an instrumental variable for treatment received.









Example: Exogenous Shocks





An exogenous shock is an external event or intervention whose occurrence is not caused by the variables under study. Examples might include an unexpected policy change, natural disaster, or randomized intervention.
We can represent an ideal exogenous shock \(Z\) as a node with no incoming arrows, potentially affecting treatment \(A\) and outcome \(Y\):
\[
Z\rightarrow A\rightarrow Y.
\]
However, exogeneity is an assumption, not something established by drawing a node without incoming arrows. Natural experiments require careful justification that the shock is sufficiently independent of relevant unmeasured causes. If we want to use \(Z\) as an instrumental variable, we also need assumptions such as exclusion.









Example: Measurement Error





DAGs can distinguish between a variable’s true value and what we actually measure. Let \(X\) denote the true variable, \(X^*\) its observed measurement, and \(\varepsilon\) a source of measurement error.
\[
X\rightarrow X^*\leftarrow\varepsilon.
\]
For example, a patient’s true physical activity might affect their health outcome \(Y\), while researchers only observe self-reported activity \(X^*\).
\[
X\rightarrow Y,
\qquad
X\rightarrow X^*\leftarrow\varepsilon.
\]
The graph makes clear that the measured variable is not necessarily the same as the underlying causal variable. Additional assumptions, such as \(X^*=X+\varepsilon\) with independent measurement error, specify how the measurements relate to the true values.

title: What is Causal Inference?
text:
ICH E9 (R1): Estimand Types
ICH E9(R1) complements PICOTS by considering how intercurrent events can affect the interpretation or existence of the outcome, such as treatment discontinuation, rescue medication, or death before assessment. ICH E9(R1) describes five strategies for addressing these events when defining the estimand:







Strategy
Effect of interest




Treatment policy
Outcomes regardless of the event’s occurrence, where those outcomes remain defined.


Hypothetical
Outcomes under a specified hypothetical scenario, such as no rescue medication.


Composite
Incorporate the event into the endpoint, such as counting rescue medication as treatment failure.


While on treatment
Outcomes before the specified event occurs.


Principal stratum
Effect within a subgroup defined by potential intercurrent events under specified treatment conditions.



These strategies define what effect we want, rather than merely how to analyze the data. Specifying that effect does not, by itself, establish its identification.

title: What is Causal Inference?
What is Causal Inference?
section: ATE: Standard Causal Identification Assumptions SUTVA, positivity, and exchangeability/ignorability
text:
ATE: Standard Causal Identification Assumptions SUTVA, positivity, and exchangeability/ignorability
To identify the ATE as a functional of the observed-data distribution through standard covariate adjustment, we typically invoke SUTVA/consistency, positivity, and exchangeability (ignorability/no unmeasured confounding).
These assumptions require justification rather than being automatically established by the analysis. Clearly defined interventions and attention to interference support SUTVA; covariate-overlap and propensity-score diagnostics help assess positivity; and randomization or substantive causal knowledge supports exchangeability. DAGs make the latter assumptions explicit and help determine an appropriate adjustment set, but do not verify the assumptions they encode.






Assumption: SUTVA



Here, I use the stable unit treatment value assumption (SUTVA) to include:

No interference: one individual’s outcome does not depend on other individuals’ treatment assignments.
No relevant hidden treatment versions: the treatment labels distinguish versions that could produce different potential outcomes, or versions grouped under a label yield the same potential outcome.
Consistency links the potential outcomes to the observed outcome: \[
A=a\quad\Longrightarrow\quad Y=Y(a).
\] Equivalently, \[
Y=AY(1)+(1-A)Y(0)=Y(A).
\tag{2}\]









Assumption: Positivity



Let \(e(x)=P(A=1\mid X=x)\) denote the propensity score. For identifying the ATE by covariate adjustment, a standard positivity condition is \[
0<e(X)<1\qquad P_X\text{-almost surely}.
\tag{3}\]
Both treatments must have positive probability at almost every covariate value in the target population. This is a population-level support condition, not a requirement that a finite sample contain treated and untreated individuals at every exact value of \(X\).


SUTVA and positivity alone do not make treatment groups comparable. Their observed outcomes may differ because of baseline prognosis or selection on treatment benefit. To justify the usual covariate-adjusted comparison, we need exchangeability!






Assumption: Conditional (Strong) Exchangeability



\[
\{Y(0),Y(1)\}\perp\!\!\!\perp A\mid X.
\tag{4}\]
Given \(X\), treatment assignment carries no additional information about the potential outcomes. This is often called unconfoundedness, ignorability, or no unmeasured confounding relative to \(X\).








The Bayesian meaning of ignorability



The missing-data interpretation explains the word “ignorable.” Suppose, conditional on \(X\), the full-data model factors as \[
f_\theta(y_0,y_1\mid x)\,g_\psi(a\mid x),
\] where exchangeability removes potential outcomes from the assignment model. Integrating the missing potential outcome yields \[
f_{\theta,a}(y\mid x)\,g_\psi(a\mid x).
\] With distinct parameter spaces and independent priors \(\pi(\theta)\pi(\psi)\), the assignment factor does not affect the posterior for the outcome-model parameters \(\theta\). This is a likelihood-based meaning of ignorability, not permission to ignore \(X\) or assume away confounding. A prior also does not by itself establish identification. See Chapter 10 of Fan Li’s course notes.

title: What is Causal Inference?
text:
ATE Estimators: Regression and Weighting
Together, these assumptions connect the causal means to observed-data quantities.






Theorem: Identification by Standardization



Define \(m_a(x)=E[Y\mid A=a,X=x]\). Assume \(E[|Y(a)|]<\infty\) for \(a=0,1\). Under consistency, conditional mean exchangeability, and positivity, \[
\begin{aligned}
E[Y(a)]
&\overset{\text{iterated expectation}}{=}
E_X\!\left[E[Y(a)\mid X]\right]\\
&\overset{\text{exchangeability and positivity}}{=}
E_X\!\left[E[Y(a)\mid A=a,X]\right]\\
&\overset{\text{consistency}}{=}
E_X[m_a(X)].
\end{aligned}
\tag{5}\]
Thus, \[
\boxed{ATE=E_X[m_1(X)-m_0(X)].}
\tag{6}\]
Positivity ensures that the observed-data conditional means are determined across the covariate distribution over which we average.








Theorem: Identification by Standardization



Personally, I find the role of positivity less obvious in the standardization argument. The observed-data distribution determines \(m_a\) only \(P_{X\mid A=a}\)-almost everywhere, while the integral averages over \(P_X\). Inverse probability weighting (IPW) makes this support requirement explicit through a change of measure.
Write \(e_a(x)=P(A=a\mid X=x)\). Positivity, \(e_a(X)>0\) \(P_X\)-almost surely, ensures absolute continuity: \[
P_X\ll P_{X\mid A=a}.
\] Any covariate region absent from arm \(a\) must therefore also have zero probability in the target population. By Bayes’ rule, the Radon–Nikodym derivative is \[
\frac{dP_X}{dP_{X\mid A=a}}(x)
=\frac{P(A=a)}{e_a(x)}.
\] Starting from the standardization formula, \[
\begin{aligned}
E[Y(a)]
&=\int m_a(x)\,dP_X(x)\\
&=\int m_a(x)\,
\frac{P(A=a)}{e_a(x)}\,
dP_{X\mid A=a}(x)\\
&=E\!\left[\left.\frac{P(A=a)}{e_a(X)}Y\right|A=a\right]\\
&=E\!\left[\frac{\mathbf{1}(A=a)Y}{e_a(X)}\right].
\end{aligned}
\] Consequently, with \(e(x)=P(A=1\mid X=x)\), \[
\boxed{ATE=E\!\left[\frac{AY}{e(X)}-\frac{(1-A)Y}{1-e(X)}\right].}
\]
The weights transform the covariate distribution within arm \(a\) into the target distribution \(P_X\). Exchangeability and consistency supply the causal interpretation. If a target covariate region is absent from arm \(a\), neither weighting nor standardization can recover its counterfactual mean without additional assumptions: weighting lacks the required change of measure, while standardization has an undetermined integrand in that region.

title: What is Causal Inference?
section: ATT and ATU: changing the target population and causal identification assumptions
text:
ATT and ATU: changing the target population and causal identification assumptions
Different estimands can require different identification assumptions.
Under SUTVA, including consistency, the following mean-exchangeability and positivity conditions are sufficient. Write \(e(X)=P(A=1\mid X)\) and assume finite potential-outcome means and \(0<P(A=1)<1\).









Estimand
Mean exchangeability required
Positivity required
Counterfactual means to recover




ATE
\(E[Y(a)\mid A,X]=E[Y(a)\mid X]\) for \(a=0,1\)
\(0<e(X)<1\), \(P_X\)-almost surely
Untreated outcomes among those treated and treated outcomes among those untreated


ATT
\(E[Y(0)\mid A,X]=E[Y(0)\mid X]\)
\(e(X)<1\), \(P_{X\mid A=1}\)-almost surely
Untreated outcomes among those treated


ATU
\(E[Y(1)\mid A,X]=E[Y(1)\mid X]\)
\(e(X)>0\), \(P_{X\mid A=0}\)-almost surely
Treated outcomes among those untreated



For the ATT, consistency already identifies the treated potential-outcome mean among those treated; only their untreated mean must be recovered. For the ATU, the reverse applies.
Under the full set of assumptions used for the ATE, the same conditional contrast can be averaged over different target populations: \[
\begin{aligned}
ATT&=E[m_1(X)-m_0(X)\mid A=1],\\
ATU&=E[m_1(X)-m_0(X)\mid A=0].
\end{aligned}
\] These effects need not equal the ATE under conditional exchangeability: the covariate distributions being averaged over differ, and treatment effects may vary with \(X\).






Remark: Weaker Exchangeability Conditions



For identifying average effects, joint conditional independence of \(\{Y(0),Y(1)\}\) and \(A\) is stronger than necessary. It is sufficient to assume treatment-specific conditional independence, often called weak exchangeability, \[
Y(a)\perp\!\!\!\perp A\mid X,
\qquad a=0,1,
\] or even the weaker conditional mean exchangeability restrictions, \[
E[Y(a)\mid A,X]=E[Y(a)\mid X],
\qquad a=0,1,
\] provided the relevant expectations exist. Together with consistency and positivity, either condition identifies the average effects.


Each estimand, however, requires identification of only one missing counterfactual mean. For the ATT, \(E[Y(1)\mid A=1]=E[Y\mid A=1]\) is already observed under consistency. We need only identify \(E[Y(0)\mid A=1]\), using the one-sided conditions in the table. No exchangeability assumption for \(Y(1)\) is required. With \(p=P(A=1)\), this gives \[
\boxed{ATT=\frac{1}{p}E\!\left[AY-(1-A)\frac{e(X)}{1-e(X)}Y\right].}
\] The treated outcomes already represent the target group; the untreated outcomes receive odds weights \(e(X)/\{1-e(X)\}\).
Similarly, the ATU requires mean exchangeability only for \(Y(1)\) and treated support over the untreated covariate distribution. Then \[
\boxed{ATU=\frac{1}{1-p}E\!\left[A\frac{1-e(X)}{e(X)}Y-(1-A)Y\right].}
\] In these one-sided weighting expressions, ratios need only be evaluated in the arm whose outcomes they weight; the corresponding summand is defined as zero outside that arm.
We can also relax the no-interference component of SUTVA to study spillover effects, where one person’s outcome depends on other people’s treatments. This is more subtle than simply dropping an assumption: we must expand the potential-outcome notation to represent those treatment assignments, define the effects of interest, and justify identification assumptions for them. Consistency still links the observed outcome to the potential outcome under the treatment configuration actually received.

title: What is Causal Inference?
text:
Identification: More Details
We now look more closely at what separates an observed contrast from a causal effect, what exchangeability buys us, and how the assumptions change with the estimand.
The key thing to understand here is that you can easily fool yourself if your es9itmand is causal and you take a naive obsewrved data contrast as the estimator without estabilshing thge necessary identifcation assumptions. below we use ATE and ATE_obs as an example of this when






Example: The Perfect(Confounded)-Doctor



Suppose larger outcomes are preferable. A doctor knows both potential outcomes and treats exactly those who benefit.
Person | \(Y(0)\) | \(Y(1)\) | \(\tau\) | \(A\) | Observed \(Y\) | |—|—:|—:|—:|—:|—:| | 1 | 13 | 14 | 1 | 1 | 14 | | 2 | 6 | 0 | −6 | 0 | 6 | | 3 | 4 | 1 | −3 | 0 | 4 | | 4 | 5 | 2 | −3 | 0 | 5 | | 5 | 6 | 3 | −3 | 0 | 6 | | 6 | 6 | 1 | −5 | 0 | 6 | | 7 | 8 | 10 | 2 | 1 | 10 | | 8 | 8 | 9 | 1 | 1 | 9 | Treating these eight people as an equally weighted finite population,
\[
    ATE=\frac{40-56}{8}=-2,
\] but \[
    ATE_{\mathrm{obs}}=\frac{33}{3}-\frac{27}{5}=11-5.4=5.6.
\] The doctor’s individualized policy is beneficial relative to treating everybody—or nobody. But that is a different comparison from treating everyone versus treating no one, which is what the ATE describes. The observed treated-minus-untreated contrast is positive even though the ATE is negative.



Decomposing the observed mean difference with minimal causal assumptions
Assume consistency, finite potential-outcome means, and \(0<p=P(A=1)<1\). No exchangeability assumption is needed for the following decompositions.








Quantity
Representation
Interpretation




Baseline selection bias, \(B_0\)
\(E[Y(0)\mid A=1]-E[Y(0)\mid A=0]\)
Difference in untreated potential-outcome means


Treatment-effect selection bias, \(B_\tau\)
\(ATT-ATU\)
Difference in mean treatment effects



“Baseline” here means the outcome under no treatment, not necessarily an outcome measured before treatment.
The law of total expectation gives \[
ATE=p\,ATT+(1-p)\,ATU.
\] Rearranging, \[
ATT=ATE+(1-p)(ATT-ATU)=ATE+(1-p)B_\tau.
\tag{7}\]
Using consistency and adding a “fancy zero,” \[
\begin{aligned}
ATE_{\mathrm{obs}}
&=E[Y(1)\mid A=1]-E[Y(0)\mid A=0]\\
&=E[Y(1)\mid A=1]-E[Y(0)\mid A=1]\\
&\quad+E[Y(0)\mid A=1]-E[Y(0)\mid A=0]\\
&=\boxed{ATT+B_0}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{8}\]
This equation explains why an observed treated-versus-untreated difference need not represent a treatment effect. Substituting Equation 7 into Equation 8 gives an even more detailed decomposition, \[
\boxed{ATE_{\mathrm{obs}}=ATE+B_0+(1-p)B_\tau.}
\tag{9}\]
Equal untreated means and \(ATT=ATU\) are sufficient for equality of the observed contrast and ATE. They are not necessary: the two bias contributions can cancel.






Example: The Perfect(Confounded)-Doctor cont.



In the perfect doctor example above, \(p=3/8\), \(ATT=4/3\), and \(ATU=-4\). Therefore, \[\begin{aligned}
B_0&=\frac{13+8+8}{3} - \frac{6+4+5+6+6}{5}=\frac{29}{3}-\frac{27}{5}=\frac{64}{15}\\
B_\tau&=\frac43-(-4)=\frac{16}{3}\end{aligned}
\] Consequently, \[
ATE_{\mathrm{obs}}
=-2+\frac{64}{15}+\frac58\frac{16}{3}
=5.6.
\]








Remark: What Does a Test of the Observed Mean Difference Test?



The question is then: are you testing what you think you are? Statistical significance can give a veneer of mathematical legitimacy to a causal conclusion that the research design does not support. A paper need not mention causal inference in its methods to make causal claims in its conclusions: saying that an intervention improved outcomes is a causal claim, even if the analysis is described only as a comparison of groups. Neither a small p-value nor a large sample closes that identification gap.
A valid test of \[
H_0:ATE_{\mathrm{obs}}=0
\] tests equality of the observed treatment-group means. Without further assumptions, it does not test \(H_0:ATE=0\). The decomposition above shows why: this null concerns the sum of the causal effect and the two selection terms, rather than the causal effect alone.
When \(ATE_{\mathrm{obs}}\neq 0\), a consistent test will reject with probability approaching one as the sample size grows, under suitable sampling conditions. It is correctly detecting an associational difference; interpreting that rejection as evidence of a treatment effect without establishing identification is the error.




What does exchangeability actually give us?
Under consistency and unconditional exchangeability, \(\{Y(0),Y(1)\}\perp\!\!\!\perp A\), both \(B_0\) and \(B_\tau\) vanish, and \[
ATE_{\mathrm{obs}}=ATE=ATT=ATU.
\] Under conditional exchangeability given \(X\) and positivity, the corresponding within-\(X\) biases vanish. The marginal biases need not vanish because treated and untreated groups can have different distributions of \(X\). Example: Conditional Exchangeability Does Not Justify a Crude Comparison



Suppose \(X\in\{0,1\}\) distinguishes two groups with different baseline outcomes. Treatment adds \(2\) to everyone’s outcome: \[
Y(0)=10X,\qquad Y(1)=10X+2.
\]









Group
Outcome under control, \(Y(0)\)
Outcome under treatment, \(Y(1)\)
Treatment effect




\(X=0\)
0
2
2


\(X=1\)
10
12
2



Thus, \(ATE=ATT=ATU=2\). Within either group, everyone has the same potential outcomes, so treatment assignment cannot provide any additional information about them once we know \(X\). This is conditional exchangeability.
Now suppose half the population receives treatment, but the treatment groups have different compositions: \[
P(X=1\mid A=1)=0.8,\qquad
P(X=1\mid A=0)=0.2.
\] In words, 80% of treated individuals belong to the higher-baseline group, compared with only 20% of untreated individuals. Both values of \(X\) occur with positive probability in both treatment groups, so positivity holds.
Under consistency, we observe \(Y(1)\) for treated individuals and \(Y(0)\) for untreated individuals. Using the table, \[
\begin{aligned}
E[Y\mid A=1]
&=0.2(2)+0.8(12)=10,\\
E[Y\mid A=0]
&=0.8(0)+0.2(10)=2.
\end{aligned}
\] The crude difference is therefore \(8\), even though treatment adds only \(2\) for everyone. The remaining \(6\) comes from the different baseline compositions: \[
\underbrace{ATE_{\mathrm{obs}}}_{8}
=
\underbrace{ATT}_{2}
+
\underbrace{B_0}_{6}.
\]
To recover the treatment effect, compare treated and untreated outcomes within each value of \(X\), then average those comparisons over the target population. Since half the population receives treatment, \[
P(X=1)=0.5(0.8)+0.5(0.2)=0.5.
\] Standardization therefore gives \[
ATE
=
\underbrace{0.5}_{P(X=0)}\underbrace{(2-0)}_{\text{contrast within }X=0}
+
\underbrace{0.5}_{P(X=1)}\underbrace{(12-10)}_{\text{contrast within }X=1}
=2.
\]
Conditional exchangeability justifies the comparisons within \(X\). It does not make the crude treatment groups comparable when their distributions of \(X\) differ.

title: What is Causal Inference?
text:
Biostatistics: Randomized experiments
Random assignment supplies a known assignment mechanism. Under simple randomization with a common treatment probability, treatment is independent of pretreatment characteristics and potential outcomes. Blocked or unequal-probability designs require analysis that respects their assignment rules.

Fisher’s and Neyman’s modes of inference
The lecture distinguishes testing a sharp hypothesis from estimating an average effect. Both can use the randomization distribution; “exact versus asymptotic” is not the whole distinction.








Approach
Typical target or null
What randomization supplies




Fisher
\(H_0:Y_i(1)=Y_i(0)\) for every \(i\)
Under this sharp null, all missing outcomes are imputable, allowing a finite-sample randomization test


Neyman
\(\tau_N=N^{-1}\sum_i\{Y_i(1)-Y_i(0)\}\), or \(H_0:\tau_N=0\)
Unbiased estimation and randomization variance; commonly large-sample confidence intervals and tests



A zero average allows positive and negative individual effects to cancel. It does not make the null sharp. A Fisher test of no individual effects is therefore not automatically a test of zero average effect under heterogeneity.






Result: Complete Randomization and the Difference in Means



For \(N\) fixed units, completely randomize exactly \(n_1\) to treatment and \(n_0=N-n_1\) to control. Then \[
\widehat\tau=\bar Y_1-\bar Y_0,\qquad E_A[\widehat\tau]=\tau_N,
\] and \[
\operatorname{Var}_A(\widehat\tau)
=\frac{S_1^2}{n_1}+\frac{S_0^2}{n_0}-\frac{S_\tau^2}{N}.
\] Here \(S_a^2\) and \(S_\tau^2\) are finite-population variances with denominator \(N-1\). Because individual effects are unobserved, the usual variance estimator omits the last term: \[
\widehat V=\frac{s_1^2}{n_1}+\frac{s_0^2}{n_0}.
\] Its expectation is at least the true randomization variance. A normal-approximation interval requires additional large-sample conditions; conservative variance estimation alone is not an exact coverage theorem.


For a Fisher test, compute the statistic under each allowed assignment using the outcomes imputed under the sharp null. Compare the actual statistic to this distribution. Enumerating the assignments gives finite-sample type-I error control, potentially conservative because of discreteness. The permutations must follow the actual design.
Randomization supports inference for the trial participants. Generalizing to another population requires additional sampling or transportability arguments.


G estimation - revisting contingency table cell means and regression


RCT
Adjustment for prognostic pretreatment covariates can improve precision and power; it is not needed to repair confounding created by simple randomization. Chance covariate imbalance can still occur in a realized trial.
One approach fits arm-specific regressions and evaluates both at the overall covariate distribution. For fixed-dimensional linear adjustment, fit \[
Y_i=\alpha+\beta A_i+\gamma^T(X_i-\bar X)
+A_i\delta^T(X_i-\bar X)+\varepsilon_i.
\] The treatment coefficient is the adjusted contrast at \(\bar X\). Under standard complete-randomization regularity conditions, this fully interacted estimator is consistent and asymptotically no less precise than the unadjusted estimator, even if the linear outcome model is misspecified. Use design-appropriate, heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors. This is not a universal finite-sample improvement guarantee, especially with many covariates.

Target populations and overlap weighting
For a nonnegative function \(h\), define \[
\tau_h=\frac{E[h(X)\tau(X)]}{E[h(X)]},\qquad 0<E[h(X)]<\infty.
\] The normalized weighted contrast uses \(w_1(X)=h(X)/e(X)\) and \(w_0(X)=h(X)/(1-e(X))\).



Target
\(h(X)\)
Treated weight
Untreated weight




ATE
\(1\)
\(1/e(X)\)
\(1/\{1-e(X)\}\)


ATT
\(e(X)\)
\(1\)
\(e(X)/\{1-e(X)\}\)


ATU
\(1-e(X)\)
\(\{1-e(X)\}/e(X)\)
\(1\)


ATO
\(e(X)\{1-e(X)\}\)
\(1-e(X)\)
\(e(X)\)



Overlap weighting targets \[
ATO=\frac{E[e(X)\{1-e(X)\}\tau(X)]}{E[e(X)\{1-e(X)\}]}.
\] It emphasizes covariate profiles with plausible assignment to either arm. Its weights are bounded, but its estimand generally differs from ATE. With a finite, unpenalized logistic maximum-likelihood fit including an intercept, the score equations imply exact weighted mean balance for included covariate columns under overlap weights. This does not establish unmeasured balance.
Extreme inverse weights signal unstable comparisons. Trimming changes the represented population; truncating weights generally changes the estimating equation and can introduce bias. Report the target and examine balance and weight distributions. A useful weight diagnostic is \((\sum_i w_i)^2/\sum_i w_i^2\), computed within each arm.



Augmented weighting and doubly robust estimation
Outcome regression predicts missing outcomes; weighting corrects representation. Augmented inverse probability weighting combines predictions with weighted residuals.






Estimator: AIPW for the ATE



\[
\begin{aligned}
\widehat{ATE}_{\mathrm{AIPW}}
=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\Bigg[&\widehat m_1(X_i)-\widehat m_0(X_i)\\
&+\frac{A_i}{\widehat e(X_i)}\{Y_i-\widehat m_1(X_i)\}\\
&-\frac{1-A_i}{1-\widehat e(X_i)}\{Y_i-\widehat m_0(X_i)\}\Bigg].
\end{aligned}
\tag{10}\]


Under the causal assumptions and regularity conditions, consistency holds if either the propensity model is correct or both outcome mean models are correct. Double robustness concerns nuisance-model misspecification, not protection against unmeasured confounding or absent overlap.

Why double robustness works
For candidate functions \(q(X)\in(0,1)\) and \(r_a(X)\), consider the treated-mean contribution \[
U_1=r_1(X)+\frac{A}{q(X)}\{Y-r_1(X)\}.
\] Conditioning on \(X\) gives \[
E[U_1\mid X]
=r_1(X)+\frac{e(X)}{q(X)}\{m_1(X)-r_1(X)\}.
\] Subtracting the desired \(m_1(X)\), \[
E[U_1\mid X]-m_1(X)
=\frac{q(X)-e(X)}{q(X)}\{r_1(X)-m_1(X)\}.
\] This is zero if either factor is zero. Repeating the calculation for the untreated mean yields the ATE bias identity \[
E[U_1-U_0]-ATE
=E\left[(q-e)\left\{\frac{r_1-m_1}{q}+\frac{r_0-m_0}{1-q}\right\}\right].
\tag{11}\]
This identity is for fixed candidate functions; convergence of fitted models and control of empirical fluctuations are additional steps in proving estimator properties.


Inference with flexible nuisance estimates
Under both nuisance functions being consistently estimated, suitable overlap and moment assumptions, cross-fitting, and sufficiently small nuisance-error products, AIPW has influence function \[
\begin{aligned}
\phi(O)=&\ m_1(X)-m_0(X)-ATE\\
&+\frac{A}{e(X)}\{Y-m_1(X)\}
-\frac{1-A}{1-e(X)}\{Y-m_0(X)\}.
\end{aligned}
\] A typical sufficient rate requirement is \[
\|\widehat e-e\|_2
\left(\|\widehat m_1-m_1\|_2+\|\widehat m_0-m_0\|_2\right)
=o_p(n^{-1/2}).
\] Cross-fitting trains nuisance models outside each observation’s evaluation fold. Under these conditions, \[
\sqrt n(\widehat{ATE}-ATE)\rightsquigarrow N(0,E[\phi(O)^2]),
\] with standard error estimated by the sample standard deviation of estimated influence values divided by \(\sqrt n\). Consistency under only one correct nuisance model does not automatically justify this particular standard-error formula; nuisance-estimation contributions may then need separate treatment.

title: What is Causal Inference?
section: Computer Science: DAGs, Structural Causal Models, and Causal Discovery
text:
Computer Science: DAGs, Structural Causal Models, and Causal Discovery
A prominent tradition in computer science and artificial intelligence emphasizes structural causal models, directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), and algorithms for reasoning about interventions.
I find DAGs useful, and working through the conditional independences they imply is a very useful exercise. Personally, though, I find the potential-outcomes formulation a cleaner starting point for defining treatment effects. It makes the target comparison explicit before introducing the graphical machinery.
These approaches are compatible. A structural causal model generates potential outcomes by replacing a variable’s structural equation with a specified intervention. The graph represents assumptions about the causal structure; potential outcomes express what would happen under particular interventions.

What does a DAG give us?
Consider the causal structure \[
X\longrightarrow A,\qquad
X\longrightarrow Y,\qquad
A\longrightarrow Y.
\] Here, \(X\) is a common cause of treatment and outcome. Under the causal assumptions represented by this graph, adjusting for \(X\) blocks the backdoor path from \(A\) to \(Y\). With consistency and positivity, the resulting identification formula is the familiar standardization formula: \[
E[Y(a)]
=
\int E[Y\mid A=a,X=x]\,dP_X(x).
\]
The graph therefore helps justify the adjustment set. It does not verify that the assumed causal structure is correct, and it does not tell us to adjust for every available variable. In particular, conditioning on a collider can create an association, while conditioning on a mediator can change the effect being targeted.
Do-calculus provides rules for transforming expressions involving interventions into identifiable expressions involving observed distributions, when the graph permits it. This goes beyond ordinary covariate adjustment. The notation can take some getting used to, but the underlying question is familiar: can the causal quantity be expressed using the data distribution under these assumptions?
Despite the term “Bayesian network,” these graphical representations do not require Bayesian estimation or priors. A probabilistic graph describes a factorization; a causal interpretation adds assumptions about what happens under intervention.


Causal discovery is a different task
Using a proposed DAG to identify an effect is different from attempting to learn the graph itself. Causal discovery uses features of the data, together with assumptions, to infer aspects of causal structure.
For example, the two graphs \[
A\longrightarrow Y
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
A\longleftarrow Y
\] do not imply different conditional-independence restrictions when these are the only two variables. Observational association alone therefore cannot select the direction.
More generally, conditional-independence-based methods often identify a Markov equivalence class rather than a unique DAG. Distinguishing members may require interventions, temporal information, or additional functional assumptions. Common assumptions include the causal Markov condition and faithfulness; some methods also require no unmeasured common causes, while others allow latent confounding.
The word “discovery” should therefore be read carefully. The output remains conditional on the assumptions and on how well the data support the statistical decisions made by the algorithm.
There are much fuller introductions to DAGs than I will give here. Judea Pearl’s An Introduction to Causal Inference develops the structural-model perspective.

title: What is Causal Inference?
text:
Psychometrics: Measurement and Construct Validity
Psychometrics approaches a question that is easy to skip once we have a dataset: what are we actually measuring?
Our scientific hypotheses may concern latent attributes such as happiness, sadness, anxiety, or mathematical ability. But the data contain questionnaire responses, test scores, or observed behaviors. Connecting those measurements to the attribute we care about is part of the scientific problem, not merely a preliminary formatting decision.
There are several competing views of validity. Personally, I find the causal account developed by Borsboom and colleagues especially compelling: an attribute must exist, and variation in that attribute must causally produce variation in the measurement outcomes. This directs attention toward the process that generates the score, rather than treating a collection of correlations as sufficient validation.






Example: An Effect on a Score Versus an Effect on a Construct



Suppose a randomized intervention is intended to reduce anxiety, and the outcome is a questionnaire score \(S\). Randomization may identify \[
E[S(1)-S(0)].
\] But the scientific claim may concern a latent anxiety attribute \(L\): \[
E[L(1)-L(0)].
\] These are different estimands.
For illustration, suppose the measurement process is \[
S(a)=\alpha+\lambda L(a)+\gamma a+\varepsilon(a),
\qquad E[\varepsilon(a)]=0.
\] Then \[
E[S(1)-S(0)]
=
\lambda E[L(1)-L(0)]+\gamma.
\]
The term \(\gamma\) represents an effect of treatment on questionnaire scores that does not operate through anxiety—for example, changing how participants interpret the questions or how willing they are to report symptoms. Even a perfectly randomized trial cannot, by randomization alone, separate that reporting effect from an effect on anxiety.
Under this illustrative model, recovering the latent mean effect would require additional measurement assumptions, such as \(\gamma=0\) and a known nonzero scale factor \(\lambda\). The latent scale itself also needs a definition.
Factor analysis and item response theory provide tools for relating latent attributes to observed responses. Measurement-invariance analyses examine whether aspects of that relationship remain comparable across groups or occasions. However, good model fit, high reliability, or strong prediction does not by itself establish the intended causal measurement interpretation.
This is why I think measurement deserves much more attention in discussions of causal inference. We can identify an effect on the recorded outcome and still overstate what that effect tells us about the scientific construct.


For the causal perspective on validity, see Borsboom, Mellenbergh, and van Heerden’s The Concept of Validity.

A genome-wide association study (GWAS) examines whether single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), locations in DNA where individuals can differ by a single nucleotide (e.g., A versus G), are associated with a particular trait or disease. There are generally thousands or even millions of these SNPs to investigate in a genome for each individual.
Humans generally have 23 pairs of chromosomes, including 22 pairs of autosomes and one pair of sex chromosomes. For each autosomal pair, an individual inherits one chromosome from their mother and one from their father. These two chromosomes contain corresponding DNA sequences at the same locations, but the sequences are not necessarily identical. In particular, an individual may inherit different nucleotides from each parent at the same location in the genome.
A single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) is a location in DNA where the nucleotide varies across individuals in a population (e.g., A versus G). Because an individual has two copies of each autosomal chromosome, they carry two alleles at each SNP location, one inherited from each parent.






Figure 2: A single SNP



A genome-wide association study (GWAS) examines whether these genetic differences are statistically associated with particular traits or diseases. This is done by measuring the genotypes of many individuals at a large number of SNP locations across the genome and testing whether differences in genotype at each SNP are associated with differences in the outcome of interest.






Figure 3: Many inidivudals SNP, GWAS is just this along with demographic info and outcome data on a bunchn of individuals/SNP

Suppose we want to investigate whether a SNP is associated with diabetes. We record each individual’s genotype (AA, AG, or GG) and whether they have diabetes. We can then fit a logistic regression model,
\[
\operatorname{logit}\{P(Y_i=1\mid G_{ij},X_i)\}
=
\alpha_j+\beta_jG_{ij}+\gamma_j^\top X_i,
\]
where \(Y_i\) indicates diabetes status, \(G_{ij}\in\{0,1,2\}\) is the number of G alleles individual \(i\) carries at SNP \(j\), and \(X_i\) contains relevant covariates such as age, sex, and genetic ancestry. Testing \(H_0:\beta_j=0\) determines whether the SNP is statistically associated with diabetes under this additive model.
This process is repeated separately for each SNP across the genome, allowing researchers to identify genetic locations associated with the outcome. Because so many hypothesis tests are performed, multiple-testing corrections are necessary. Importantly, finding an association does not establish that the SNP itself causally affects the disease.

title: Intro
section: 1a) O’Brien (Rank Sum of endpoint-wise ranks across all endpoints individually)
text:
1a) O’Brien (Rank Sum of endpoint-wise ranks across all endpoints individually)
O’Brien creates a patient-level score by ranking each endpoint separately and then summing those ranks, treating all endpoints as the same “priority level” (unless you add weights).
Let \(Y_{ijk}\) be endpoint \(k\) for subject \(j\) in group \(i\), and let \(R_{ijk}\) be the pooled rank of \(Y_{ijk}\) among all subjects for endpoint \(k\) (ties get midranks). Define \[S_{ij}=\sum_{k=1}^K R_{ijk}\] Then compare the observed \({S_{ij}}\) between treatment arms using Wilcoxon rank-sum / Mann–Whitney \(U\). The interpretation is: treatment is tested for a shift in a latent additive rank-utility (the sum of endpoint-wise ranks). There is no explicit hierarchical priority, each endpoint contributes additively.






Example (demonstrative example)



Here if we have endpoint-wise ties we assign average ranks, then in the baove data we can rank individuals within each endpoint, with the convention that (1 = worst, 7 = best),

title: Intro
section: 1b) Sun (Average Z-score across all endpoints individually)
text:
1b) Sun (Average Z-score across all endpoints individually)
Sun et al. create a patient-level score by putting endpoints onto a common standardized scale and averaging, again treating endpoints as the same “priority level” (unless you add weights).

First align direction so that “larger is better” for every endpoint; for time-to-event endpoints, one typically replaces \((t,\delta)\) by a logrank/Gehan-type score so censoring is handled appropriately.
Standardize each endpoint \(k\) across all subjects: \[Z_{ik}=\frac{X_{ik}-\bar X_k}{s_k}\]
Form the average Z-score: \[A_i=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^K Z_{ik}\]
Compare \({A_i}\) across arms via Wilcoxon rank-sum / Mann–Whitney \(U\)

Interpretation: treatment is tested for a shift in a latent additive standardized utility (the average of standardized component scores). Again, like O’Brien, this does not encode a hierarchy unless you explicitly weight endpoints.






Example (demonstrative example)



First we align all directions,

For endpoints where “bigger is better”: use the value as-is (Death, Stroke, Amp, MI, Hosp, QoL).
For Rescue rate where “smaller is better”: use (\(X_{\text{Rescue}^\star}=-\text{Rescue}\)) so larger is better.

For the censored ((365)), we have the option to treat it as 365 but Sun et al. discuss logrank-type scoring for censoring which we opt to perform. That is we’ll implement the “logrank-type scoring” explicitly for the 5 time-to-event endpoints (Death/Stroke/Amp/MI/Hosp), then do regular Z-standardize on the \(2\) others For each time endpoint (\(k\)), each subject has (\((t_{ik},\delta_{ik})\)) where (\(\delta=1\)) if the event is observed and (\(\delta=0\)) if censored at 365.
Use the pooled Nelson–Aalen cumulative hazard for endpoint (k): \[\widehat\Lambda_k(t)=\sum_{t_{(j)}\le t}\frac{d_j}{Y_j}\] where (\(t_{(j)}\)) are distinct event times, (\(d_j\)) is the number of events at (\(t_{(j)}\)) (here always 1), and (\(Y_j\)) is the pooled risk set size just before (\(t_{(j)}\)).
A simple per-subject logrank-type score (a monotone transform of the Cox/no-covariate score residual) is \[L_{ik}=\widehat\Lambda_k(t_{ik})-\delta_{ik}\] This has the right direction: larger (\(L_{ik}\)) = better (late censoring gives large (\(\widehat\Lambda\)) with (\(\delta=0\)); early events give small (\(\widehat\Lambda\)) but (\(\delta=1\)), so negative).

title: Intro
text:
2a) Felker (Hierarchical Composite)
Felker defines a single ordinal rank per patient using the pre-specified hierarchy and within ordering then compares arms using a rank test.

Construct a ranking map \(R_i=g(Y_i)\), where \(Y_i\) is the patient’s outcome vector.
Compare \(\{R_i\}\) across arms using Wilcoxon rank-sum / Mann–Whitney (equivalent).

Key feature: the hierarchy is built into \(g(\cdot)\). Lower-priority endpoints are used only to break ties among higher-priority outcomes.






Example (demonstrative example)



Using our data above we perform the global rank test indicated above with g defined as \[g(Y_i) = R_i^{\text{global}} = 1 + \# \{j: Y_j \prec Y_i\}\] where \(\succ\) and \(\prec\) are a lexicographic ordering where two patients \(i\) and \(j\) we have \(i \succ j\) iff at the first component they different in the hierachy (in order) \(i\) is better.

Here according to our ordering the global best to worst ordering is \[T3 \succ C3 \succ C1 \succ T2 \succ C2 \succ T1 \succ C4\]
This global ordering is determined by going event-by-event and comparing remaining contenders. Numerically, if we assign higher ranks to better outcomes (according to the lexicographic ordering), we obtain

Treatment: \(R_T={2,4,7}\)
Control: \(R_C={1,3,5,6}\)

The Wilcoxon rank sums are \[
W_T = 2+4+7 = 13,\qquad W_C = 1+3+5+6 = 15.
\]
With \(n_T=3\) and \(n_C=4\), the corresponding Mann–Whitney \(U\) statistics (using the shift relationship) are \[
U_T = W_T - \frac{n_T(n_T+1)}{2}
= 13 - \frac{3\cdot 4}{2} = 13-6 = 7,
\] \[
U_C = W_C - \frac{n_C(n_C+1)}{2}
= 15 - \frac{4\cdot 5}{2} = 15-10 = 5.
\]
Among the \(n_Tn_C=3\cdot 4=12\) cross-arm comparisons induced by this global ordering, treatment has \(U_T=7\) “wins” and control has \(U_C=5\) “wins.” The induced probability-of-treatment-superiority parameter is estimated by \[
\hat\theta_T = \frac{U_T}{n_T n_C}
= \frac{7}{12}
\approx 0.5833,
\] and equivalently \[
\hat\theta_C = \frac{U_C}{n_T n_C}
= \frac{5}{12}
\approx 0.4167.
\]
To determine the exact one-sided p-value (in the direction “treatment tends to have larger ranks”), note that treatment could be any \(3\) of the \(7\) ranks with assumed equal probability under the null of exchangeability \(F_T=F_C\), so there are \(\binom{7}{3}=35\) equally likely allocations. The observed \(U_T=7\) is equivalent to \(W_T=13\), and the subsets of \(3\) ranks with sum at least as large (\(\ge 13\)) are exactly the \(15\) subsets: \[
\{1,5,7\},\{1,6,7\},\{2,4,7\},\{2,5,6\},\{2,5,7\},
\] \[
\{2,6,7\},\{3,4,6\},\{3,4,7},\{3,5,6\},\{3,5,7\},
\] \[
\{3,6,7\},\{4,5,6\},\{4,5,7\},\{4,6,7\},\{5,6,7\}
\] Therefore the exact one-sided p-value is \[
p_T=\Pr(U_T\ge 7)=\Pr(W_T\ge 13)=\frac{15}{35}\approx 0.4286.
\] This is equivalent to focusing on controls: \[
p_C=\Pr(U_C\le 5)=\Pr(12-U_T\le 5)=\Pr(U_T\ge 7)=\frac{15}{35}\approx 0.4286.
\]
For larger samples we typically do not enumerate all \(\binom{n_T+n_C}{n_T}\) allocations. Instead we use the normal approximation for the Mann–Whitney \(U\)-statistic. Under \(H_0\) (exchangeability), the null mean and variance are \[
\mathbb E_0[U_T]=\frac{n_T n_C}{2},\qquad
\operatorname{Var}_0(U_T)=\frac{n_T n_C (n_T+n_C+1)}{12}.
\] Equivalently, for the rank-sum \(W_T\), \[
\mathbb E_0[W_T]=\frac{n_T(n_T+n_C+1)}{2},\qquad
\operatorname{Var}_0(W_T)=\frac{n_T n_C (n_T+n_C+1)}{12}.
\] So a large-sample \(z\)-statistic for “treatment better” is \[
Z=\frac{U_T-\frac{n_T n_C}{2}}
{\sqrt{\frac{n_T n_C (n_T+n_C+1)}{12}}}
\overset{H_0}{\sim}N(0,1).
\]
In this toy example, \(n_T=3\), \(n_C=4\), \(U_T=7\), so the normal approximation yields \[
Z=\frac{7-6}{\sqrt{3\cdot4\cdot (3+4+1)/12}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{8}}\approx 0.3536,
\] and a one-sided p-value of \[
p_{\text{asym}}(T)=\Pr(Z\ge 0.3536)=1-\Phi(0.3536)\approx 0.362.
\] This differs from the exact value \(15/35\approx 0.4286\) because the normal approximation is poor at such small \(n\), which is why the exact enumeration is preferable here.

title: Intro
text:
2b) Modified Kernel + U-statistic “Win” methods
Just as Felker U statistics built from a pairwise kernel taking in both treatment and control patients and comparing them while considering the hierarchy specifically
Using this pairwise kernel across every treated–control pair \((i,j)\) in the specified priority order decides win (\(+1\)), loss (\(−1\)), or tie/indeterminate (\(0\)) then aggregating over pairs gives us the standard win statistic building blocks. These aggregated kernel comparisons are naturally order-2 U-statistics






Example (win kernels and U-statistics)



Fix a prioritized pairwise comparison kernel on full patient outcome records (possibly multivariate, with hierarchy/censoring rules built in). In a two-arm trial this is naturally written as a two-sample order-2 kernel \(\phi:\mathcal Z_T\times\mathcal Z_C\to\{-1,0,+1\}\) (win/tie/loss), or \({0,1}\) if you only code “treated wins.”
For treated patient \(i\) and control patient \(j\), define the pairwise score \[
s_{ij}=\phi(Z_i,W_j)\in{-1,0,+1},
\] where \(+1\) means “treated wins,” \(-1\) means “treated loses,” and \(0\) means tie/indeterminate. The win statistic is the average of this kernel over all treated–control pairs, \[
U=\frac{1}{n_T n_C}\sum_{i=1}^{n_T}\sum_{j=1}^{n_C}\phi(Z_i,W_j),
\] which is exactly a two-sample order-2 U-statistic. (Many practical variants—stratified/matched designs, inverse-probability weighting, nuisance-adjusted estimators—keep the same underlying order-2 kernel but modify how pairs are aggregated.)


A standard hierarchical kernel is lexicographic for example,

Compare Death (larger time is better); if resolved, stop.
Else compare Stroke; if resolved, stop.
Else Amp; then MI; then Hosp.
Else Rescue (smaller is better).
Else QoL (\(\Delta\)) (larger is better).

Its useful to note that in general censoring can occur when the ordering cannot be determined for an endpoint and you move on.

2b1) Finkelstein–Schoenfeld (FS) net benefit / win difference
FS aggregates the pairwise scores: \[U = \frac{1}{n_T n_C}\sum_{i=1}^{n_T}\sum_{j=1}^{n_C} s_{ij}\] Here \(U\) targets \[E[U]=P(\text{win})-P(\text{loss})\] often called net benefit / win difference / net treatment benefit






Example (demonstrative example)



Compute \(s_{ij}\) for all \(n_T n_C = 3\cdot 4=12\) treated–control pairs. The table also records which endpoint first resolved the comparison. Define the estimator \[\hat\Delta
=\frac{1}{n_T n_C}\sum_{i=1}^{n_T}\sum_{j=1}^{n_C} s_{ij}
=\widehat{P(\text{win})}-\widehat{P(\text{loss})}\] (where ties/indeterminates contribute 0 to the difference).
This is a two-sample U-statistic. A standard asymptotic variance estimator uses the Hoeffding projection:
Compute row/column averages \[\bar s_{i\cdot}=\frac{1}{n_C}\sum_{j=1}^{n_C} s_{ij},\qquad
\bar s_{\cdot j}=\frac{1}{n_T}\sum_{i=1}^{n_T} s_{ij}\]
Then an asymptotic estimator of \(\mathrm{Var}(\hat\Delta)\) is \[\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat\Delta)
=\frac{1}{n_T(n_T-1)}\sum_{i=1}^{n_T}\left(\bar s_{i\cdot}-\hat\Delta\right)^2
+
\frac{1}{n_C(n_C-1)}\sum_{j=1}^{n_C}\left(\bar s_{\cdot j}-\hat\Delta\right)^2\]
So \[SE(\hat\Delta)=\sqrt{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat\Delta)},
\qquad
Z=\frac{\hat\Delta}{SE(\hat\Delta)}\approx N(0,1)\ \text{under }H_0\] and a Wald CI is \[\hat\Delta \pm z_{1-\alpha/2}, SE(\hat\Delta)\] Though in cases with a small amount of patients we can find the direct CI and P-values as we do below using permutations.

The FS net benefit estimate is \[\hat U

\widehat{P(\text{loss})}=\frac{5}{12}\approx 0.4167\]
Exact one-sided p-value (randomization / permutation). Under \(H_0\), the treatment labels are exchangeable among the 7 patients, so there are \(\binom{7}{3}=35\) equally likely labelings. Recomputing \(\#W\) (or \(\sum s_{ij}\)) under each labeling, only 15 of 35 labelings give \(\#W \ge 7\) (equivalently \(\sum s_{ij}\ge 2\)). Therefore, \[p = P(\#W \ge 7) = P!\left(\sum_{i,j}s_{ij}\ge 2\right)
= \frac{15}{35}\approx 0.4286\]
(Here, because there are no ties/indeterminates, \(\#W\) is exactly the Mann–Whitney \(U_T\)) on the induced ordering, so the same exact p-value appears.)
We also have the asymptotic and as wald CI as ????





2b2) Pocock win ratio
The win ratio emphasizes the ratio of win to loss probabilities: \[WR
=\frac{P(\text{win})}{P(\text{loss})}
\approx \frac{\#W}{\#L}\] typically with the same hierarchical comparison kernel. It is a function of two U statistics with kernels ????






Example (demonstrative example)



From the pairwise table above, \(\#W=7\) and \(\#L=5\), so \[\widehat{WR}=\frac{7}{5}=1.4\]
Interpretation: in this sample, treated patients win about 1.4 times as often as they lose when compared pairwise against controls under the prioritized endpoint hierarchy.
Let \[\hat p_W=\frac{\#W}{n_T n_C},\qquad
\hat p_L=\frac{\#L}{n_T n_C},
\qquad
\widehat{WR}=\frac{\hat p_W}{\hat p_L}=\frac{\#W}{\#L},\] ignoring ties in numerator/denominator (ties just reduce \(\#W+\#L\) below \(n_Tn_C\)).
Large-sample inference is typically done on \(\log(WR)\). One common approach (used in generalized pairwise comparison software) again treats this as a U-statistic functional and uses influence-function / projection variance. A simple, serviceable approximation that is often used when ties are not dominant is a delta-method style: \[\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\log \widehat{WR})
\approx
\frac{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat p_W)}{\hat p_W^2}
+
\frac{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat p_L)}{\hat p_L^2}
-2\frac{\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}(\hat p_W,\hat p_L)}{\hat p_W\hat p_L}\] where \(\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat p_W)\), \(\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat p_L)\), and the covariance are computed via the same projection idea (replace \(s_{ij}\) with indicators (\(I{s_{ij}=+1}\) and \(I{s_{ij}=-1})\).
Concretely define \[w_{ij}=I(s_{ij}=+1),\qquad \ell_{ij}=I(s_{ij}=-1)\] Then \(\hat p_W=\frac{1}{n_Tn_C}\sum w_{ij}\) and \(\hat p_L=\frac{1}{n_Tn_C}\sum \ell_{ij}\) are again two-sample U-statistics, and you can estimate \(\mathrm{Var}(\hat p_W)\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(\hat p_L)\) using the same row/column projection formula as above (with \(w_{ij}\) or \(\ell_{ij}\) in place of \(s_{ij}\)), and similarly estimate \(\mathrm{Cov}(\hat p_W,\hat p_L)\) via cross-products of the corresponding row/column means.
Then \[SE(\log \widehat{WR})=\sqrt{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\log \widehat{WR})},\] a Wald CI on the log scale is \[\log \widehat{WR}\pm z_{1-\alpha/2}SE(\log \widehat{WR}),\] and exponentiating gives a CI for (WR).
Practical note: in real analyses, most people either (a) use the established generalized pairwise comparison variance estimator (projection-based) implemented in software, or (b) use a permutation/randomization test if the design supports it, or (c) use a bootstrap (cluster bootstrap if clustered).

title: Intro
section: 2c) DOOR (Desirability of Outcome Ranking) and related “benefit–risk ranking” frameworks
text:
2c) DOOR (Desirability of Outcome Ranking) and related “benefit–risk ranking” frameworks

Core idea
Construct an ordinal desirability ranking that jointly encodes benefit and harm categories, then compare arms via a probability-of-better-outcome estimand (again essentially a Mann–Whitney-type object).
DOOR is widely used in infectious diseases and emphasizes explicit benefit–risk tradeoffs in the ranking categories. (OUP Academic)


Where your tied-tier rules fit
DOOR is basically a global rank framework with carefully designed categories. If you allow co-ranked regions, your rules determine:

how categories are formed (or how ties within a category are broken),
whether you treat multi-attribute categories as Pareto/majority/score-based.

So your framework generalizes DOOR too, but most DOOR applications bake the rule into the category definitions.



Win graph with co-ranked regions and majority rule
